content:
20 things I wish I knew in my early 20s:

1. Confidence is a skill. Train it like any other, and it maxes out over time.

2. Authenticity is the highest form of vibration. Partners, colleagues, investors, customers, friends - all drawn to the most authentic version of anything.

3. Everything compounds. Where you put your energy in your 20s pays off for years. Choose carefully.

4. Become financially literate.

5. Fix your health habits now. You don't want to be building them later.

6. Be proud of failure. It means you tried, and that's a muscle too.

7. Speak unprocessed thoughts out loud. Left alone, they turn into bad bacteria in the brain, same as food left to rot in your stomach.

8. Stop people-pleasing. Your life gets infinitely better.

9. Get into leadership and into real relationship. That's where transformation happens. Not from following, not from standing outside.

10. As above, so below. Fix what's going on in your mind and body, and the outside world follows.

11. Hire people better than you in everything you do. If you don't you become the ceiling, quickly.

12. Talk to 100 real customers before you build anything. Deeply listen, don't suggest. Save yourself a lot of wasted time.

13. Cash in the bank buys time to build value.

14. The team you build is the company you build.

15. Say no to almost everything, so you can say yes properly to what matters.

16. A broken team can never build a functioning business.

17. Your first version will embarrass you later. Ship it anyway.

18. Ask for help before you're drowning. Not after.

19. Investors back conviction, not certainty.

20. The hard part of scaling is holding day-1 standards on day 1,000.

35 feels like the first year I actually know what I'm doing. Ask me again at 45.

content:
Apparently, humour is allowed in B2B now.

Some of us have been 'risking' our professional reputations with memes for a while 😂

Marketing Week has a piece on how B2B brands are using humour to cut through. It’s very much what I’ve been saying, and experimenting with here lately.

People come to LinkedIn for work. They still appreciate a laugh, especially when it’s about something they’ve experienced themselves.

A good meme about an unnecessary meeting can say more about your understanding of working life than 800 words on organisational efficiency. And there’s a good chance someone will send it to a colleague with “this is us”.

But good humour is hard. You need to understand your audience, notice something familiar and get the timing right. Anyone who’s sat through a corporate video trying to be funny knows how badly it can go.

It’s also why I think good humour will be one of the last things we fully outsource to AI. AI can generate a joke. Knowing which joke to tell, to whom, and whether you should tell it at all takes judgment.

And yes, humour has ROI on LinkedIn.

It gives people a reason to connect or a way to start a conversation. Someone who’s never commented on your serious posts might finally reply because you’ve captured their Tuesday perfectly.

That can open a door you’ve been trying to open for months.

I spend plenty of time talking about expertise and trust here. Having a personality helps too. I want people to know their stuff, but I’d also quite like to enjoy talking to them.

You can take your work seriously and still be funny.

The Marketing Week piece, for anyone who needs approval before posting their next meme.

content:
Seven global businesses. One Strategy: Invest in brand to grow.

Unilever's Fernando Fernandez says the days of underinvesting in brands to squeeze out more profit are over.

Procter & Gamble’s CFO Andre Schulten puts long-term brand strength at the center of its growth strategy.

Nike's Elliott Hill is redirecting investment towards brand storytelling and consumer connection.

adidas's Bjorn Gulden says top-of-funnel activity has improved performance further down the funnel.

At AB InBev, Michel Doukeris calls creativity a competitive advantage that helps grow the beer category. LVMH's legendary Bernard Arnault thanks brand desirability and creative passion for growth.

Tapestry's Joanne Crevoiserat directly connects Coach’s disciplined brand building and creativity to compounding growth.

Different businesses and categories, some protecting strong positions while others rebuild them. But the people in charge keep coming back to brand.

The compounding effects of proper positioning achieved by creativity and broad-reach emotional storytelling is only becoming more important as AI lowers the barriers to entry and levels the technical playing field.

Specifically the role of advertising in changing behaviour to create future demand. In my research with System1 and Effie Worldwide (The Creative Dividend) we found that long-running distinctive ad campaigns that are emotional are 7.5x more likely to lead to profitable business growth.

We must plan in years, not quarters.

Thanks to Aline Meloni for sharing similar on innovation. I agree, businesses that focus on consumer value creation and long-term brand strategy will win.

author.name: Jon Evans
author.headline: Interviewing the World’s best CMO’s & Business Owners on the Uncensored CMO podcast, inspiring marketers at events like The Calling and hopefully speaking at your next event

content:
Guinness is a world-class example of consistency AND coherence

Last week at the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) Effectiveness Conference, Orlando Wood shared his POV on brand coherence with System1 and The Whole-Brained Marketer. It’s an important addition to the consistency conversation, and Guinness is a brilliant way to explain why.

Conveniently, I own the T-shirt. One of my favourites!

Guinness has used the harp since 1862. Look at how much it has changed without becoming something else entirely. Consistency leaves plenty of room for creativity when you understand what’s worth keeping.

What I particularly love is that, after years of simplification, the 2016 redesign brought back detail and craftsmanship. Design Bridge and Partners worked with Gerry Barney, who drew the 1968 version, along with harp-makers and a letterpress studio. A more thoughtful brief than “make it work as an app icon.”

That's where consistency meets coherence. The craftsmanship in the identity belongs with the care in the pour, the anticipation of the first sip, and the beer's character. The design reinforces the experience. It gives the familiar symbol more meaning.

Orlando shared Paul Simonet's framework, which looks at a brand’s heart, face, voice, and actions. What it stands for, how it looks, how it communicates and what it does should add up to a recognisable character. That goes well beyond advertising; it's part of the brand strategy process.

You can put the same logo on five unrelated ideas and still have five unrelated ideas.

This new initial, exploratory study of 21 IPA award-winning brands found that brands whose coherence improved (consistently delivered across Paul's framework over time) were more likely to report effects: a small study, but an interesting direction for the industry to pay attention to.

This builds on the case for consistency. My 'Compound Creativity' work over the past 4 years with the IPA, System1 and Effie Worldwide found that the most consistent UK and US brands reported an average ROI of 8.8, versus 2.1 for the least consistent. There is considerable commercial value associated with building on what you’ve already established.

There's now significant empirical evidence for what marketers have always known is best practice.

COHERENT BRANDS: Be clear on who your brand is, what it stands for, and what it looks like. Make sure the brand lives up to this across its products, partnerships, communications and customer experience.

CONSISTENT CAMPAIGNS: Give good campaign ideas time to develop. Keep building the assets, characters and associations people recognise. 

We need both. The person buying a pint doesn’t care whether something came from the brand team, the social agency or the partnerships team. It’s all Guinness to them.

Links to both pieces of research in the comments.

content:
Suri might be one of the most thoughtful brands I've ever encountered.....


I was fortunate enough to host last week's Up World talk with Ana Caeiro from Suri Dental and came away dripping in insight that I need to share. 

Here are the top 7 killer takeaways:

1. 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞’𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭’𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐬𝐤.

Suri looked beyond brushing to the other things that matter to the customer when it comes to their toothbrush - the everyday bathroom experience (the mirror magnet keeps the brush clean & the sink area tidy), what to do when they travel (their smart cases are designed to be as compact as possible so you don't have to compromise when you're away), and the day to day essentials (like great battery life that's easier with all the pointless extra features that don't add value stripped out). 

2. 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐥 𝐢𝐬 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐬 𝐩𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐮𝐥 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐟𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐬.

Ana told me that the dominant toothbrush brand in the category has 90% prompted awareness but when asked, most people couldn't remember the brand of their toothbrush. Suri saw an opportunity to build affinity, not just awareness. 

3. 𝐁𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐭𝐨𝐨 𝐭𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐯𝐨𝐢𝐝 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐜.

Early product gifting brought out personal stories Suri could never have scripted. One creator’s five-brush setup became a best-performing ad format. Always make sure you give creators room to show you what resonates. 

4. 𝐈𝐟 𝐲𝐨𝐮'𝐫𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐠𝐨 𝐛𝐢𝐠, 𝐠𝐨 𝐛𝐢𝐠 𝐛𝐢𝐠.

When your brand is ready to go above the line, don't just dip your toe, and don't spread yourself too thin. A tiny above-the-line test may seem like a good idea but realistically it will tell you very little and waste a lot of your budget. ATL channels need proper investment, consistency & reptition (see challenger examples of this in action from Lucky Saint or Pip & Nut).

5. 𝐓𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞.
Ana told us that Suri onboards its customer-service team on the brand and its values, while using customer-voice reports to understand what people like and what isn’t working. 

Loved the chat, and so much I'm taking into my next projects.

Thanks so much to Ana for joining us.

content:
Sooo... a little announcement from today.

It's been one year at Shake. And what a year it’s been  🙌 

A year ago, I left LinkedIn to join a small agency with big ambitions. Since then, we have grown, launched things, worked with brilliant people and had a lot of fun along the way.

The question I’ve been asked most is: “What’s it like going from a huge company to a small one?”

So I wanted to share a few reflections for anyone considering a similar move.

First, this comes from someone who loves LinkedIn. I’m a proud former employee and ambassador, and I’ve always said it’s an AMAZING company to work for. I miss many things about my time there, especially the people.

These are personal observations about my own experience, rather than a verdict on where anyone else should work.

1) Autonomy suits me
I like having room to make decisions, try things and take responsibility for what happens next. I’m usually happier testing an idea than spending weeks discussing whether we should test it.

Big companies have more people and priorities to account for. I understand why. But I’ve realised how much I enjoy working somewhere that moves at my pace.

2) I spend less time proving I’m doing the work
In a large organisation, doing good work and making sure the right people know about it can become two separate jobs.

3) I have become more comfortable being myself here
My LinkedIn content has become funnier, occasionally more unhinged, and a lot more enjoyable to create. I have tried new angles, made more jokes and explored commercial opportunities I probably wouldn’t have pursued before.

4) Ideas have somewhere to go
An idea can become something people actually use within days. We’ve launched parody tools, our Best Time to Post tool and the What Just Happened Podcast. Some ideas start as a business opportunity. Others start with “this would be funny”.

I really like having the ownership to follow that curiosity and help build the thing.

5) The impact feels closer
You see a conversation turn into a client. You see someone use a tool you helped launch. You see how your work contributes to the business growing. I cared deeply about my work at LinkedIn too. At a smaller company, the connection is just easier to see and feel.

6) You have to enjoy things changing
More meetings out of the office, different challenges each week, priorities moving as opportunities come in. That can be messy. It also suits me. I’ve learned that variety gives me energy, even when it makes the calendar slightly ridiculous.

If you are considering a similar move, think about the conditions in which you do your best work. How much structure do you want? How comfortable are you with uncertainty? What gives you energy?

This year has helped me answer those questions for myself.

A huge thank you to the whole Shake Content team, especially James Farnfield and Harry Williams, for the trust, support, guidance and room to run with things.

It’s been a brilliant year. Here’s to many more ✌️

content:
A while back I gave a talk in London, and at the end I opened the floor to questions.

A man with a friendly face and wise eyes put his hand up and asked, "When you started presenting Formula 1, who was kind to you?"

Nobody had asked me that in all the years since I started the job. What a lovely way to ask about such a big moment in my life.

I hate the phrase "self-made man". I've never met one. When I got the BBC F1 job I was far from alone. Niall, my boss, put his arm around me. Mark the producer gave me years of wisdom. David and Eddie, my pundits, gave me the confidence to stand shoulder to shoulder with them on TV.

And still it was lonely. The contract was 12 months. I knew I was a risk for the BBC, and that one misstep could cost me the job and maybe my whole career. I was young for it, and the next hour felt like it would decide everything.

The loneliest moment came about 10 minutes before we went live in Australia. I walked away from David and Eddie and stood on my own in a pretty empty pit lane. Ear defenders on, six or seven voices in my head, the PA counting down, no autocue, and one voice telling me I was about to mess it up.

With about five minutes to go I couldn't take any more. I took my earpiece out and made a call. When it was answered, all I said was, "I'm scared Dad."

My parents were up early at their cottage in the Norfolk countryside, ready to watch their son host live TV on BBC One. Only a few years before, their boy had been struggling with life and not much was expected of him. I still get emotional thinking about what they said next.

"We're having tea and toast, it's still dark, and the dog is curled up on the floor. Life here is exactly the same as it always has been, and you can always come home. No matter what happens today we love you, always will, and our door will never close. So go and enjoy yourself, knowing that."

My life had changed, but life itself hadn't. Knowing I could just go home, no judgement, no failure, lifted the weight completely.

I put the earpiece back in, listened to the minutes tick down, and went live to millions.

Who was kind to you when it really mattered? It might be worth telling them ❤️

content:
💾Gabriel Davis at Anthropic published data analysing 2.5M+ Instagram posts, and the numbers are pretty crazy.

Between Jan 2025 and May 2026:
1) Likes dropped 73% for carousels and 81% for reels
2) Comments fell 39% to 46% across the board
3) Even top 1% accounts saw 50-65% drops in engagement

My take: Instagram is increasingly built for passive consumption and private sharing. 

LinkedInis moving in the exact opposite direction. It is s becoming more conversational.

Active discourse and comment sections have become the real engine for reach, authority, and pipeline.

Yes, AI has also created an supply of generic posts and painfully predictable comments. But the growing importance of the comment section is still an encouraging signal.

LinkedIn isn’t rewarding people for simply consuming content. It’s creating more value around people contributing to it. 

The future of LinkedIn may belong less to the people with the biggest audiences, and more to those who start the best conversations.

content:
One of the most underrated things in content is being recognisable.

I have spent years working with founders, executives and brands on LinkedIn, and it's something I come back to constantly.

Think about the people and companies you instantly recognise in your feed. Sometimes you don't even need to see their name to know who's behind the content.

Their personality, their style, the way they communicate. All of that builds familiarity over time. And familiarity is a big part of how trust is built.

Which is why I find Synthesia's latest launch quite cool.

They've just introduced Syren, which lets you generate videos from a prompt using your existing brand identity.

You upload existing videos as Brand Context, and Syren learns things like motion, pacing, tone of voice, colours and fonts.

Then you give it a prompt, and it creates a new video using that context.

Pretty impressive when you see it in action.

We've spent years talking about the importance of building a recognisable brand. But maintaining that identity across different channels, formats and types of content takes a lot of work.

Technology that helps teams carry that identity into more of what they produce is genuinely interesting.

Especially as video becomes an increasingly important part of how brands communicate.

Of course, the ideas, creative direction and understanding of your audience still matter enormously. Those are the foundations of good content, regardless of how it's produced.
But I love seeing how tools like this are expanding what's possible for creative and marketing teams.

Selfies on LinkedIn can lead to more opportunities. I know. I’m still a bit conflicted.

Business Insider just covered creators using selfies and unscripted videos to build an audience, get speaking invitations and even land jobs.

Having spent 4+ years at LinkedIn working closely with creators, I have seen how much it helps when people get to know the person behind the posts. A face adds familiarity. A personal story gives people something to connect with beyond a job title.

And with so much AI content around, I understand the appetite for something that feels more human.

But I’m less enthusiastic about the takeaway becoming: “Attach a selfie. Get more reach.”

A random selfie attached to an unrelated business lesson because someone told you it performs better? That’s where you lose me.

I have always liked the idea of “personality yes, personal optional.” You should be able to build a reputation through your ideas and expertise without feeling obliged to put your face on every post.

I use photos of myself too, so this is also a question for me: how much is helping people get to know you, and how much is fishing for attention?

Where do you land? Do selfies make you more interested in someone’s content, or does it depend on what they have to say?

content:
Best ad I've seen this week

I'm a SUCKER for this kind of work

FMCG is a brilliant case for relative differentiation. Sour Patch Kids aren't the ONLY sour sweet, but they've committed to the positioning and focused on saying it louder, in more places, in as many interesting ways as possible.

Most brands have to invest in brand characters. They have a cast of them sitting in their product. Simple, well-branded, fun and perfect for outdoor.

We've just put this into System1 testing to see what the consumers think and feel about them, but this really does nail three key OOH brand-building principles Beth Marchant and I found in our research with JCDecaux

1. Be distinctive: the power of a character. Brand characters give OOH ads a 3x higher chance of rapid brand recognition. We also found that the goal is to use fewer than 7 words on this type of billboard because attention is lower.

2. Don't be dull: tug of war, tennis, a dramatic scene (the kid's literally torn in half). AKA right-brain showmanship. The top 20% OOH campaigns for showmanship drove +167% more brand association lift than the dullest in our analysis.

3. Be consistent: same yellow, same pack, same line, every time. Whether it's a digital screen or a poster, you know it's Sour Patch Kids before you've read a word. Fresh executions, familiar frame. In my work with the IPA, we found that brands that are more consistent with their assets see 2x the average profit growth.

We need big multi-channel campaigns, built around a tension-unlocking insight. But we also need hard-working outdoor like this that does a lot of heavy lifting on the plan, and really takes advantage of the public power of posters. I love it, VCCP!

I'm glad they didn't stop at the cool Oreo special build (what CMOs love for internal decks!) but bought loads of placements for real reach. Will share the results in the comments tomorrow.

author.name: Mark Ritson
author.headline: Founder MiniMBA

content:
I think that the thing I most regret about having decades in advertising is just how much energy we put into getting people to aspire to living THE Good Life – vs. A Good Life.

THE Good Life is easy to define and easy to sell. 

It’s about acquisition and status. It’s comparative. You never get there, there’s always something else to buy to get you closer. 

As an ad person, you just keep reminding people that other people are living better – that they have a better car, a better house, better clothes, better shoes, better life insurance, better food, better coffee, a more functional kitchen and more beautiful hair.“

You are falling short” is the message. 
“Buy this and catch up” is the sell.

We called it “aspiration.” 
Of course we did. “

Aspiration” sounds better than “a hamster wheel of envy and longing from which you will never escape”

And we knew that it made people unhappy. The science has been in for a long time. There is no greater thief of joy than comparison.

We knew and we did it anyway. 

Trade that Toyota for a Lexus, your instant coffee for Gold Blend, for Nespresso, for this $6500 Italian Chrome piece of Barista Nirvana.

We defined The Good Life as something that was just, tantalizingly, out of reach, but close enough to warrant continued pursuit. 

And people ended up angry, upset, depressed in debt and with a storage unit full of things that arrived via Amazon.

And I get it, no one ad did it. 

But billions and billions of dollars were spent over decades telling people that they were an upgrade away from happiness – and that has an effect. Ads rarely shape culture, the cumulative effect of ad spend against dangerous ideas does.

I didn’t do a lot of that stuff. But I did enough, and I’m sorry.

content:
Huge research out the IPA Effectiveness Conference today

Nature is healing. Ad Awareness is taking on a new, practical role marketers can use.

For a while marketers were 'Ad Awareness' mad. Focusing too much on it. And we correctly moved on.

It's not an outcome metric like profit. And everything Robert Heath showed us (people don't even need to look, think or notice ads for them to work) meant a total focus on Ad Awareness created campaigns to boost recall, not emotion and brand growth.

But we clearly over corrected. Which we always do in marketing: this or that, long or short, brand or performance. The answer is always both.

This is why I think this is the most important effectiveness research I've seen in a while.

It's robust AF, econometric modeling with huge datasets from Ebiquity plc, Gain Theory, Thinkbox, YouGov & WPP Media 

But it crucially doesn't overclaim anything but gets to genuinely practical findings for marketers doing the job:

1) Ads and ad awareness have a small direct sales effect but a much larger effect through brand.

2) It's not the entire way advertising works or can be measured, but it clearly explains part of how advertising works, with ad awareness explaining up to 65% of brand consideration depending on the category.

3) Advertising works through three main brand effects (quality, value, and reputation). Which helps explain how useful ad awareness is for each category. If your category is in the above chart, awareness is a useful intermediary metric you should bother reporting.

Looking forward to exploring this more in my own research. Creativity will clearly have a role here.

You can read more about the full research with the key charts in my column today: https://lnkd.in/eDABpPba

content:
$0 to $1m ARR. 0 marketing budget. 12 months

When I started working on Connectd, no one knew who I was. 

Although I previously had an exit, it was in the world of sports and gaming - out as far from the "future of work" you can get.

I'd never posted on LinkedIn. New market, no contacts, basically starting again.

No marketing budget, no sales team, no credibility in the space.

I realised I had to fill the gap of network and connections with content and thought leadership. 

So I took the plunge, started posting, and started building a community 

Every post did three things:

Credibility: I'd sold a company and Id spent a few years working fractional and as an advisor.

Pain: demonstrating that I understood the pain of our customer base as a fractional trying to build a career or as a founder looking for the right people at the right time 

Conviction: showcasing my worldview: why I felt the market was missing what we were doing and why we were the answer

Slowly it started to land. Connection requests started got accepted. Conversations started to happen organically in comments and inboxes and inbound started to pick up. 

Within 12 months: 300 customers, over $1m ARR

If you're on the fence about posting, just remember: a few years ago we had nothing. Now we have the privilege of servicing over 10,000 community members.

It doesn't matter what your journey is. You can build credibility from your own reality, just be authentic. 

Shoot your shot, tell your story in the comments

Yesterday, we launched Snapshots. 

I think it's a really good example of one of the things I love most about Granola overall – simple on the surface, but lots of technical complexity underneath to make it work just right. The team really sweat the details to make it feel perfect *and* as non-invasive as possible.

Snapshots put the slides, docs, decks, designs – whatever's shared on screen – right into your Granola notes.

A company tells me they can’t invest in LinkedIn because the ROI is too difficult to measure.

Two weeks later, they spend a small fortune on a billboard in San Francisco.

I always wonder how they measured that one.

Did the billboard guarantee qualified leads? Did they track how many drivers remembered the company? Could they attribute a specific deal to someone seeing it for the third time in traffic?

Probably not.

They bought it for visibility, recognition and familiarity.

LinkedIn can deliver all three, with a lot more data attached.

The problem is that companies still expect a straight line from post to pipeline.

Buyers don’t work like that.

They see your CEO’s post. Hear the company mentioned on a call. Ignore a video. Visit the website. Close the tab. Reply to your salesperson two months later because the name feels familiar.

The modern buyer journey is more pinball machine than funnel.

content:
I've been working a lot with brands and agencies recently to help plan creator campaigns more effectively, and still the biggest challenge is branding

So here are the facts and some practical advice...

1) Branding early is a very sound strategy. I've seen some creator agencies say it decreases View-Through Rate, so you shouldn't brand early. Yet View-Through Rate isn't an effectiveness outcome. And that treats all types of branding as equal. Yes, attention matters, but it's not the outcome; memory is. I'd rather have 1sec of branded attention vs. 10 secs of creator brilliance that isn't at all distinctive (what a lot of people advocate for without realising).

2) Brand-made ads that successfully get brand recognition in the first 2 seconds see +47% Brand Memory Lift (ie., awareness and campaign recall gain). Creator ads that do the same see a TRIPLING of brand lift outcomes. This clearly shows the lowest-hanging fruit here is to work with creators in a way that creates well-branded content.

3) I was at a wonderful Creator dinner (much love Amelia Christie-Miller and Bold Bean!!) the other day, and I asked 7 creators what their biggest gripes were when working with brands. No. 1: A brief that doesn't just let them create whatever they want (ie they want "no brief"), and No. 2: Being asked to brand early. This dramatically highlights the value of proper agency and marketing talent working with creators; we must brief in a way that is on strategy without losing the creator magic. And if a creator tells you they won't brand early, I will go so far as to say: find another creator. Imagine your creative agency telling you the same?

4. The most pratical insight here: it's about how you brand. In the Creator Effectiveness Playbook with TikTok, System1 and WPP Media we found editing a logo early causes so much skipping that it harms brand outcomes. Yet using on-screen brand names, speaking the brand name and integrating the logo or product into the creative idea itself drives brand outcomes. I get grilled on this a lot, but platform users have developed heuristics to skip certain assets, and some assets force you to be clunky and ruin the creativity you've paid for (ie editing a logo into an edit in post).

Hopefully that sheds some light on a rather confused debate on social and creator branding. Full research on this is clearly explained and free here: https://lnkd.in/eu_HM8hT

content:
You don’t need everyone on LinkedIn to know you. You need the right people to know what to come to you for.

I think we’re going to see more “nichification” of content. And LinkedIn is particularly well suited to it.

People who have spent years doing something, sharing things the rest of us wouldn’t know to ask about. The decisions, details and lessons that come from doing the work.

Take Mohammad Taher, aka The Airport Guy. An aerospace engineer who brought people behind the scenes of aviation. His expertise gave people a reason to watch. His personality gave them a reason to keep watching.

You hear 'airports' and think of him. That’s a powerful association to build.

There’s room for the equivalent in almost every industry. Someone who understands procurement. Someone who can explain the economics of running a restaurant. Someone who knows why construction projects go over budget.

On LinkedIn, that knowledge has an audience of people who buy, hire, invest and make decisions in those industries.

That’s why I encourage more people to aim for industry influence, rather than measuring themselves against the idea of being an 'influencer'

A few thousand relevant people who trust your judgment can do more for your career or business than a huge audience with little interest in your work.

And with AI making it easier to publish a plausible take on almost anything, I’m more interested in hearing from someone who can say: “I have dealt with this. Here’s what happened.."

Being known for something specific doesn’t mean you can never talk about anything else. It gives people a reason to remember you, recommend you and come back.

My first exit at 26, but that doesn't tell the full story.

RealSport had millions of monthly users.

A community that actually showed up every day.

What we hadn't solved was the shift the whole industry was going through, moving off eyeballs model onto subscription.

I knew exactly what that meant if we didn't act.

Gfinity had what we didn't: a reliable way to monetise the audience we'd built and relationships with the biggest sports right holders in the world.

It meant a chance to work more deeply with the Premier League, NBA, F1, do better by our community, and change our lives.

When the deal came together, I took it.

Although it was life changing financially, it didn't feel like a win when it happened. Honestly, it felt like getting out from under something.

The lesson for any early-stage founder: build something that survives on its own, not on someone else's risk appetite or whatever's in fashion that year. It's the one thing I've built differently at Connectd.

content:
If you're in the midsts of retailer planning season - this one's for you.
Yesterday, Andy Page delivered the first of North Star's mini-series of webinars focused on helping you nail retail planning season and the recording has just gone live...


It was a great session, with some of the key takeaways below:
 
1. Know both agendas: Your retailer and your buyer each have their own priorities, goals and ambitions. Your job is to find these out, and build a plan that shows the thread between the two.
 
2. Do the homework before the meeting, not in it: Results statements, investor presentations, IGD and the trade press will tell you what the retailer is chasing. Then ask the buyer directly whether the category is about footfall, margin or growth, and where they're under pressure.
 
3. Category first, not brand first: Category story, shopper evidence, numbers that add up and marketing that drives shoppers to the fixture. "We'd like a new listing" becomes "here's how we grow your category".
 
4. Get in store: Buyers spend less time on the shop floor than you'd think, so get in there and observe something interesting you can take them that they may not have seen.
 
5. Ask for more than the listing: Shelf position, online, convenience and quick commerce, aisle ends and secondary space are often in the buyer's gift too.

You can watch the replay on our retail planning minisite: https://lnkd.in/ebWKeCRh

Marketers don't know what an insight is. And consumers don't care.

It's ad effectiveness awards season around the world. Judging, celebrating and sharing campaigns that worked.

It can cause marketing anxiety. How have other marketers created such world-changing campaigns? What did they do to unlock such an insight that changed the future of their brand?

Rest assured, how bad marketers are at finding an insight should give us total faith that most marketing works in the total absence of one.

Seriously. There's always something in the box marked "insight". But it was usually just an assumption about a category or a fact from research, not the grand, tension-unlocking revelation we’re told an insight needs to be.

Some of the best cases I saw this week grew sales, profit, price elasticity and share with no "insight" at all.

This argument is as old as planning itself. In the 60s, JWT built long-term strategy from grand consumer insights. BMP fiddled with execution. Stephen King called them "ad tweakers".

Yet BMP gave us the Honey Monster that was ridiculously successful. Same story with Jaffa Cakes' Full Moon Half Moon, Compare the Meerkat and Geico's Gecko. None started with a grand revelation.

Effective campaigns start with a clearly identified problem for consumers, the category, or the brand itself. And the brief makes it interesting and emotional for the right audience.

Because the customer never sees your insight slide or strategy deck, they just see the execution.

This is also why creatives should be invited into the planning process, and strategists should work closely with creatives.

Let’s celebrate work that worked, not pretend and retrofit strategy or insights to them.

content:
The results are in

I was wrong. Again. Sort of.

Earlier this week, I shared this new McDonald's outdoor campaign from the Netherlands. I said I wasn't sure about it, with clear reasons from 3+ years researching thousands of OOH campaigns with JCDecaux and System1 (all of which you can find in the book we ended up making free here: https://lnkd.in/gesN9nJ4)

1. Outdoor gets bursts of 2 seconds of attention. You need to land the brand in that time, or it's hard for anything good to happen.

2. You also need to try to attract attention, make people feel something, and build a relevant memory structure. Often, the best way to do this is to put on a show.

3. This led to a boom in outdoor ads where big brands played with their distinctive brand ads. This is trying to do that (the fries box, McFlurry tub, Happy Meal, etc).

I wasn't sure if the shadows were distinct enough, whether anyone cared, and then putting the logo in the bottom left is also a challenge because usually no oone looks there in 2sec and if they do, they ain't looking at the idea.

So I tested it with System1 on hundreds of people. The results are super interesting. I've attached all the reports in the comments.

1. The Happy Meal creative is clearly the best one. 88% of people get the brand in a few seconds. It is one of the most emotional OOH ads we've tested, but interestingly, women LOVE it, and it nearly gets 5 Stars. Men, not so much, at 2 Stars. I guess it captures a snapshot of the lovely moment between the father and his kid. It is a snapshot of a story; it is putting on a show. It's a good ad.

2. The other executions, not so much. Most people (55%ish) don't link the ads to McDonald's quickly enough. They do after quite a lot of attention, though, so maybe cross-track placement would work. And they don't get much of an emotional response (1 Star), as the Happy Meal creative is a snapshot in time between two characters; the others are people eating food.

3. Now I know this isn't fair, but I saw everyone shouting about "it relying on the logo and the shadows are not distinctive". So we tested the Nugget Box ad with the logo removed, and only 2% knew it was for Maccers after a few seconds. 7% after we forced them to stare for 12 seconds. Not sure if that is a useful insight, these things are running with the logo on them.

Final thought - there may not be an overarching idea or insight here. It may not be campaignable. But a large brand like McDonald's needs to remind people it exists, capture attention and emotion, and keep salience alive by linking to relevant occasions. 

The Mappy Meal ad does that very well. But let me know what you think below.

PS. Still think the dad needs clown shoes, a nose, and wig.

content:
One of the questions I’ve heard most over the years on LinkedIn:

"Am I really the best person to talk about this?"

My honest answers:  Probably not... and that’s completely fine.

There is almost always someone who knows more than you. Someone with more experience, a bigger title, a longer track record.

If being the #1 expert was the requirement for posting, LinkedIn would be a very quiet place. 

I have seen this hold back some incredibly smart executives and leaders. They assume expertise is binary: either you’re the authority on something, or you shouldn’t talk about it.
I used to feel it myself.

The way I started thinking about it was a 1–10 scale. 

You might be a 7/10 on a particular topic. That still means there are a lot of 2s, 3s, 4s and 5s who could learn something from your experience.

You can also disagree with the 8s and 9s. You can bring a perspective they don’t have. You can explain something differently because of the industry you work in, the mistakes you’ve made or the people you’ve worked with.

The goal of posting on LinkedIn isn’t to prove you know more than everyone else. It’s to contribute something worth hearing.

content:
9 silly career hills to die on

I hosted a talk on Tuesday for "The Inbetweeners", possibly the nicest group of marketers I've met (brought together by Richard Robinson🔥 and Ingenuity+) who are between roles.

Senior marketers who find themselves now looking for that next job. And right now, a lot of people find themselves in this spot.

I usually present research on effectiveness, but instead I put together 9 career moments with lessons (silly career hills I'd die on). I thought I'd share them here in case they were helpful.

1. Always wear the same thing to work. I got booed after this. But I've always just worn the same stuff at work, same green suit to present in it. I just find it helps with mental load (please don't mention the Zuk), and it makes you easy to remember for others. It's partly why TV shows make people wear the same stuff.

2. The Tuesday Evening Rule. Work out what you love, the kind of stuff that keeps you fill Tuesday evenings with, the stuff you sit up till 1am doing without being told to. And then make that your career. I used to make my own bathtub gin. It's how and why I started working on booze brands.

3. Shoot your shot. I posted about this yesterday, how I'd messaged Jon Evans asking for a role at System1 4 years ago. I'm now Chief Growth Officer. Don't miss your chance!

4. Don't be a sponge. Not all feedback is feedback. You can never please everyone. Be yourself. Respect everyone, but accept they have their game to play as well.

5. Team meetings in the pub. Obviously.

6. No Man! My favourite film is Yes Man! Where Jim Carrey says yes to everything. I think marketers have become the same. Yes, to a new channel. Yes, more ads. Yes, no logo. Yes, creative review. We do better when we are choiceful.

7. Reciprocity. If you do something for someone, they usually return the favour in a much bigger way.

8. Be second best. A few puzzled looks here but I stand by it. I find the idea of becoming an expert in ONE area of marketing very risky and strange. Especially now everything changes so much. I think the job of an effective marketer is understanding everyone's job enough (2nd best) to operate across the mix to create genuine value and behaviour change.

9. Post every day on LinkedIn. Someone threw a sausage roll at me for this one. But the process of growing a network, writing every day, sharing my work, and hiring people on LinkedIn has changed my career/life. You're at the world's biggest always-on free marketing conference.

Ace to meet the other people who shared as well Richard Sherwood, Caroline Smith, Mike Thorne

Let me know your silly career hill you'd die on below!!

The aftermath of that exit left me exhausted.

When I started Connectd I was committed to helping more founders get it right the first time.

I myself had to learn and unlearn some things:

→ how to work with my (ADHD) brain
→ when to step back and let the team run things
→ how to recognise the people I can rely on
→ when to be honest that I didn’t know something

Now, we’re an $19M ARR business with a headcount of over 130 people.

It’s crazy now to look back at over eight years of being an ‘exited founder’.

Which is why it’s so important to build a company where you’re excited for the journey as well as the outcome.

The passion.

Good account teams and managers are legends, ensuring they don’t burn out by letting them enjoy 6-12 margaritas on a sun lounger without hitting them with “Sorry to bother you while you’re away” is crucial.

content:
As more AI technology emerges, the last real advantage will be brand and strategy

Most AI ads still haven’t clocked it yet. A lot of it is just feature soup: endless claims, vague superiority, and functional gobble only the writer could love.

So when I went see Smartlead's new Shoreditch wall wrap, I was pleasantly surprised. Because there’s a real strategic thought in it. It’s trying to educate people on what AI pipeline tools even do before making the usual superiority claim. Full thoughts below!

1. I see a LOAD of total shite B2B ads, and AI ads that simply try to tell you a list of features or a line about how they are somehow superior. This tries to do more than that.

2. I genuinely think there's a smarter strategy here. It's trying to educate us on what AI pipeline tools even do before claiming it's the best one. I'm still half in an Excel file I save in my download folder to manage a lot of my CRM. So there's a strategy here, but I'd have liked to have seen this all laddered up to something more emotional and human. Like: getting home to your dog on time (no bad ideas here, guys).

3. I like the contextual creative and media placement, using famous tube lines to make this massive new technology seem familiar. And I like how it's attempting to tell the story (in a very literal sense) of the process of getting stuff done with the tool.

4. Yes, this is mega "distinctive"; it looks straight out of their brand book. But my build to move this on is: showmanship. B2B buyers are still human, so we should assume they don't care much about the CRM journey. They want character, story, a clear sense of place. This will take the idea to the next level, making it more emotional and attention-grabbing.

I’d run this through System1 testing, but I’m not entirely sure how I’d test a gigantic wall in Shoreditch. So comment below with your thoughts.

content:
I'm not sure about this new campaign from McDonald's

I see where it's coming from, the recent strategic moves by a lot of brands to own a "category entry point" and simply showing their brands near it will build salience. Here, it's sunny weather = get a Maccers!

And the recent move, especially in outdoor, for large brands to have some fun with their very famous Distinctive Brand Assets to earn that double-take and an emotional payoff (made very popular again last year by a few agencies, including Uncommon). Hiding or changing bits of their logos.

But putting yourself in the consumer's shoes for a minute, an act a marketer must do daily for several hours: could you tell this was for McDonald's without the logo? Maybe for the Happy Meal execution (I reckon this would have been a brilliant summer campaign for Happy Meal, but I'd still want to see one of the shadows being Ronald McDonald spreading his joy).

In all my research, logos at the bottom of OOH really don't help much at all, due to outdoor usually getting 1-2seconds of attention. The idea itself must be branded enough to work. Reminds me of an old Bill Bernbach quote: “A picture of a man standing on his head would get attention, but the reader would feel tricked by the gimmick. Unless we were trying to sell a gadget to keep change in his pocket.” Ie. the idea should be branded, or what's the point?

Anyway, I've put it into System1 testing to see if it gets that emotional payoff. And it's distinctive enough to grow branded memories. Will share results tomorrow but let me know what you think below. I could be totally wrong (I often am).

content:
AI can write your posts. It can polish your profile. It can make you sound like an expert in almost anything.

It can’t give you the career you claim to have had.

LinkedIn is testing a feature that lets former colleagues and classmates confirm your work and education history. It’s also giving companies more control over fake accounts claiming to work for them.

When it gets easier to look credible online, people need better ways to check what’s real. A job title or company name can open doors on LinkedIn. You should be able to trust that the person behind it actually earned it.

Of course, verification can’t tell you whether someone is good at their job. That comes through in what they say, what they’ve done and what other people can vouch for.

Trust is the currency on LinkedIn. 

That’s why I call it trust media. And as AI makes content easier to create, the people who can back up their words with real experience will stand out even more.

content:
The best founder decision I made this year was not having an assistant.

Tried it once. Brilliant, but doesn’t suit how my brain works. 

But running a $19M ARR company that has a team of 130+ work across 13 timezones (California to Mumbai) means there’s a lot of admin.

I was wasting hours every morning digging through messages, call notes, task lists to figure out what was urgent.

Having ADHD means that I could easily lose hours to context switching.

I have to start my day with meditation and a clear to do list.

Now I have an AI Chief of Staff to take care of that list.

It runs every day and creates a briefing for me with:

- Urgent team flags requiring my attention
- Action points from recent calls 
- Briefs for meetings on my schedule

It’s smart. It pulls the context I need from my schedule and meeting notes and acts like a very smart assistant, it’s not just an automated list task.

This used to need an hour of my time.

Now it’s five minutes while I have a matcha.

I’ve broken down the exact structure and how I built this in this month’s newsletter. Founders - steal it. Build your own version. 

Link in the comments 🙏

content:
This is the real public brief launched by the Ben & Jerry's founder to "free the brand" from the Magnum Ice Cream corporation

It's a brilliant example of our continued failure, skipping strategy and going straight to execution: 80% of marketers think they're awesome at briefing, but only 6% of agencies agree (BetterBriefs data).

Ben & Jerry's founder (Ben Cohen) needs a proper strategy. Not a public creative brief.

My column this week in The Drum: https://lnkd.in/e9NzJGgG

TL;DR

1) 57% of marketers rely on creative reviews to fix strategy, quite like this brief is doing. We must sort strategy before execution.

2) The opening context reads like it's been written by an upset lawyer, it should inspire and share emotion and history.

3) There's no clear task beyond "increase pressure". What problem are we solving?

4) A third of marketers aren't who their target audience is, neither is this brief.

5) The judging criteria for a winning idea is essentially "make me viral". We must give creatives a real sense of how winning will be measured.

6) One thing I love: outcome-based payment. The winning idea will get a lifetime supply of ice cream if Magnum hands Ben & Jerry's back. It needs to be more than a few scoops of ice cream, and we need clear intermediate behaviour and metrics to track. But outcome-based work is where agencies must head in the "age of AI".

A great strategist could transform this brief. Get ya wallet out, Ben. I know a few I can intro you to.

Let me know what you think of the brief below, it's always fascinating to hear what people think of briefs. Briefing is an art!

content:
The traditional CV is “dead”, replaced by cakes, social videos & letters 

BUT these *fun* formats could have very serious consequences!!

My social feeds recently have been filled with brands doing hiring differently:

→ SULT ran a whole public social media campaign for their recent hire
→ Jamie Laing hired someone who wrote him a letter
→ a reel of a cake CV gained 10 million+ views 

The UK job market right now is tough (Sky News just reported job vacancies hit their lowest level in 5 years) 

& in a world where anyone can generate text for their CV at a click of a button, I can’t say it’s surprising candidates are finding new ways to stand out 

BUT where is the line?? When employers are *idolising* going above & beyond, we risk overlooking people who can’t afford:

→ additional time (especially women, who statistically take on more of the household & care duties than men)
→ to publicly announce they’re job hunting, at the risk of losing their current role 
→ the monetary investment to (potentially) multiple jobs

& the most worrying part of all, is this is often exploitative of juniors who are desperate for a job (even if it’s minimum wage)

If you’re asking your candidates to go above and beyond, you better be rewarding them accordingly!! For me, this looks like: 

💸 Paying candidates for compulsory tasks completed in applications, even if they’re unsuccessful 
⏱️ Setting tasks with a time limit (so those with extra responsibilities are not disadvantaged)
💓 Not *automatically* discounting people who can’t go above & beyond 

What would you add to this list?

content:
"A wrong answer is better than no answer"

This comment by the awesome Karen Blackett CBE really jumped out at me when we were talking about leadership on Uncensored CMO

Was she really saying it is better to be wrong than not make a decision?

She went on to explain that the most damaging thing for a business is indecision because it leaves the organisation in a state of paralysis

It's better to make a decision and learn from it than make no decision at all

As someone who loves to leave a decision longer just in case new information emerges this really challenged me

It also reminded me of 2 other helpful decision making approaches

THE 2 WAY DOOR

I learnt this from Grace Beverley who said that decisions are either one way doors (you can't go back) or two way doors (you can). In reality most decisions are two way doors so it is better to try something knowing that you can always reverse that decision later

THE 10-10-10 RULE

I remember someone telling me the best way to make a decision is pretend it has already been made and then try and see how you feel about it.

I then came across a slightly more developed version of that called the 10-10-10 rule

Imagine the decision is made and ask yourself how it might feel in

10 days
10 months
10 years

In my experience changing the timeframe has a huge impact on decision making since we tend to always optimise for the short term. What is right in the long term usually means making greater sacrifices today - short term pain for long term gain!!

I would LOVE to know what decision making frameworks you use?

content:
LinkedIn is testing a feed with two tabs: 

Network and For You

Quite a few people have asked me what I think so here is my take...

1) What’s changing:
Network shows posts from people you have connected with or chosen to follow. For You is designed to help you discover relevant practitioners and ideas, including people outside your network.

It’s a test, so we don’t yet know how posts will be ranked in each tab or what it will do to reach.

2) The pros
I’d like a better way to keep up with people I chose to connect with. Too often, I realise I haven’t seen a post from someone I value in months.

I also want LinkedIn to keep introducing me to people I don’t know. Some of the best voices I follow were strangers when I first came across their work. Giving connection and discovery their own space makes sense to me.

3) The cons
A separate Network tab only helps if people actually open it. If everyone stays in For You, it won’t do much to help us stay connected. And For You needs to be good at finding relevant people. If it keeps showing us the same familiar takes, a second tab won’t make the feed more useful.

4) The implications for reach
This is the bit people are worried about, understandably. Will posts from your connections get fewer views if they spend more time in For You? Will it become easier or harder to reach people outside your network?

I wouldn’t claim to know yet. LinkedIn hasn’t shared enough about how the tabs will work to call this a reach win or a reach disaster.

5) The opportunity
I think this is a useful reminder that people read your posts for different reasons. Someone who knows you may want to hear what you have been working on. A stranger needs a reason to care before they know anything about you.

The best posts can do both: give your network something worth responding to and give a new reader a clear idea they can take away.

Overall, I’m positive about the test. I want to see more from the people I chose to follow, and I still want to discover people who challenge how I think.

Whether this works comes down to a much less exciting question: will either tab be good enough that we choose to open it again tomorrow?

If you have got the new design, which tab are you using more?

content:
The UN//SCENE Festival is a brilliant thing. 

At its heart it’s looking to create a pipeline of fresh voices and fresh opinions by allowing people who don’t usually get offered a stage a bloody great big one.


The fact that they now have a directory of those speakers and are negotiating slots for them at other industry events speaks volumes – these are people looking to inject freshness into industry conversation, not to extract a quick buck from industry narcissism.

I was there last week and what I loved was the fact that so much of what people were discussing was work in progress. 

There were no tablets of stone being handed down from a stage by people who believed that if advertising had a Mt. Rushmore they’d be on it. 

Instead we had people saying “this is interesting”, “we’ve been playing with this”, “we’re trying to do this”, “this seems to be working” – and then inviting others to participate, to add, to build and to take what works for them and use it however they wanted to.

That was refreshing. But what was really refreshing was just how many of the people talking were do-ers. Every person that I watched or spoke to was out there in the world making things happen. They had companies and communities, events and entertainment. They had followers and fans, customers and colleagues. They had evidence of action. And I loved that. 

The common thread I found was that all of the people on a stage or running a session were out in the world putting their thinking into practice. 

They valued impact over ego.

And if spending time with people like that wasn’t worth £99, I don’t know what is.

content:
The two biggest unlocks for me as a founder:

1. Working weekends
2. Working on my mental health

There was a time I wouldn’t have shared that.

It’s easy to miss nuance online.

We assume anyone working weekends automatically means having no work life balance.

There was a time that was true for me.

Working 24/7. No boundaries. Exhausted.

But investing in my mental health after I sold my first company gave me perspective.

I learned how to better support the team.
I learned where I have weaknesses.
I learned about how I operate best.

And interestingly I discovered that if I followed every rulebook and avoided thinking about work on the weekends, I would struggle.

It’s not how I’m wired.

The people I’m most proud to work with think similarly. It’s not that everyone has to work weekends or go to therapy (I do recommend the latter).

It’s understanding how you work best.

So you can better support the people around you.

Gen Z & older generations build their careers entirely differently

I only worked a 9 - 5 for 7 months before the COVID lockdown

→ working from home
→ in comfy clothes
→ on my phone

BUT 7 years on from that lockdown I have a successful career because the principle of visibility is the same, mine is simply *digital* instead

I’m showing up in email chains, online meetings & your LinkedIn feed 

& as the first woman in her bloodline to be able to work *anywhere* in the world from her laptop AND still be visible, I have high hopes for better inclusion at work:

→ people building their own visibility through personal brands, without relying on senior managers with unconscious bias 
→ teams built from more diverse demographics (as they’re not confined to one region) producing less-biased outcomes
→ better flexibility for people* who need flexible working, *currently predominantly women

There’s a lot of divisiveness between Gen Z & older generations 

BUT I think we’re a lot more similar than we’d like to admit… we both want to be visible, we just achieve it differently

content:
An AI out-of-office agent has racked up $10,000-a-day bill

A key modern skill: deciding when to NOT use AI

Direct from the The Wall Street Journal's Leadership Institute, Isabelle Bousquette, interviewing David Hsu who discovered one of his team has gone on holiday and instead of using a standard OOO feature in Outlook. They built an agent to deal with it.

The agent would search through thousands of chats every time it got an email, burning through tokens to decide whether to reply, and with what. Costing them 5 figures a day. For one employee.

What better example is there of: just because we can, doesn't mean we should.

It's not a new lesson. Strategy is about choosing what we DON'T do. The same needs to be applied to AI.

I have agents that read the news to keep me up to date, digest complex academic releases, and find the insight in huge datasets. These things are gold dust, save me hours and importantly make me more effective.

But we need to start asking how much they cost, what the return is, and if it's worth it. Especially as token prices eventually reach their real cost.

The full 'Companies Struggle to Explain Their Own AI Investment Return' is well worth the read.

content:
Think 121s are useless?

5 tips to make them actually meaningful again.

James Gregory, System1's CEO, has been in the business for 5 years. As I hung up our usual Monday morning call this morning, I realised we hadn't talked about projects, to-dos, or our weeks ahead. And I realised I've accidentally started finding 121s incredibly useful.

Now, I've always found them a massive drain on time and resources, as I'm clear on what I need to do; otherwise, I wouldn't be any good at my job. So I wanted to share 5 ways we make the most of our recurring meeting.

1) Fluid strategy. I don't believe a strategy is ever static, or maybe it could have been, but the marketing world is in so much rapid flux that strategy needs to be open to discussion. What are we not doing? What are we doing again? How do we create value for our customers (marketers) better than anyone else?

So our conversations are mostly about being super clear on our strategy (being the most predictive and useful creative measurement platform), whether the decisions and investments are really leading to that, and what we should NOT be doing in favor of being true to our strategy. This usually comes down to the simple questions: where are we playing, how will we win, and what systems do we need to deliver it.

2) The Venn diagram of talent. Businesses grow or shrink based on how motivated talent is. Having open, honest discussions about where I and others in the business get personal value is important. But the magic comes from the overlap of what people want and what the business wants. Spending time aligning those things feels like the difference between a job and a career.

3) Future gazing. Sounds horrendous, but bear with. Most strategy falls down because people don't 1) think far enough and 2) consider that the competition will also make their move. We spend a LOT of time talking about developments and where the market will PROBABLY end up. And what our business has to look like in 5 years to deliver on our promises. This is probably the most creative and fun part of any senior role, we have a few long-term bets that I'm very excited about.

4) Time is irrelevant. A lot of the time it's a 10min call. Sometimes it stretches into 2 hours. The call aligns thinking and the plan. If that's done in 10mins, I'm onto the next thing.

5) Don't discuss urgents. If you're discussing project details and urgent stuff on the 121, you're not using comms channels effectively. I've found the value of a 121 is NOT discussing this sort of stuff. We can all manage the short, but we win if we get the long right. That's what these meetings are for!

Clearly this will be different across businesses and categories. But I've finally got them working for me, thanks to James, so I wanted to share. But let me know your tips or if you still think they are useless below.

NB: Picture from my favourite 121, running around Central Park discussing me joining our Exec team, before leaving James in my dust  🏃

content:
A good day for creativity! Creatively awarded campaigns are TWICE as likely to win effectiveness awards

WARC's latest report, The Health of Creativity 2026, reveals that 45% of the most creatively awarded ideas win effectiveness awards, versus 21% of creatively awarded work overall.

I mean, it's not a controlled experiment, but a good sign that our industry still recognises and values the impact of creativity. And I'm a big proponent of the rigour that goes into the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) and Effie Worldwide effectiveness awards, so creativity (as judged by creatives) is clearly delivering the goods in some way.

There is a far more interesting finding than the above for marketing nerds though. 37% of the best work ran for 1+ years, versus just 15% normally.

Massive survivorship bias (good work gets used longer) but also a timely reminder that great advertising needs conviction, and the best marketers are putting more resource behind winning campaigns.

This, for me, is the best thing that creative and effectiveness awards do. Alongside the type of consumer creative testing System1 does. Giving confidence in the work so marketers are compelled to run great ideas for longer, with enough media cash for them to work.

In my research with System1 and Effie, The Creative Dividend, we found emotional and distinctive campaigns that ran for over 3 years were 7.5x more likely to report incremental profit growth.

content:
Talking about the logo should be banned in creative reviews

Honestly, how many times have you met to review creative ideas or post-shoot, and the conversation has descended into inane chat about the damn logo.

Distinctiveness is the lowest and most obvious form of creativity. It's easy. My 4-year-old nephew could have a go commenting on it.

And when we let the conversation go that way, it gets in the way of the more important things: is this on strategy? How does it make people feel? Does it put on a show? Is it consistent and coherent? Better still: is it suitable for the touchpoints we've identified?

In The Creative Dividend, my research with Effie Worldwide and System1, we found that the most funded but creatively deficient campaigns fall behind in distinctiveness 3% of the time. But they are either not emotional enough or don't use enough showmanship almost half the time.

We must raise the creative bar. Ban logo chat. And push ourselves to make work that actually works.

content:
The best ad I've seen this week

Demonstrating 5 creative effectiveness principles

To celebrate IKEA Italy's 30th birthday, Ogilvy Italia has turned their iconic blue bag into a creative device and so much more.

Probably my favourite campaign I've seen in a while, I hope this gets loads of media reach.

1. Clear brand strategy. Ikea's business goal is to sell affordable things across many home categories to everyone. So the strategic unlock for this brand has really been: Democratic Elevation. Taking the completely mundane, overlooked moments of daily life and making them feel meaningful, beautiful, and worthy of celebration.

2. Genuine creative platform. The creative idea is really just an elevation of this idea in markets around the world, quite like the award winning "Wonderful Everyday". A very stretchy idea that creatives can really have fun with, while remaining consistent and coherent with core Ikea brand.

3. Repeatable creative device. The local execution is where it gets really exciting for me, and we've seen other markets do the same (a good test that the strategy is sound). Moving the blue bag from a simple brand asset into a creative device, used to demonstrate how Ikea lives in these special everyday moments.

In my research with System1, Effie Worldwide and IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) I found the creation of something like this takes a few years to pay back in emotion as they become more fluent, so the game now is really consistency.

4. Pump the drama. To attract attention and make an idea really worth talking about, a key creative principle is finding a tension or really pumping the drama in the situation. Brilliantly demonstrated here. Crucial to delivering on their strategy and idea here.

5. Director's treatment & craft. What makes this campaign worth talking about, really. A lot of the time, marketers rush through this part, but Ogilvy brought in Salvatore Matarazzo to shoot the whole thing like a high-fashion ad. It's dripping in taste that is hard to prove in numbers. But this is why it delivered so well on the brief (in my POV), this isn't Ikea's 30th. It's Ikea Italy's 30th. And the direction makes this blatant, while giving the work value simply because it's beautiful.

Really love this, have put it into System1 consumer creative testing to see if they agree. Hope this gets plenty media spend!

content:
HubSpot flew me to Boston to attend their annual UNBOUND (prev. INBOUND) conference, and here’s the BIGGEST takeaway about the world of marketing, AI, and human intelligence ✈️👋🎙️📌 ad

(Also can we just celebrate the fact that HubSpot was one of the first brands to take a chance on me as a little B2B creator four years ago, and now we’re still here working together.) 

There’s so much pressure to learn every AI tool, agent and capability as quickly as it arrives through the fear of being left behind, or not adopting fast enough but the message from HubSpot was actually to… Take a deep breath and, uh, not use more AI. 

Instead, it was to use AI more intentionally and with the right context because that’s the difference between businesses who are transforming right now vs. those that aren’t.

In fact, in a survey they ran, HubSpot found that using AI with bad context (not giving it enough information about you, your business, your customers, your ethos, etc) was WORSE than not using AI at all. 

Let that sink in. 

It makes sense, then, that most of us start with the low-stakes stuff: drafting an email, creating content or getting ready for a meeting. It feels safer when the AI does not yet know your business properly.

But that’s the gap (!!) we're using AI for what is easiest to delegate, rather than what is most impactful. And that’s where the conversation got really interesting:

→ The most popular AI use cases are not always the most impactful: Sending emails, producing content and preparing for meetings are some of the most common ways people use AI. But the bigger business gains come from delegating less obvious work: analysing campaigns, understanding customer feedback and prioritising pipeline.

→ Context is what turns AI from fast into valuable: AI needs to understand your business context like brand voice, positioning and goals, customer context like conversations, personas and buying signals and team context like roles, processes and approvals. With poor context, it’s actually worse to use AI than not use it at all. 

→ The human role is becoming more important, not less: AI may help us complete work in a week that once took two. But it’s human judgement, creativity, thoroughness and context that’s the crucial difference between whether your output is good, or terrible. 

What a calming and reassuring but motivating message from a legacy brand. 

Keep your eyes out for a roundup post about the conference in the next couple of weeks! I’m spilling some secrets… 🤭

content:
Agency profitability is a hot topic, with most blaming AI for creating a race to the bottom, but it could obviously be helping instead

The biggest shock to me when leaving client-side marketing was how hard people work in agencies. I won’t embarrass the person who did this, but I literally was on a creative review a few years back, and someone on the senior creative team took the Zoom call…from the dentist's chair.

You can see these incredibly passionate people who care about creativity, are super involved in their clients' businesses, and genuinely want their agency to succeed. But the immense pressure of the market shifts and sheer volume of admin are rather crippling.

I shared a few months back how I’d been using Productive to explore how AI could free us all from the manual BS of project workflows, timesheets, etc. But I genuinely think it can now address the bigger issue: agency profitability.

Getting to the end of a project and finding out a client or project has not made any money, or worse (admittedly, I had this once or twice…) cost money is terrifying. Tying all the work and processes together upfront and throughout to reliably know there’s profit at the end of the rainbow.

It’s a bit of an AI-judo-flip. Sure, it’s causing pressure on costs and prices. Everyone’s trying to work out where gen-AI sits in all this. But using AI to plan accordingly and using it for what it’s good for (repetitive, complex tasks and maths) makes sense to me.

content:
A "view” on Facebook Reels can be one millisecond.
 
On LinkedIn, it’s two seconds. On Spotify, it’s 30.

So when someone says their video reached one million views, the honest follow-up Q is:
 
A million what???
 
One million milliseconds adds up to less than 17 minutes. One million LinkedIn views adds up to roughly 556 hours. One million Spotify podcast views would represent 8k+ hours.
 
The same word is being used to describe very different levels of attention.

And even the more demanding definitions still set a fairly low bar for the work we do at Shake Content.

When we create content with a CEO, exec, or senior leader, the goal isn’t (merely) to get someone across the platform’s threshold for a view.

We want the idea to STAY with them.

Would they remember the argument later that day? Has it changed how they think about the leader or company? Could it start a conversation internally? Does it build familiarity and trust over several months? Can any of that eventually contribute to a relationship, an opportunity or a decision?

A two-second view is the beginning of the measurement. The more interesting part is what remains once the video is no longer on the screen.

That’s where staying power, trust and business impact begin.

Shoutout to Matt Navarra for putting together.

content:
I had a splendid drink with a fantastic advertising person last night. As usual they were talking eloquently about "Great Work". And as usual Guinness Surfers came up as the zenith of great advertising. 

It's a great ad if you work in the industry and like self congratulatory cinematography and daring leaps of creativity that completely ignore consumer feedback.

If you see advertising not as a career, or art, but as a tactical tool for brand building and sales then Guinness Surfer is a bad ad. Not even average. It's bad. 

If, like my drinking amigo, it's one of your favourites  - good for you. But don't conflate what the industry thinks with what the consumer thinks. The first law of marketing is market orientation and it teaches you - if you are prepared to learn - that you are not the consumer. If you work in marketing you are the opposite of it. Everything you think is not just biased, it's wrong. 

It's the reason your packaging is too generic. You don't run your ads long enough. You underprice your products. You overcomplicate your positioning. You spend too little on windows. The list goes on and on. But it starts with Guinness Surfers as the acid test for market orientation. 

Good or Bad?

With thanks to Andrew Tindall (who is now hiding under his East London sofa), System1 and my mate Dennis who inspired this post.

content:
If you’re still putting QR codes in your ads, you’re a moron

My column this week: https://lnkd.in/eA9qREyA

Admittedly, one of the spiciest titles in my years of writing it. But plenty of data backs it up.

Research shows CTV QR code scans have fallen 60%, to 0.004%. Imagine how low it is for channels like OOH.

Marketers already know this. Obviously, QR codes in ads don't work. Consumers know this. So why are we still doing it?

Why am I force-fed ads between CTV, BVOD, and even YouTube that assume I'll leap out of bed and scan to buy Febreze that very second?

The increasing need for media to be "shoppable" reveals a deep misunderstanding of how advertising works. It has a tiny, almost irrelevant effect on nudging a sale today. And a huge, lasting, compounding effect on memories that create sales in the future.

You see this in the research exploring what happens to brands when they stop advertising. They don't plummet to the ground that quarter; it takes years for the damage to reveal itself.

Slapping a QR code on an ad, or into a media format, isn't just chasing the smallest role of advertising. But it decreases the chance of achieving the more important role of advertising. It also assumes that a customer would ever care about your ad or brand. They don't.

In my column this week, I shared a load of evidence for why this needs to stop. And ask a simple question.

If you’re so insecure that your ad won’t work that you feel obligated to slap a QR code on it, why are you advertising in the first place?

content:
Never trust a planner who opens with “that’s off brief”

It’s a sign that they’re more in love with making an argument then they are with advertising. A sign that they’re more at home with logic than with magic.

A brain that automatically closes down an idea because it can’t make an immediate, logical connection to some words on paper is a brain better suited to finance than strategy.

A strategist’s first response would be “okay, that’s not what I was expecting, tell me what you’re trying to do with this, explain it to me” – they would meet the idea with curiosity, not with suspicion. They’d look past the execution and towards the idea.

In essence a planner that opens with “that’s off brief” is the kind of person who buys the show-home on a new development, because they didn’t like the color of the walls in the bathroom on the place over the road.

One way to spot them, other than to follow the sound of creative people grinding their teeth, is that they also look for magic words, rather than real magic. They’ll overlook the way that a spot feels, the emotion in it, the way that it looks, the music, the ideas you have to make this open in people’s minds rather than just on the page – and then get hugely excited about a pun, the way one line of copy is phrased or a play on words. 

Worse, they’ll spend more time on the slide you threw together to introduce the idea than they do on the idea. If they ever ask you to go back to it, that’s a red flag bigger than the one you’ll find on the North Korean side of the DMZ border.

There are more and more of these people wandering amongst us, Ghouls in glasses more concerned about the deck than the work, about the template than any kind of emotional tempest. 

They can’t be avoided, but they must be ignored; because if they win then every ad becomes their brief minus the bullet points. And the world becomes a less artful, less beautiful, less interesting place.
