content:
ChatGPT has launched a campaign to convince the world it helps children learn. We've tested it to see if it will work

This has to be one of the most interesting ads launched this year. There's huge pushback (and evidence) right now that AI is getting in the way of children learning.

So, OpenAI's ChatGPT has launched what is objectively world-class marketing:

Their business goal is razor-sharp: mass adoption of their tools.

They're clear on the customer problem: AI is perceived as stopping children from learning and disrupting our school system.

Marketing challenge: flip the script and ensure ChatGPT is seen as a tool that helps children learn, not hinders them.

Their execution is twofold, which is impressive, as most marketers would have just seen this as a comms problem, but they've leaned into more than one of the 4Ps. Launched a new product, "Study Mode," that doesn't give the answers but shares questions and quizzes shown to reinforce learning. An ad campaign making it feel social, easy, and attractive.

The marketers at OpenAI clearly know what they are doing. System1 have tested the ad with hundreds of people and we predict it will be effective for a few key reasons:

1. It's one of the most "right-brained" tech ads we've tested in a while. Character acting, a clear story, a recognisable place, humour. Instead of trying to rationally convince with features and facts, they lean into making it feel human.

2. It works. There's some negative emotion from cognitive dissonance, where people can't reconcile what they are seeing with how they feel about AI and learning. But a large majority are won over and feel incredibly positive. This puts it in the top 13% of Software ads for emotional response, predicting a good amount of long-term behaviour change.

3. They are leaning into the EAST framework, which I learned from Richard Shotton. A framework to help organizations change behaviour. Easy, Attractive, Social and Timely. Specifically, they are making it look social, social proofing so it looks like everyone is doing it and it's normal. They show it being used in a real school environment. Attractive, no feature lists but warm humour and emotion from real teachers. And easy; it's just a click away to solve this current issue.

I recognise this is controversial and a tough topic, but I also recognise the skill of the marketers at OpenAI so I wanted to share the research behind it.

A lot of marketers challenging the Sydney Sweeney ad BUT not their own organisations☕️

(THAT’S where we can make real change!! I’ll prove it) 

The first 3 years of my career I ran the social media for Loughborough Sport, that’s:

→ number 1 university in the WORLD for sport
→ BUCS champions since it’s inception 
→ (at the time) Sports Uni of the Year

AND it has a skewed male student population

(so I fear I have the credentials to speak on this topic) 

& at the time, where sports clubs had a gender split ALL the male clubs had the “main” Instagram handle, think: 

“@lbororugby” vs “@lborowomensrugby” 

It wasn’t malicious, it was simply “the way we’ve always done things” & *nobody* questioned it…

…until I did 

I advocated that all clubs with a gender split should follow the rule of @lboro(sport)(gender), think: 

“@lbororugbymens” & “@lbororugbywomens”

Not ONLY was this better for equality, it was better SEO for the clubs!!

(prioritising sport before gender, meaning audiences searching for men’s sides would discover women’s sides & vice versa)

& guess what? This change is still in place 4+ years after I’ve left the organisation!!

Marketers are BEYOND powerful & we have to lead from the front 

Want to make a difference? Start in your own organisation: 

💓 get CREATIVE with it, not all change is made in a post 
💭 question “the way we’ve always done things”
📣 speak up, even when others don't

All it took was ONE person (the *least* senior marketer in the team btw) to speak up to challenge the status quo 

BIG changes are made by taking small steps!!

Posting on LinkedIn is free. Sharing your founder story, your insights, your mistakes - that's content. Post 3-5x a week before spending a penny on ads.

2. Find advisors before hiring employees.
The conversations will save you from expensive mistakes you'd make alone. Find people who've done what you're trying to do. Ask specific questions. Do it before you're desperate.

3. Hire fractional before full-time.
Get someone who's done it 10x before to spend 1-2 days a week getting things right before you hire someone to scale. Fractional = senior expertise at a fraction of the cost.

4. Track three metrics obsessively. Ignore the rest.
Pick the numbers that actually matter right now. Revenue, churn, CAC - whatever moves the needle. Solve for them obsessively. Everything else is noise.

5. Build relationships before you need them.
Don't wait until you're fundraising to start talking to investors. Founders who move fast and are successful have been building those relationships for months.

6. Get comfortable being uncomfortable.
If you're not slightly terrified by what you're building, you're playing it too safe.
Most early-stage failure comes from trying to do too much with too little.

Focus. Find the right people early. Move fast on what matters.

—
I’m Roei. ADHD founder helping other businesses grow.

content:
A public apology.

This week I shared one of many reactive ad ideas (this one a spec ad) for the new foldable Apple phone launch. I said the idea was brilliant.

After System1 testing I can confirm that this idea is sadly not brilliant.

It's left me with some very hard-learned lessons.

1. The Apple foldable news may be big on LinkedIn, my corner of Instagram and even with marketers. But alas, the general public doesn't know or care much about it yet. Leading to a very low emotional response. Which is an issue, because we've shown with JCDecaux that the emotional response to outdoor ads has a clear, significant relationship with sales and brand effects.

Lesson 1: You are not the customer, Andrew.

2. Despite the ad having a central image of the product itself, with a massive logo. 40% of people aren't sure it's for The Economist, because this looks nothing like previous Economist work. In 'Compound Creativity' with the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) and Effie Worldwide, we found that consistency is a key "law" of effectiveness.

Lesson 2: Obviously, consistency and coherence matter.

3. Only 23% of respondents built a memory around anything to do with the category (news, finance, etc.). Almost half built "magazine," but I'm not really convinced that is actually a relevant category entry point anymore for The Economist. This will struggle to build much salience; it only preaches to the choir of current customers.

Lesson 3: Even with fun ads like this, we can't leave strategy at the door.

4. All the above could be true, but the idea and execution could simply tell an engaging truth well to attract attention and elicit emotion. Which has always been a silly hill i'll die on: sometimes great execution can do weird things and trump everything. This was not the case.

Lesson 4: Great creativity matters, and makes our industry what it is today.

Here's the full research for yourself, which I presume Damon Hutson-Flynn will print out for his fridge next to the dartboard with my headshot stuck on it: https://lnkd.in/dmFhUR7C

content:
No one agrees if gen AI makes ads more effective

Over the past 10 months, there's been 4 key pieces of research exploring if gen-AI makes advertising more effective. As Chris Aarons has shared, they appear to disagree with each other.

1.  NYU Stern School of Business looked at Click-Through Rate in a very impressive controlled causal experiment, showing that AI ads perform up to 19% better until the consumer is told it's AI; then they get hammered by -35%. Ie people struggle to tell AI was involved until they are told, and good AI ads shouldn't give it away.

2. Taboola ran a very large observational study looking at Click-Through Rate of 500m+ impressions, broadly finding AI ads saw slightly more engagement. But the best AI ads were the ones people didn't think were AI, and people still couldn't really tell what those were.

Useful large studies but largely on performnce/display platforms looking at CTR, a performance metric. So the other two studies are useful.

3 & 4 Ten months ago I tested 20 AI ads with System1's tools vs our huge haman-made ad database, a similiar study was shared last week in Harvard Business Review which concluded the total opposite outcome. But they agreed on the same thing again, people really can't tell if AI was inolved till prompted.

The marketing industry must move on. Consumers do not care how an ad is made, because they do not care about advertising. We shouldn't be sloppy and rub it in their faces, whcih has led to some backlash and headlines recently, but that's about as nuanced as our take is going to get.

Which prompts the next more important, useful and practical question for the industry.

If humans can’t spot good AI ads. Can AI indentify good human ones?

For this I sat in my underpants till 2am last night running a new experiment and writing it all up in for my column this week. 10 human ads, tested with System1's human testing. Retested with System1's new AI predictive testing trained on 18mil human emotional responses (called Test Your Ad Screen).

AI was largely pretty good, but it fails in some places, which are obvious in hindsight. This raises important questions for eager marketers going all in on AI creative testing that always has an answer, no matter what. Read the whole thing free here: https://lnkd.in/eG2BeRzm

Some come from 4+ years working inside LinkedIn. Others come from helping founders and executives use it every day.

1) B2B brands should spend less time trying to sound human and more time letting actual humans speak

content:
Last night Byron Sharp confused marketers into believing that advertising and its quality don't reliably grow brands by misreading my research again

Given this was the British Brands Group 23rd annual lecture, an organisation that exists to help British marketers, it's time I cleared up this blatant and recurring misinterpretation.

My study, built from Effie Worldwide award data & System1 creative testing, shows that media investment combined with creative quality (emotion, distinctiveness, showmanship) explains 60.1% of reported campaign Business Results. Spend enough, choose the right channels, make good ads, and campaign outcomes are within your control.

Sharp keeps putting my chart next to Joseph Korkarnes' (great but different) research showing ad sales elasticity is "close to zero" (ie it doesn't move sales much), and framing my findings as make-believe. These pieces of research don't contradict each other. They measure completely different things.

1. Read the chart title. This is a study on "campaign Business Results", not total business growth or sales. It never claimed to explain all of business performance. Multiple times now I've watched Sharp claim I'm saying ad spend and quality explain the majority of business growth. This is simply wrong.

2. Comparing owls to kangaroos. My research shows spend alone is a weak predictor of campaign success, because you might have terrible ads. That's the point. The elasticity research Sharp cited measures media spend alone. Adding creative quality to that model would be a genuinely useful academic contribution. If Byron's serious about evidence, that's the paper he should be pushing for.

3. Different time horizons. Elasticity studies measure same-period sales shifts, typically over weeks. The Creative Dividend measures campaign outcomes over years. Advertising compounds. Short-term spend elasticity being near zero is not evidence ads don't work. Everything on ESOV shows it's a law-like pattern when you zoom out.

Kockarnes's finding that spend-alone elasticity is close to zero is the reason creative quality research exists. If raw spend predicted results perfectly, creative quality wouldn't matter. The paper Sharp cited is part of the motivation for The Creative Dividend research. Why are we chronically pretending making good ads doesn't matter?

British brands are struggling. Own-label took majority grocery share for the first time this year. Brand Finance's top 250 British brands just lost 3% of value. Kantar BrandZ shows British brands now contribute less to total company valuation than global peers.

The last thing British marketers need is to be told effectiveness data can't be trusted and advertising doesn't work.

It was rather strange to sit in a lecture theatre, watching someone I respect clearly misinterpret my research and use it to mislead a room full of marketers.

Well-invested, well-planned, creative advertising reliably compounds to help brands grow.

content:
Stanley Tucci joins Birra Moretti in their new campaign

I can already smell marketers climbing on their high horse about this one. And I get why; research clearly shows celebs, in general, don't automatically lead to higher effectiveness.

But when a celeb is used as part of the strategy or creative idea to draw attention, increase fame, build emotion, and the right type of memories the brand wants to borrow, good things do happen.

So instead of assuming, I put this ad into System1 testing last night with hundreds of people, and the results are very clear.

1. It sits in the top 10% for predicted long-term effects because of how this manages to engage the public and leave them feeling great about the brand. I think it comes down to the simple but unique idea that beer marketing is losing its authenticity (other brands have really picked up on this recently), and how comically on-the-nose Tucci is for the brand. And to be fair, truthful insight that he very much embodies: don't let life get in the way.

2. If you work in booze or even marketing, you're probably itching to comment on the "lack of authenticity" of this "Italian" brand. But it's very clear, consumers do not feel this. This is really well loved. Especially with men, and 18-54yo, where this actually lands a 5-star. Any negative reaction to the ad (and there's very little) is from beer rejectors. Consumers love this sort of Foreign Consumer Culture Positioning (FCCP - Google it!) in beer. There's bubbling pushback against this sort of brand strategy, sure, but it has not gone mass public yet.

3. It builds all the right positive memories for the brand. Stuff that will build salience: "beer", "lager", "refreshing", "together". As well as what makes the brand relatively different: "outdoors", "italian", "quality". All seen as highly positive.

In summary, our testing shows this has been a massive first success. People like the pairing, the idea and the execution. And the strategy looks to be coherent with what the brand has stood for over time. Congrats to Lucky Generals, quickly becoming the go-to agency and understanding how the Brits view culture and tying that to what a brand stands for.

content:
Instagram claims your feed is still somewhat in a chronological order 👀👋📌🎙️ 

Adam Mosseri has a new series breaking down why Instagram ranks content and how the ranking actually works. Here's a summary of the key points in his latest video:

Why does Instagram rank content?

→ Ranking is about making the most of users' time and helping them find what they're interested in more easily. For creators, it's about increasing the size of the pie with more reach to go around overall, since content is served to an audience that actually wants to see it, rather than being shown to everyone.

→ “A bunch of things are true": if IG didn't rank content, the feed would get overrun by accounts that post most often, and businesses/brands post far more than creators and everyday people. IG would shift from a friend and creator-oriented platform to a more business, news, and publisher-oriented one, which Mosseri doesn't think fits IG's identity as a creative platform.

→ Without ranking, people see a lot less content overall, and average reach for creators drops significantly as the total pie shrinks.

📈How does Instagram rank content?

→ “People often say 'the algorithm'" but there isn't just one. There are many, each ranking different types of content differently. Broadly, there are two: one ranks content from accounts you follow, and one ranks content from accounts you don't.
IG makes an educated guess about your interests based on your historical behaviour on the platform, then predicts how likely you are to like, comment, send to a friend, or watch a video to the end — these actions act as proxies for interest.

→ Those predictions become a relevancy score for every post you could see, and posts are ordered by that score. Mosseri confirms that the recency of a post still matters a lot, which is why feeds are roughly, but not strictly, chronological.

→ Mosseri highlights that the existing systems aren’t perfect and that Instagram is constantly iterating on ranking but mentions how they give you tools to shape your own algorithm: Favourites, the Following feed, adjusting your interests, and more.

You can watch his video here: https://lnkd.in/eQ2ViGwt

If you feel like you’re struggling with reach because of the “algorithms” I thought now was a good time to reshare what helps reach on the platform AND what I think helps reach — tried, tested + iterated over the last few years on both my own accounts and client accounts 🙂‍↕️

content:
Nike Booted Out Of The S&P100

On 21st September Nike will no longer be in the list of mega businesses that occupy the S&P100 list

This is a really sad day.

It's a sobering reminder of how the mighty have fallen as Nike was one of the most loved and admired brands in the World, especially amongst marketers who try so hard to emulate them

There was no single reason for the fall which wiped over $200BILLION of their valuation and a decline in stock value of -76.5% over the past 5 years

The summary for me is actually a neglect of the 4 P's

 👟 Excessive Discounting

If you look at their margin in 2016 it stood over 46% and is now down around 40%. That points to a lot of discounting and in management reports they have admitted discounting heavily. The issue here is once you start its' very hard to come back from this.

 👟 Lost focus on Innovation

They seem to be losing the race for innovation which was exemplified when adidas won the battle for the first Sub 2hour Marathon. Nike dismantled the previous focus on sport (running, football etc) for more generalised categories.

 👟 Wholesale Neglect

It is well documented how Nike doubled down on a direct-to-consumer model and neglected their relationships with the wholesale trade. This left the door wide open for competitors to take space in store that Nike never won back.

 👟 Competitors turned up the heat

Just as all this was happening adidas raised their game with innovation and advertising, easily winning the World Cup this year for earned and paid. Then newer brands like ON did a brilliant job of stepping into culture and being super focussed by sporting tribe.

 👟 Brand OFF and Performance ON

The irony here is that Nike is perhaps THE poster child for brand building. Instead of doubling down on this advantage they turned on the performance drug and whilst they may have converted a lot of demand they stopped creating it.

So in essence they turned their back on the 4 P's

content:
Dyson trained AI on 450k+ dental images and put it inside a toothbrush with a camera that flosses for you

The launch campaign for it is impressive for 3 reasons

The $499 CameraJet is Dyson's first move into toothbrushes, with a really tiny lens that takes 28 pictures a second while you brush, detecting the gaps between your teeth within milliseconds to fire jets and floss for you.

The price tag and technology sound like a rather difficult step for consumers to understand, which I think has informed the launch campaign brilliantly.

1. Fluent Innovation. The comms in all channels have a simple message: it's a toothbrush that flosses for you, enabled by the innovation you are familiar with from James Dyson himself. The job of marketing here is to make this rather surprising innovation to feel as comfortable, familiar and obvious as possible.

2. Social Proofing. I've been HAMMERED with influencer ads in my feed for this over the past week. From the more obvious health and tech creators, to wider choices like fashion and food. In my research with System1 and Effie Worldwide the use of creators in a campaign massively drives brand effects. Showing people you are familiar with using the toothbrush makes choosing to use it far more appealing, without anyone really realising.

3. The ad asset used in the launch (below) manages to turn a rather techy announcement into a story, System1 tested it with hundreds of consumers and it's landed in the top 8% of Personal Appliance ads for emotion and predicted long-term brand effects. It's again managed to take a rather intense bit of new technology and use the narrative of how and why they did this to make it appealing to everyone. content:
Creativity in the age of AI

How ten human ideas found their way to Times Square

If you need some human positivity, this story delivers big. A few weeks ago, Kushagra Oberoi shared a brilliant ad idea for Parker Pen. It went viral, mainly because it highlighted the tension between the human thinking you can do with a great pen. Vs getting AI to do the thinking for you.

It caught the attention of creatives worldwide who wanted to get involved, so I worked with System1 and One Minute Briefs to challenge the creative community to share their ideas with one very simple but powerful brief: In the age of AI, #SellMeThisPen

Hundreds of ideas were shared. It then caught the attention of the Parker Pens team. We all worked together to select the ten winning ideas, and they've funded the work to put them in Times Square, New York.

This is creativity and bringing human creatives together at its very best. Showing the power of great ideas.

Here's the ten ads that got selected, and if you scroll to the end, you'll see Simon Sinclair and Manish Dodani's idea then scored highest in System1's consumer creative testing, which we predict will be the most effective.

A great lesson in something that a lot of effective advertising has in common: finding a shared tension and getting to a simple idea that dramatises it. And of course, no matter how good technology gets, there will always be a place for human creativity.

Congrats to all the creatives involved: George Smith, Ross Brodie, Mohammed Afri, Amruth Ganesh Achar, Sherice Jacob⚡️, Liam Biesty, Steve Wyatt, Paschalis Katsaitis, Ester Scattolini. And thanks to Nick Entwistle, Newell Brands and Megan Williams for supporting this.

content:
LinkedIn reach is reportedly down 47% year on year.
 
But as you all know... I am still more bullish on than I’ve ever been.
 
Because reach, audience and reputation are three different things.
 
Reach is how many people LinkedIn distributes your post to. That number will fluctuate as the platform, competition and feed change.
 
Your audience is the group of people who repeatedly recognise your name, ideas and expertise.
 
Your trust/reputation is what those people eventually believe about you.
 
We’ve spent years treating the first one as the main measure of success, partly because it’s the easiest to see. But the second and third are where most of LinkedIn’s value is created.
 
A post can receive fewer impressions and still reach the person who mentions you in a meeting three weeks later.
 
Someone can read ten of your posts without liking any of them, then contact you when they have the right problem.
 
A potential client can discover you through someone else’s comment, visit your profile and decide you understand their industry.
 
None of that fits neatly inside the performance of one post.
 
This doesn’t mean reach is irrelevant. You need distribution to build familiarity in the first place.
 
But a 40+% decline in average reach doesn’t necessarily mean LinkedIn has become less valuable. It makes relevance, recognition and reputation more important.
 
The opportunity on LinkedIn is still enormous. The people you want to work with are here, professionally identifiable and consuming ideas connected to their work.
 
The goal is to give them enough useful evidence to remember and trust you.
 
Reach is rented one post at a time. Reputation can keep working long after the post disappears from the feed.

content:
THE CRISIS IN AUTHENTICITY: We are entering Late Stage Influence

There's a reason this POV on influencers is going viral: it's true. And challenges where the creator industry must head next

stephen buranyi's latest long read on The Guardian is well worth the read but it basically nails where (food) creators came from, and what I refer to as Late Stage Influence really means. And how we've got there in some categories quicker than others.

- Social made it possible for anyone to become an influencer, without any qualifications, experience or even taste. To start with this was filled with credible people like Topjaw
- The influence is real. If you'd have asked Gordon Ramsay 10 years ago if he'd have welcomed influencers in with phone cameras to judge his food, he'd have told you where to shove it. Now, he's out making desserts on creators' foreheads. The right content can make a restaurant literally millions. It's honestly a really cost-effective form of reach if it goes well, with a post costing a brand anything from £300.
- Traditional media has felt it; one video alone can match the entire reach of print media in the UK. An industry where you'd go to Uni to study it, and spend years responsibly honing your craft.
- "While influencers’ audiences are continuing to grow, their relentless positivity and seemingly total lack of critical faculty has led to a viewer backlash that one influencer described to as a “crisis of authenticity”."
- The market is getting flooded, and the economics really don't stack up. Lots of creators are now starting to go back to day jobs.
- Consumers will eventually (if they haven't already) question the overly positive reviews of everything anyway.

The solution? Quite like most industries, yet marketing seems to try forget this: hire f****g experts. Proper planning teams with creator expertise.

I've spent years researching how creator content actually grows brands with System1, TikTok and WPP Media. The findings from our most recent study (https://lnkd.in/eUkFTuN8) are brutally simple:

- An authentic fit between the brand and the creator is crucial. Pay-to-play leaves a bad taste. We need expert agencies and teams to plan for this.
- Content execution (entertaining, emotional, well-branded content) explains most of the outcomes for a brand. We must work with quality creators who know what they are doing.
- Fame and follower count are important, but authenticity and creative quality are far more important. Aka size barely matters.

I believe we are entering Late Stage Influence. The boom has happened. The reach and opportunity are there, but now it's time for professionals to step in and credibly scale this industry.

content:
There are two types of slop right now.

1. Content slop (the one we all know)
Generic, fluffy content that uses lots of words to say very little.

2. Context slop
This is harder to spot because the content itself might be really good. Smart, well written and full of interesting insights. But the person posting has zero earned credibility on the topic.

This one is much more dangerous IMO...

If I suddenly shared a deep take on quantum computing, it might be a brilliant post. But what the f* do I know about quantum computing?

Of course, we should all explore new subjects. You don’t need a PhD to be curious.

But there’s a difference between sharing what you are learning and borrowing expertise you haven’t earned.

AI has made it easy for anyone to sound like an expert on anything. 

And that might be the more dangerous kind of slop.

content:
Bringing a campaign from the 1950s back to life

How Guinness keeps a legacy alive

Throughout the 1900s, John Gilroy created various iconic posters for Guinness. Including the famous "Guinness For Strength" girders and the brilliant exotic zoo posters featuring seals and a toucan with "My Goodness My Guinness" and "Lovely day for a Guinness".

Like everything the Guinness team at Diageo, breathing new life into this line with "Lovely Day For A Guinness" and now just "LoVely" is world-class stuff, alongside AMV BBDO.

Often the secrets to a brand's future are buried in the past.

But the strategy behind "Lovely Day for a Guinness" is smart, it focuses on building memories around lighter, daytime and summer occasions. It breaks Guinness out of the winter/Christmas pint it's become so known for.

The new, even simpler execution is now live across the UK, and Ireland works even harder outdoors. It's the same idea but executed perfectly for OOH which has less time to land the idea, so focusing on the beauty of the product after consumption with one killer word makes a lot of sense.

But this only works because consistency compounds creativity. Using the original line from the 1950s, the past few years of the new "Lovely Day For A Guinness", and their unique and famous harp that's been built over decades. This groundwork has allowed them to create something this simple in 2026.

It's obviously cracking work. Thanks Sonnie S. who sent this over because my "personal brand" (ie loving the Guinness brand, and pint) is so strong that this ad made them think of me!

content:
Timothy Taylor's rebrands logo with bearded hipster to target Gen Z

Reminding us that time is a marketer's best friend

As a Yorkshireman and marketer who's spent years researching consistency, I've finally managed to pull myself together enough to write this.

Timothy Taylor has gone from 8th to 1st biggest cask ale in the UK recently because no one's falling for "craft beer" or "Spanish" lager brewed in Tadcaster anymore, so they are returning to authentic cask ales. Brands with legacy, stories, location and history.

In fact, 25% of 18-24 year olds now drink cask ale. A 50% boom in a year.

So why is the gut reaction to rebrand and move away from the very thing driving the growth? Young drinkers are finally rediscovering cask ale, why does a 170 year old brewery need a newer font? Why must the Landlord look like he's now taken GLP-1?

The redesigns look fine, but they might find they've tidied up the very thing driving growth. If there's cash to spend, why not dramatise the brand's quirky old Yorkshire routes instead? Invest in telling the stories that already exist?

In my 'Compound Creativity' research with System1 and the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) we found change must come in the face of hard data showing year on year brand decline. Gen Z pouring into a brand is the opposite.

My column this week, I share the history of this titan of brand, a damning new review from The Telegraph on the change, but uncover some gold hidden in one of the quotes from an angry Taylor's fan that reveals time and consistency really are a marketer's best friend: https://lnkd.in/eXht67Tf

content:
I was informed yesterday, by someone who is paid for their marketing knowledge, that “the role of promotion is to make people fall in love with the brand.”

Now I thought that this kind of wishful, woeful thinking had been safely contained within the pages of “Love Marks” – a book that almost nobody owns and even fewer people ever open. But alas it seems that somebody opened their copy of that bastard book and allowed this cursed idea back out into the world.

There is not a single brand in my house, garage or life that I wouldn’t consider replacing if I needed to buy again. Some are stickier, but not because I love them, more because I’m somehow locked into the system. Switching out of Hasselblad would leave me with expensive lenses that no longer had a home on a camera, but hey I switched out of Sony & Canon & Leica. My phone? Nah. My car? I hop between marques. My ketchup? I have a preference, but if they’re out I wouldn’t go into mourning.

And I’m not strange (in this regard) – people aren’t in love with brands that they buy daily. They don’t have the depth of feeling, loyalty and chemical attachment to brands that marketing people think that they do.

Sure, 20 years ago about 0.0000001% of Nike fans had the brand tattoo’d on their legs. Even they bought and used other brands. 

We simply aren’t in love with brands. Nor should we be. We have preferences. We have (limited) loyalties. We even have favourites. 

But “love”? 

C’mon now – it’s that kind of hyperbole that led to people thinking that bleach should have an app full of games, that people would watch a Geico sitcom and that nobody would ever switch out of BlackBerry.

Get a grip, now.

content:
I’m shooting a series of pictures at the moment, tentatively titled “after the thrill has gone”

It’s an exploration of whether desire can survive domesticity. 

I’m looking at how the things that used to push buttons grow wearisome when the ironing is 
 in your eyeline. Think kink in the kitchen, puck-boy romance novels as you unblock the shower, chastity when you’re already in separate rooms.

In truth it’s a project that’s bigger than I am, I don’t really have the skill level to pull it off – but that’s not the point. The point is that I’m trying to make something. And I’m building a little community as I do it. Getting to know people, getting invited into their projects, finding new venues and new people inside of them.

Almost everyone I know outside of work is busy working on something. They’re writing and staging plays or variety shows, they’re scoring movies, they’re organizing strip karaoke or bringing art and science together for a show on stage. They’re designing clothes or booking DJs and acts. They’re getting together to rhinestone costumes, or to walk with other men who need space before they can talk. I’m lucky to know so many beautiful communities.

Almost everyone I know who's still working in an agency is too exhausted to do anything outside of work. They work late, often in isolation. They feel the weight of deadlines upon them every minute of every day, and bristle at how little time they have after meeting about the work that needs to be done, to do it. 

They walked into their agency years ago with a lifetime of experience in their pocket and have had it wrung out of them by unrealistic demands on time and unambitious demands of the work.

They are dry sponges. 

And I get it. But I hate it. 

I hate seeing beautiful, brilliant, quirky minds robbed of input and stimulus and inspiration. Robbed of the time to read or write or sculpt.  I hate seeing people zooming in from the same seat, in the same box room, in the same apartment every day. 

The answer is simple. But impossible. Go out. Drum. Paint. Dance. Strike a pose. Write some code. Serve some soup. 
Impossible I know. But do it anyway. You are what you do. Do interesting things. Do them often. Do. Do. Do.

$1BILLION IN UNDER 200 DAYS

Yesterday's announcement is significant news for anyone with a media budget

It's a very large number for a brand new media channel. To put that in context it is almost as much as the UK largest commercial TV network gets per annum in ad spend.

But it's also a very small number as it represents only 0.4% of global Ad spend on Google search which just highlights the scale of opportunity that exists

Here are a few thoughts 

 🚀  Speed of adoption - ChatGPT is still less than 4 years old and yet in 200 days has built enough trust with advertisers to commit to an annualised $1billion. This is effectively a proof of concept that signals potential.

 🚀  OpenAI are listening - Last year we saw a very traditional Ad campaign (TV and OOH) using very human led creative work. They understand the consumer audience and now this suggests they understand the advertising one too.

 🚀  Media at the point of decision making - People are using AI to make decisions on a level not seen before and this provides advertisers with a chance to influence that decision like never before.

 🚀  Earned and Paid unite - One of the biggest changes in marketing over the past couple of years has been to gain share of digital search organically. That can now be perfectly complemented by paid spend.

It's worth noting that the ability to advertise on ChatGPT is still being rolled out across the world so there is more supply becoming available

Will ChatGPT spend be incremental OR are we seeing spend being switched from other media and if so who will lose out?

Everyone told me fundraising would be brutal. For me it was the part I loved.

I get why that might sound unusual. So let me explain

I did stand-up comedy for 18 months so getting in front of a room and holding attention.. that part never scared me.

Pitching has always felt very natural.

Connectd has now raised $23M. A lot of that came down to figuring out early that my pitching style didn’t have to look like everyone else's. 

Some investors weren't for it but the right ones absolutely were.

Two things I made non-negotiable going into every pitch:

- Knowing my numbers 100% - this gives you huge confidence

- Being honest with what I didn’t know. People can tell when you’re bluffing

You're not trying to impress every investor in the room. 

You want to find the right ones.

When you remember it’s a two way street and that it has to work for YOU as well, it feels a lot less brutal.

- Arianna Huffington launched HuffPost aged 55

If you spending the long weekend trying to decide whether to take the jump, then just do it. 

Age is just a number

Dolly Parton’s death hit a lot of people harder than they expected.

People whose Dolly interactions may have been little more than tapping along to “9 to 5” in the car found themselves weirdly affected by her death.

It happens.

Dolly Parton was one of the last things that America had in common. Everyone had an opinion on Dolly, and it was the same one. She was warm and human, generous and open, funny and forgiving – a good soul with a huge heart. Pretty much the embodiment of the America that people want to live in.

There aren’t many of those kinds of icons out there. Who’s left as a beacon of all that a nation hopes to be? There was Dolly and there was Oprah (maybe) and that’s about it.

So, it was no surprise that lots of that sentiment leaked out across people’s social feeds – as they looked to share the news, share the loss and connect with others who had been surprised at just what a gut punch this was. So deep was the feeling that it even reached LinkedIn, giving us a brief respite from the “humbled and proud” and “ain’t Jaguar shit” posts designed to feed the algorithm; replacing them with simple, honest, human posts mourning the loss of a very human icon.

Enter cos-play curmudgeon Mark Ritson

Mark Ritson was not happy that people weren’t using LinkedIn in the way that he believed it should be used.

8 out of 10 people don’t believe brands when they explain why they used AI.

New research shows consumers think businesses did it because it was easier or cheaper, no matter what you tell them. 

A new academic paper tested what happens when brands disclose AI use in ads. They tried different explanations to try convince people, like “We used AI to personalise this for you.”, “...to reduce environmental impact" or "to improve the experience" etc.

The finding is brutal. No matter what was claimed, people still assumed the same thing: the company used AI because it helped the company. Not the consumer or society.

In one study, 90%ish of people thought the main winner from AI use was the brand itself, regardless of what the disclosure actually said.

Marketers are still trying to force AI claims into ads and brand positioning.

No one cares or believes you.

AI has now become table stakes; we assume every business is using it. We must move on to proper positioning that creates relative difference around what customers care about.

If AI is used to achieve that, I'm not sure there's any benefit in even mentioning it. This is just classic marketing training: lead with the customer benefit, ideally emotional. Not functional stuff about how you achieved it.

I’ve looked at easily 20,000 LinkedIn posts over the last 5 years.

Most flopped posts are actually well-written. The grammar is clean, the structure makes sense, and they were published at the 'optimal' time on a Tuesday morning.

The issue is they make the reader feel absolutely nothing.

You read the post, nod politely, and forget it existed two seconds later.

Now that AI can generate infinite informational posts on demand, generic tips have almost zero commercial value. What actually stops the scroll and builds authority is an emotional reaction.

Shaan Puri framed this better than anyone with the 7 emotions:
1) LOL (makes you laugh or smile)
2) OHHH (connects dots you hadn't seen)
3) WOW (mind-blowing achievement or stat)
4) AWW (genuine warmth or vulnerability)
5) YAY (celebrating a shared win)
6) WTF (calling out industry absurdities)
7) FINALLY (saying what everyone was privately thinking)

Every good post (usually) hits at least one of these.

I did a full breakdown of how to use this framework in Issue #5 of my newsletter.

author.name: Matthew Kilgour
author.headline: Officially puts the rat in creative strategy for b2b brands (c)

content:
An incredible example of defeating Marketing Myopia, a key marketing principle of the last century

Excellent work from everyone involved

Marketing myopia is on the syllabus of every decent MBA for a reason. If you work in business, you need to understand it.

Theodore Levitt first introduced it in a now-iconic 1960 Harvard Business Review article. It's when a company defines its business by its products rather than the customer needs it satisfies. A failure of strategic vision.

The company looks inward at its own production capabilities instead of outward at the always changing market. That's why Mark Ritson calls the solution 'market orientation': look at your business through the customer's eyes. Not from your desk. 

A more popular modern term has arrived though: salience, to look at how a brand occupies space in a consumer's mind. Brand salience is the degree to which a brand is thought of when a customer is making a decision. It is about being top-of-mind in specific buying situations.

It comes from 'salire', the Latin verb 'to leap'. So when a brand leaps to mind in the right occasion via a category entry point.

Haagen-dazs stopped seeing itself like an ice cream and realised what else it's actually competing with: pints. Connecting with friends. A night in over a moment. Seems simple AF but look at the rest of the category that just advertise like ice cream.

The campaign's going so well in Canada that Stella Artois are now doing reactive ads back at them.

Lovely work, dramatising the moment you're replacing. A brief that would surely work for any brand.

Nestlé Courage AB InBev Labatt Breweries of Canada Harvard Business Review

content:
This is BANG ON from Jamie Laing: the power of audio in marketing is undeniable

I've been researching this for years. As our world gets more (visually) cluttered, one simple human insight holds true: you can close your eyes, but you can't close your ears.

There's also a lot more nerdier science about how the brain processes audio, which means we recall the audio of ads more than the visuals (see: ITV's "Earning Attention" research).

And the nerdier media stuff: audio media channels are usually hugely broad in reach, high-attention, trust-building, and capable of emotional storytelling (like TV), but usually at a 5th of the price per reach (literally radio!).

I did new research on this that I launched with Mark Ritson at Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity this year, using wonderful Effie Worldwide data. It's not just mine or Jamie's opinion; the research showed:

1. Audio distinctive brand assets are generally the most powerful for getting brand recognition in advertising. Even on TikTok, they work without causing skips.

2. Global campaigns that include audio in their media mix report profit growth +75% of the time. Which only increases the larger the campaign is (audio works harder through mass scale!)

3. Emotional campaigns report DOUBLE the profit outcomes if they use audio, putting an emotional idea into audio works wonders.

Marketers are finally waking up to the power of audio, and it makes me very happy.

content:
Most leaders treat LinkedIn like a slot machine. 

(post something, hope it hits, repeat)

Then they wonder why they have 20K impressions and zero pipeline.

The problem is almost never effort. It's that every post is trying to do the same thing. Or worse, trying to do everything at once.

The founders, executives, and leaders I see turning content into real commercial pipeline have something different. They don't just have a posting habit. They have an architecture. 

Every post has a specific job, and those jobs are usually distinct.

Here's how I think about it:
1) Point-of-view posts. These are your top-of-funnel engine. A sharp take on something your industry is getting wrong, a trend you see forming, a belief you hold that others don't. These pull in relevant strangers. Timely newsy reactions + insights tend to work here as well. 

2) Operational insight posts. These speak directly to the person who has budget and a problem right now. You are describing the specific pain they are sitting with, and you are showing them you understand it at a level that makes them think "this person gets our situation." These don't go viral. They don't need to. They need to land with 50 of the right decision-makers.

3) Proof posts. Client outcomes, before and afters, the specific result that happened and why. These exist to de-risk the conversation. By the time someone reaches out, they have already seen evidence that you've done this before. The selling happened before the conversation even started.

Most people I talk to are stuck on type 1. They are building visibility but not converting it, because there's nothing in the system that bridges attention to trust to action. Or they jump straight to type 3, posting case studies to an audience that doesn't know them yet, and wondering why nobody engages.

The system is what connects them. Point of view builds the room. Operational insight earns the nod. Proof closes the gap.

This is the core of what we build at Shake Content. Not more content. Better architecture.

content:
Viktor gave me back 6 hours this week.

I gave him three jobs. By Friday, I started to get the whole "AI employee" thing.

We already use plenty of AI tools. Everyone has something that writes, researches or summarises when you ask it to.

And for the first couple of days, that's basically how I used Viktor too. I'd ask him for something, get an answer, move on.

I wasn't particularly impressed. Then I started giving him actual jobs.

The thing nobody tells you about AI at work: the real value isn't the writing.

For me, it's all the stuff around it. The admin, the prep, the things I'm not great at.
I do strategy, storytelling, video, founder positioning. That's what I'm good at. Inbox management, meeting prep, prospect research... that's the stuff that piles up while I'm doing the actual work.

So here's what Viktor does for me now:

Every morning, he sends me a brief with cultural moments, conversations and ideas I can turn into a timely LinkedIn post or meme.

For sales, I give him a prospect and get back the research I'd normally spend an hour pulling together myself. What they're posting, how often, what's working, where we might have an interesting angle, plus relevant Shake work we can reference.

Then there's the admin. Inbox triage and draft replies, meeting prep based on who I'm speaking to and our previous conversations, and turning call transcripts into notes and actions.

And it's already spreading beyond me. Our content strategy team handed him the research: what a client's industry is arguing about this week, what their competitors are posting. They now start a strategy session with a full picture instead of 20 open tabs.

None of this sounds huge on its own. Together, it saved me 6 hours this week.

That's time I spent with clients, being creative and doing sales. The parts of my job I actually want to be doing.

I'm not technical at all either. Setting Viktor up was basically just chatting to him in Slack. I told him what I needed and went from there.

If you can send a Slack message, you can use Viktor.

And that's where the "AI employee" framing started to make sense to me.

A chatbot waits for you to explain everything again. Viktor already has the context.

One needs a prompt. The other already knows the brief.

Hire viktor.com for your team.

content:
“I think my biggest problem is being young and beautiful. It's my biggest problem because I've never been young and beautiful. Oh, I've been beautiful. And God knows I've been young, but never the twain have met. Not so as anyone would notice anyway.”

I love Torch Song Trilogy. To a ridiculous extent. 

It has a way of disguising wisdom as wit that I love. 
And the bathos. Bathos has always been my dramatic device of preference. 

Where am I going with this? I don’t know. It’s late. Dolly is dead. I’ve just wept my way through the final of The Piano & I think I’m in love with Mika (and Alice Sarah Ott’s trousers)

I wanted to talk about the idea that “We are more emotionally literate than we have ever been, whilst also being more practically fragile.” Torch Song would have been a good way into that and the points I have to make sound smart at least.

But it feels forced tonight. It’s late. I’m awake. Dolly is dead and I want to think about art and beauty. I want to write about the poetry and the passion and community that I was lucky enough to be a part of at two weddings this year – remarkable occasions that made me so acutely aware of the cost of a life moving from place to place that I just wanted to plant myself to the spot and never move.  I want to write about Dolly’s skill with a murder ballad, about Radio City Music Hall, about plans with friends who have long slipped through the cracks of a million moves to do Christmas at Dollywood. 

I have so much to share. But I can’t find the words. Or the platform. I look at LinkedIn and what it does to all of us. A hungry algorithm that is not a fussy eater consuming even the best we know. Which makes me want to share nothing, nothing that matters anyway. 

Why keep eyeballs on a platform that gives so little in return? I want to be angry. But Dolly is dead and the people still writing about Jaguar are not. 

I have nothing to say.

content:
Founders don't really do holidays

"Can't you just put your out-of-office on and tell everyone you are off"

I heard that a lot

But the reality of being a founder vs an employee when it comes to taking a break is huge

I didn't really appreciate it until now

I have accounts to sign off, invoices to chase, things to buy as August is year end.

I have customers waiting on proposals to get signed off. No proposal means no money.

I have unexpected things going wrong that I need to address quickly.

I have a daily Linkedin post to write and messages to respond too.

I have the constant pressure of knowing I have salaries to pay, VAT and tax.

Then add in the fact I do my best thinking when I start to relax and need to write it all down before I forget it

With all that said ...

When I took a week off just before The Calling my daughter Lilia said to me on the last day 

"Daddy you never jumped in the pool once"

So this time I did. Every single Day.

I also swam up to 200 lengths every day to win the battle against the late night Ouzo

I am not saying I have the answers. Far from it. I am just saying I now empathise with all the Founders who spend their holiday working. I get it.

For me the antidote was jumping in that pool.

I am grateful I have a thriving business, a wonderful team and can spend a couple of weeks in a beautiful place spending time with the family (and keeping the business afloat)

This is for every Founder out there. I see you.

content:
Why did it take so long for System1 to launch AI ad testing?

I had a daunting task when I stepped up to be our Chief Growth Officer. We've been testing advertising for over 20 years, a lot of AI ad testing tools had popped up and people wanted to see if we were joining the party.

The issue is: there's a lot of not-great AI options out there. It's a crucial time for the industry, so getting this right matters.

There are generally 2 types of AI creative testing. There's Improv AI (calling it this simply to wind up a few people) is plugged into large language models, you ask it to pretend to be a human, it says yes a lot. It changes its mind if you re-prompt it with the same ad. You can't really interrogate the data or know where it's come from.

The second type is 'Method AI', a model trained to predict a large historical dataset. We went with this type because we didn't want to launch what would effectively be a random electric bingo machine. And we've measured our wonderful Star Rating 120k+ times and know it explains brand growth.

Every prediction model produces a probability. Like the weather forecast, you don't know it will rain at 4:12pm. But you know if you should probably bring an umbrella. Somewhere along the way AI creative testing ignored all this and decided to provide long lists of exact metrics. "4.2% feeling inspirational", "78/100", etc. But the wildest part is that every AI creative testing tool on the market will always give you an answer, despite certainty wildly varying across ads. If an ad is too unique vs what's happened in the past, the model won't be able to predict it. This is how AI works.

So we had to figure it all out again to get to somewhere we were happy with. 4 years ago we published a study with Warwick University to understand how to predict human emotion with AI, and now we launch Test Your Ad Screen. It provides predicted bands for our core metrics, matching human metrics 9 out of 10 times. All trained on the most representative ad dataset available: almost every UK and US TV ad launched over the past 5+ years.

And when Test Your Ad Screen isn't confident, it will not give you a Star Rating, and we won't charge you. How refreshingly honest.

For now, we've launched this for long-form assets meant for the UK and US. More to come shortly; check it out here: https://lnkd.in/e3Eh3sys

Congrats to everyone who worked on this - big step.

Why the US mindset beats the UK one

When Najoh Tita-Reid started explaining that one of her greatest challenges was the UK mindset I was obviously going to pay attention

content:
The ad that got me fired from The Young Apprentice 15 years ago

It was a simple task: make up a hair product and a TV ad to launch it.

Then a couple people were asked which they thought was better, leading to Lord Sugar pointing the finger and firing me in front of 4 million people.

The issue is, decades of marketing research has shown us that this is a terrible way to judge advertising. There's even research showing marketers select winning ad campaigns only 50% of the time.

So I went back and tested this ad against the competition, with System1's modern emotion-first ad testing tools. My team's ad was the standout winner. Me and my sweet teenage combover were robbed.

Yes, it may be the pettiest thing I've ever done, holding a 15-year-grudge. But it teaches us a valuable marketing lesson: the customer is always wrong. We can't trust people's rational thoughts to make marketing decisions.

content:
The brief that made Coca-Cola billions

Their century-old bottle design

Most of modern marketing is busy work. Changing things. Decks. Fighting procurement. Convincing others.

Rory Sutherland  shares a lot of sage advice from his decades of experience but the best is: "Most of the value you create will come from just one or two decisions in your career."

Be it finding that insight. Creating that tagline. Launching that one new product. Or deciding the bottle of your product needs to be your most distinct asset. 

I'd argue that the real hard work and billions of value has been keeping the bottle the same shape for over a century. In my research with Effie Worldwide and System1 , we found the most consistent brands report 4 times the Return on Investment.

Marketing often isn't about doing more, it's about doing less for longer.

People love to call your dedication "luck" when they didn't see the sacrifice. 

When you finally break through, get the promotion, or land the massive contract, critics will call it good timing. They’ll say you were in the right place at the right time.

What they don't see is the "luck" you built in the dark:

The late nights honing your craft while everyone else was sleeping.

The weekend hours invested in learning while others were checking out.

The endless rejections you absorbed before getting a single "yes."

Luck happens when relentless preparation meets opportunity.

If you aren't in the room doing the work, the opportunity passes right over you. You don't get lucky by accident, you make yourself luck-prone through consistency, discipline and grit.

Let them call it luck. Just keep turning on the light and doing the work.

The harder you work, the luckier you get.

content:
You can't explore a new frontier with an old map. 

We've both been at this long enough to know the trap of an old map, 

You launch a new product, land some new customers and win a few quarters.

Then something subtle happens.

You start assuming the growth will just continue.

It won’t.

The map that got you there is useless for where you're going next.

In our latest episode of Uncensored Renegades, we unpack what it actually takes to stay grounded when success is pulling you off balance.

Here's what we learned:

EVOLVE OR DIE
The average lifespan of an S&P 500 company has fallen from 61 years in 1958 to under 20 today. The companies that last are the ones built to question everything, including themselves.

PLAY TO WIN, NOT TO NOT LOSE
When the stakes rise, most teams go defensive. They protect, they preserve, and then they shrink. The ones who keep growing stay on offense.

INCREMENTAL PROGRESS OVER LOFTY VISIONS
Big, lofty goals fizzle fast. Small, steady, compounding improvements build momentum that no single grand endeavor ever will.

The biggest takeaway?

When you reach the top of the mountain, you find yourself at the bottom of the next mountain. And the next mountain is taller, steeper, and more technical to climb. The ones who make it aren't the ones holding on to the past. They're the ones who let go of what no longer serves them so they can make space for what they need next.

That's staying grounded.

CAN YOU FACE THE TRUTH?

Have you ever been in a situation when you knew you had to say the truth but also knew it was going to be unpopular?

In the latest episode of Uncensored Renegades Kory Marchisotto and I talk about the importance of staying grounded as a leader especially when things are going well

Having been in a few high growth roles in my career I have discovered that telling the truth about your situation becomes even more important when things are going well

That’s because often complacency has started to set in and the team start assuming growth will happen automatically 

They are the precise moments when honesty really matters

But it can feel really hard

Why are you criticising a team that’s doing so well?

Teams that are truly high performing know how to give each other honest feedback even when things are going well and that’s precisely what keeps them performance high

The more successful you are the harder it becomes to maintain that level

It reminds me of something Eddie Jones, the former England Rugby, said to me

“Be touch in victory and gentle in defeat”

He set the record for the most number of consecutive England victories and knew that success depended on being self critical even when the team had won easily.

content:
When did Creative Reviews become firing squads?

When did they switch from being the Creative Dept sharing the work that they wanted the account team to sell, to a free for all where every person and their dog not only gets to have an opinion on the work but also to dictate changes that they want to see in the work?

And why do we let it happen?

“I’m not sure about black as a background”, “I’d change the headline to this”, “I think that we need x, y & z in the body copy”, “The client doesn’t like... , “I think we need to merge options 2 and 3”, “maybe we could bullet point that?”

Not your call Nigel. 

You can raise a red flag if you truly believe that something in the idea of the execution is fundamentally wrong (“no the client isn’t going to produce a special run of a billion mauve Coke cans to support this tactical promotion”, “we genuinely don’t have the budget or the ability to get Trump, Biden, Taylor Swift and Blake Lively into this direct mailer campaign”) but you don’t get to nit-pick copy or suggest creative.

But there are no "small changes" - everything dilutes. Small changes kill big ideas. And they’re always suggested by someone who is afraid that the client might not like the undiluted idea – who believes in homeopathic ideas, the weaker the better. Who thinks that a good idea is one that won't raise so much as an eyebrow in the meeting. Who believes that they could write the ads, given the chance.

I blame that enduring platitude “everyone is creative, ideas can come from anywhere.” 

Everyone is and every idea can, but advertising ideas tend to come from advertising creative departments. You may be a wizard at cross stitching. A genius at designing crosswords. You may hand make pewter crosses for Jesus to die on for your etsy store. All creative. It doesn’t make you an expert in selling 4 ply toilet tissue to households with more than three bathrooms.

The place for input and influence from the account team isn’t in the creative review. That review is there for you to see the work that the creative wants to present, so that you can figure out how best to support selling it.

The place for input and influence is in the conversations, the debates, the messy scribbles stage of the process. In the moments where the teams are looking at ways in, looking for opinions, looking for support, looking for information, looking for options on where they can take the work.

Those are the conversations that matter. And if you’re not in them – it’s because the teams don’t really think that your voice is one that’s going to help them find the way. Which also means that it’s a voice that’s going to grate in the creative review.

So just remember. Absolute red flags, raise a hand. Brilliant idea on how to sell the work, raise a hand. Burning desire to re-write the headline into something that you think the person three levels below the ultimate buyer will approve, do pipe down Trevor.

And there's no better training than the MiniMBA with Mark Ritson

After leaving medical school to pursue marketing, I was totally shocked that 80% of the marketers I worked with had never done any training. We ended up just doing what the last person had done and repeating processes. Not challenging or experimenting.

I don't think it's for everyone, though. To get the most out of it, you need to set aside time to read the core material. This isn't a paid endorsement; I had to fork out the cash to do it myself! I just think the industry will be better when the majority of marketers have done some training. This is the most accessible, modern course that covers most of what we need to know to do our jobs properly.

There is a difference between being a great founder vs. being a great boss.

I learned it the hard way in my first company.

A great founder prioritises traction over anything else
→ Scrappy, obsessive, data-driven and moves quickly.

A great boss creates an environment where their team can do their best work. 
→ They read the room. They give honest feedback. They allow people to learn for themselves.

Whether you like it or not, there’s a difference. 

The challenge of ‘stepping back’ and allowing others to do the jobs you once did as a founder can be tough. But as I learned early on, hiring people who are better than you is a blow to the ego but the best thing for the business 😉

My goal is to be a great founder AND a great boss. 

If you’re lucky, you’ll find the people that want to build with you.

Talent gets you hired but being a great human keeps you in demand. 

Skills can be trained. Systems can be taught. 

Technical gaps can be filled. But attitude, integrity, and energy are completely on you.

The colleagues who thrive long-term aren't always the smartest in the room, they're the ones who bring value without bringing drama:

They take ownership instead of passing the blame.

They listen to understand, not just to reply.

They bring solutions to the table, not just complaints.

They make hard projects feel manageable and good wins feel celebrated.

When you become reliable, empathetic, and easy to collaborate with, opportunities stop being something you hunt for. They naturally find you through the people who loved working with you in the past.

Your technical skills are your resume. Your character is your reputation.

Make sure your reputation speaks louder than your credentials.

content:
Why I was fired from The Apprentice at 15, with a key lesson for all marketers: the customer is always wrong

There are a few silly marketing hills I will die on, but none cost me more than this one. Getting fired in front of 4 million people before I'd even left college.

In my column this week, I open the old hurt locker and have a good old rummage round to share a very important marketing lesson.

Your customers are lazy liars who can't be trusted.

Claimed rational data has no bearing on what humans do, have done, or will ever do. We aren't even aware of how our feelings warp our thoughts and memories. Your customers are no exception.

Basing marketing decisions on this sort of data will not end well.

Instead, we should rely on what Daniel Kahneman won a Nobel Prize for. Understanding that our implicit, subconscious feelings influence 95% of our actions without us even realising.

I learned this the hard way 15 years ago on BBC's The Young Apprentice. We were competing to make the best ad, a couple of customers were asked which they thought was the best. They rationally thought mine was terrible, and I got the public finger from Lord Sugar himself.

I have dug out the ads and tested them with modern System1 creative testing. My ad won by a country mile. I was robbed.

You can avoid this mistake too by remembering one simple marketing truth. The customer is always wrong. Read it free here: https://lnkd.in/eRSDAG9m

content:
It’s Wednesday morning. 

After a day’s respite from the summer’s relentless heat the sun is back, already fighting to get through the blackout curtains that I mistakenly believed would allow me to sleep.

Everything in me says “head for river, drink in the last of this heat, swim naked in the fast moving water, share a picnic with a stranger, nourish yourself on the company of others who see the sun and feel the draw to be outdoors.”

But I can’t walk.

Literally.

Something has happened to my back that causes it to spasm and my left leg to give way every five steps or so. 

And so instead of heading for the quiet hedonism of a morning doing nothing I head for the doctor and the chiropractor and then the physiotherapist in a bid to find some relief.

The not being able to walk is a new thing. But the needing an army of people to keep me on track, to keep me moving, to keep me alive, is not. 

I guess I've played the ad game for too long and ignored the fact that it's designed to suck the marrow out of youthful bones and spit what's left into the trash.

It's not an industry built for long term careers.
Consequently, if you stay long enough, you will end up fucked.

The impossible hours, the manufactured stress, the pressure to stay a little later, the request to cancel that vacation, or come back from vacation early, or at least to take the call, be back for the pitch, answer the e-mail, some e-mails, all of the requests, the deck that needs to be finished today, the slack that needs to be picked up, the urgency of everything – well it will get to you.

For a lot of people I know the price was substance abuse. For others a cycle of burn-out, return, repeat. And advertising agency demands have killed more relationships than Google search histories.

And we don’t learn. I don’t anyway. I scorched my adrenal system and didn’t learn. I ran meetings from a chair in chemo and asked for faster infusion rates so that I could be back in the agency for a 4pm that was “crucial” - and didn't learn.  I’m still taking part in meetings and workshops that start at 3am for me, and the team knows that if they put in an 11pm meeting – I will be there. I never learn.

I fly too much. Swiss just congratulated me on making their top 10% in terms of mileage covered. I felt sick. I am sick. At times this job has literally threatened to kill me.

So yeah, it’s Wednesday. The sun is shining. A glittering river full of friendly nude bodies beckons and I’m in bed, working - because I can’t walk. Unable to walk, because I'm always working.

Be careful out there.

LinkedIn is changing how comments are ranked.

Instead of everyone seeing the same replies at the top of a post, LinkedIn is now personalizing comment ranking for each user. 

(I guess they are using signals like your professional interests, your connections, and your past engagement to decide which comments show up first for you).

This means 2 people can open the same post and see completely different conversations. Pretty cool  😎 

The comment that's most relevant to a marketing director in London won't be the same one surfaced to a founder in New York.

On top of that, LinkedIn is also starting to surface comment threads directly in the feed. So you might see a conversation without ever clicking into the original post.

It also gives good comments far more potential reach. A thoughtful reply may no longer depend entirely on someone finding the original post. LinkedIn can bring that conversation to them.
 
You can see why they are investing here. Time spent reading comments has increased 18% year on year, while overall content consumption is up 10%. Of course, this only works if the comments are worth reading. LinkedIn is making these changes while also trying to reduce engagement pods, automated replies and the endless stream of AI-generated agreement.
 
I like the direction. Some of the most useful ideas/insights already live in the comments. Now LinkedIn is starting to treat them as content in their own right.
 
I have been saying this for a whileeee: what you contribute to other people’s conversations may soon be almost as visible as what you publish yourself.

content:
After a decade, the Dolmio family returns. The undeniable effectiveness force of brand characters marches on.

Mars are doubling their marketing investment in Dolmio as the brand turns 40 this week, and bringing back some of my favorite brand characters: the Dolmio family. Alongside their iconic tagline.

This should get every marketing nerd hot under the collar. Here's why.

Brand Characters are having a real moment in global marketing, as more and more realise how much they really pay back. In my research with System1 and Effie Worldwide, we found that campaigns that use brand characters are 2x more likely to report profit growth or share gain compared to campaigns that don't. Or campaigns that use a celeb. Ouch. 

We are seeing a resurgence of brands reaching for their hard-working, well-loved, growth-driving brand characters. Pillsbury Doughboy's recent return in the States drove a +13% jump in cookie sales. And new brands are getting involved, with Crocs launching their first brand character (a 6-foot croc).

With Dolmio's mega multi-million investment putting the characters across OOH, TV and social, all the research points to good things now happening. But it's worth considering why...

1) Unlike how celebs are usually used, characters force you to be consistent. Finding new and interesting ways to build the same associations and memories for your brand. Because of this and a character's ability to create a unique personality for a brand, according to the Effie data, you're +50% more likely to report differentiation gains by using a brand character.

2) They help you put on a show, key for advertising to create a lasting impact with non-buyers. Ads with brand characters are, on average, 26% more emotional.

3) They omni-brand your advertising. When your characters are on screen, the idea is branded. Unlike other DBAs that are fleeting in their fluent attention. You're 3x (!!) more likely to report distinctiveness gains by using a brand character.

I spotted this 3D steaming billboard in Shepherd's Bush yesterday; thanks for sharing some of the details Aman Matharu. This is marketing using everything we know to stack the odds in your favour. I love it.

I share #advertising and #marketing insights daily, follow for more. For full data, go check out "The Creative Dividend" free online by System1 and Effie.

content:
I grew up in a seaside town in the shadow of a steel mill; the blast furnaces providing the backdrop to every donkey ride and yellow top ice-cream.

A mile out of town were the chemical plants, miles from end to end, dominated by huge cooling towers belching water vapour into the sky. As a small kid I was convinced that that’s where clouds came from.

My accent was as thick as the wet sand beneath the soon to collapse pier and the expectation was that British Steel, ICI chemicals and the industries that supplied them would provide us with jobs that would allow us to buy houses, raise families and buy season tickets for The Boro.

It wasn’t just the expectation, it felt like the only option. I didn’t see people who looked like me, sounded like me or came from places like me outside of the documentaries that occasionally popped up on the BBC, or on repeats of The Likely Lads.

Beyond the furnaces, the hissing chemical pipes and the towers full of hydrogen was a world, but it seemed closed to me.

You could smell my class on me. 
And in the UK my class was a sin. 

One advertising agency I applied to referred me to “a man that might be able to help you”, as he dealt with “young men in your kind of situation” – it transpired that he worked helping young offenders find work post juvenile detention.

Another told me that I was “terribly amusing” and “really rather interesting” but that they couldn’t imagine putting someone with my “background and accent” in front of a client.

A third recommended elocution lessons.

A 4th took a chance – putting me in the basement, in a non-client facing role, with some brilliantly funny and resourceful women. 

It sticks with you though.
Gives you a heightened awareness of the monoculture.
Makes you recognise the lack of diversity

Watching the white people leave the building at 7pm, and the Hispanic women come in to clean it at 8. Suddenly realizing that nobody you work with has ever bought the newspapers you read, the magazines you loved or watched the shows you grew up with – making your reference points alien to them. Being 15 years in before seeing a creative department run by a woman. Going to one retirement party in 30 years. Being asked to justify your opinion, because it was voiced in an accent that screamed “I don’t belong”

Which may explain why I hate that advertising remains a monoculture. 

Or maybe that’s just in me. 

But we exclude diversity of background, opinion, experience and expression at great loss to ourselves.

And as I dance in the twilight years of what might be called a career, that is what makes me saddest.

content:
Three of our clients told us the same thing this quarter: "Someone booked a call because they found me through ChatGPT."

I have been beating this drum for a while now. LinkedIn activity doesn't just build visibility on LinkedIn. It builds visibility across the entire AI search layer. Two birds, one stone.

Here are 5 takeaways that might help your AI visibility strategy:
1) Consistency is the baseline. 75% of cited authors post at least 5 times per month. If you're posting once a week and hoping for the best, you are probably invisible to these models. 

2) Depth gets cited. Posts between 500 and 2,000 words are the sweet spot. AI models are pulling from content that actually explains something.

3) Personal profiles outperform company pages. The person behind the business is more citable than the business itself. This is the entire thesis behind founder led content, and it's now backed by data at scale.

4) Original thinking wins. AI models are looking for signal, not noise. Reposting industry news with a generic caption doesn't register. Sharing what you actually know does.

5) Authority compounds. The people getting cited aren't gaming anything. They've been showing up consistently, building a body of work that AI models now treat as a source.

This has become a huge part of the conversation at Shake Content. Clients are getting surfaced in AI answers more frequently, and that visibility is driving real pipeline. Actual conversations that start with "Claude recommended your profile."

Most people still think of LinkedIn as a place to post and get likes. That's one layer. The less obvious one is that every post you publish is training AI models on who you are and what you know.

Kaleigh Moore wrote a great piece building on this data about how B2B creators on LinkedIn are anchoring AI search visibility. Worth reading alongside the Semrush study.

https://lnkd.in/e3G79jkN

I have never been more bullish on LinkedIn.

Kindness is not weakness, it is the ultimate competitive advantage. 

People often confuse kindness with being a pushover. They think leading with empathy means having low standards or avoiding hard conversations.

It doesn't.

Kind leadership is about treating people with dignity while holding them accountable. It’s about offering grace when someone makes a mistake and giving them the support they need to fix it.

Employees give you their best work, not just their minimum effort.

Teams stand by you during crises because you stood by them.

Your professional reputation becomes an unstoppable magnet for top talent.

You will never look back on your career and wish you had been harsher, colder or more ruthless.

Lead with empathy. The ROI on human decency is infinite.
