content:
What's the biggest problem facing CMOs today? 👀

Most people would guess budgeting, resources, or time.

When Jon asked 65 of the world's best CMOs, the top two answers weren't any of those it was leadership and politics.

It’s easy to assume that being a great CMO is all about marketing.

The craft, the campaigns, the classic 4 P's sitting in every marketer's rearview mirror. Product, price, place, and promotion

So, when TikTok asked Jon what their first CMO conference should cover, his answer caught them off guard.

"Don't talk about marketing."

After 270 conversations, the pattern that kept showing up was human and it was leadership.

So, we unpacked a new set of P's and even added a fifth.

PEOPLE/ The work is easy. The people are hard. CMOs repeatedly shared that leadership and politics are what hold them back, not budget. Hire for the characteristics that let someone thrive, not just their resume.

PLANNING/ As a CMO it’s easy to get stuck in the short-term cycle. The rare skill is playing the long game while still meeting the moment. When you're growing, you become the target, so move the target.

PERSUASION/ 56% say it's getting harder to make the case for investing behind their brand. Persuasion isn't a script, it's audience before content. The Jedi move? Get your CFO to sell your business case for you.

PERFORMANCE/ We have accountability but not always control. Performance comes from influence, and from the stories you tell. Kill the postmortem. Run after-action reviews while it's still hot.

PERSEVERANCE/ Kory's addition, along game of constant next-best actions. The kind that's driven 30 consecutive quarters of growth at e.l.f.

The biggest takeaway we hope you gain from this weeks episode is that it’s not about marketing after all - it’s about leadership. The greatest CMO’s are the greatest leaders. Learn how to be a leader and you’ll develop muscle necessary to succeed at every level.

Which P is holding you back, and which one are you underestimating?

content:
The world's best ads have always respected the medium they are in

As social advertising has boomed, you hear "made for platform" and "platform fit" a lot. Which people take as "shot on an iPhone in someone's kitchen with text on screen."

Hilariously missing the point. This is not new, it's a very old idea, respected by the world's best creatives.

Great advertising must respect the viewer, and respect the value exchange of the media channel.

Here's a great example from Sony in 1986 with Rowan Atkinson. Directly breaking the 4th wall, casually talking to the viewer on their sofa about their inferior screen colouring. Dramatising Sony's new product benefit.

But after seeing this, you'll notice it everywhere. Whether it's radio ads joking about how boring the traffic is, YouTube ads trying to beat the 5sec skip, or brands using creators to make incredibly entertaining TikToks to stop the scroll.

It should remind all marketers that advertising is consumed within the context of the world and culture. We must earn attention, not demand it. This really splits the good ads from the great.

This is my favourite quote about this, not no one can agree if Leo Burnett, Howard Gossage or FCB's founder John O'Toole first said...

"Advertising is an uninvited guest in the consumer's living room, and we must behave with the manners of a welcome guest rather than a loud, disruptive intruder."

author.name: Andrew Tindall
author.headline: The World’s Best Ads & Why They Work | Chief Growth Officer @ System1 | Marketing Effectiveness

content:
As an industry we pride ourselves on our ability to interest people. On our ability to make things that stop people in their tracks, get them to pay a little attention and then hang out in their brains for a while.

Attention, interest & memorability is the unholy trinity that we sell. 

And we all know that it’s a promise that’s getting ever harder to deliver upon as timelines get shorter, budgets get smaller and audiences cluster in ever smaller groups around ever more niche interests.

But we don’t help ourselves.

In a bid to be more efficient, to get more done, to meet more of the deadlines that used to whoosh past un-noticed, to drop fewer balls and co-ordinate better we’re all under more pressure to discuss less and dictate more.

AI will summarize the meeting and send out the tasks to everyone. Google allows people to work on “their bit” of a project alone, while calling it “collaboration on the deck.” E-Mail functions that started correcting spelling and grammar now offer hints and tips on content and organization. And remote working puts us all in boxes for at least half of the day.

Our internal comms are being blended to beige in a wind tunnel of tools designed to make everything consistently acceptable. And out of this unappealing soup of communication we’re expected to find the ingredients necessary to make magic.

We need to defend time to talk. And disagree. And get excited by an idea. And debate, discuss and deliberate. We need to slow down. To use the language that conveys how we feel, rather than the language that Grammarly or Gemini think best.

It’s a small thing, but it’s a real thing. 

The machines are taking over the big stuff. But they’re taking over the small stuff too, and once you outsource your voice it’s hard to get it back.

The resistance starts with choosing to keep that sentence structure.

Vive la resistance.

I was in Canva, designing some artwork worthy of the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, when I decided to silhouette an image.

Well, for the life of me, I could not find a tool or Effect that would do this. And it's quite simple, surely?

content:
Memes have a branding problem on LinkedIn.

People see them and immediately think: low effort, unprofessional, not serious content. And I get why. Most memes are lazy reposts that have nothing to do with the person sharing them.

But a good meme? A good meme compresses years of shared experience into something your audience recognises in under two seconds. That's not low effort. That's extremely high skill disguised as simplicity.

The problem isn't memes. It's how most people use them.

They grab something generic, slap it on their feed, and wonder why it feels off-brand. The memes that actually work are specific. They're about your industry, your audience's exact pain points, the inside jokes only your people would get. The more niche, the funnier.

And the best ones look effortless, which is exactly why they're not. Good humor is genuinely hard. The people doing it well have spent years developing taste for what lands and what doesn't.

A few things I have learned:

1) Keep it simple. If someone has to think about it for more than a second, it's not working
2) Don't force it. A bad meme is significantly worse than no meme. If the joke isn't there, move on
3) Memes should be part of your content mix, not the whole thing. Nobody builds authority on memes alone.. but the right one at the right time can do more for your brand than a 2,000 word thought leadership post
4) Bring it to your world. Make it about your industry, your niche, your audience's specific pain points. The more specific, the funnier

I broke all of this down in Issue #4 of LinkedIn, Actually.

content:
Zoë Bread is the perfect example of why I never bought the "brands should act like creators" line.

Her content is amazing. Probably the best content coming out of UK internet right now. It's funny, engaging, and surprisingly political. It's essential viewing, leaving brands and the rest of the media in the dust.

But it's also messy and chaotic. It skirts a whole bunch of risks that I simply don't think brands could handle. 

She calls out companies with a conviction that no Legal team would ever sign off on. Even most journalists would worry about the defamation risks of such brazen call-outs.

It's also, and this is vital, taking an actual stance on something. There's an ENEMY. Brands cannot compute this, unless the enemy is like "the dairy industry" or something equally milquetoast.

What a creator can do that a brand cannot is say "I am taking aim at this particular thing and rallying my audience against it". Brands can only operate in the safe, 'risk accepted' space of the cosplay of campaigning. Patagonia can rally against the oil industry but eventually even they have to move to protect their intellectual property and become the bad guy.

Zoë can name and shame. The consequences are on her, not a share price. That's what makes it powerful. It's real, and not in the co-opted corporate sense of "authenticity". It's also why brands can't just post through it when the spotlight's on them, as much as they might try.

Maybe I'm wrong, and a brand can rise to the occasion. But I simply don't think it's possible for a brand to do. Eventually the business needs win out.

I built a COUPLES THERAPY DASHBOARD for the CMO and CFO, because that relationship is complicated AF 

Finance and Marketing need a serious hug. They don't hate each other; they just have different love languages and timelines.


Marketing is playing the long game - date, build a relationship, lead the customer to the altar.
 

Finance wants to skip the small talk and convert on the first date.


Neither approach is wrong, but they have to align. Only care about the future, and you won't survive long enough to get there. 
Only care about today, and you won't last very long. 

Over-reliance on paid media is basically paying for love - expensive, temporary, unsustainable. You need both the art and the science to build a durable moat. Growth is nothing without durability.


The CMO's love language is Words of Affirmation ("Look at our social shares, net sentiment, brand advocacy, organic AI discoverability!").


The CFO's love language is Receiving Gifts - ROI right now ("Show me blended ROAS, contribution margin, CAC payback, today").


Normally, fixing this means a lot of counselling, 47 spreadsheet tabs, or a 12-week engineering ticket. I didn't want to wait on a dev queue to save this relationship. 

So I hopped on Lovable  to build them a shared relationship dashboard, using a fictional e-commerce brand to show how this applies to any industry.

It turns short-term performance vs. long-term brand equity into one scoreboard:
Six-Signal Trust Strip: a live health check-up mapping the journey - from initial sparks (Awareness) to commitment metrics like Defensibility and Belonging.


Budget vs. Actual Panel: toggle quarterly/annual targets, ad spend, LTV and retention blocks.

CFOs don't hate marketing; they hate surprises and a lack of clarity. Marketing doesn't hate finance; they just need a way to prove long-term value.

content:
The best ad I've seen this week

World class brand building from Burger King 👏

I'm not sure I could love this more. What a brilliant demonstration of four fundamental principles of brand growth with effective advertising. 

1. Relative difference. Burger King aren't the only place grilling their burgers. But they've selected this single association as their brand positioning for years and said it louder, longer, and in more interesting ways for decades, becoming known more for "flame-grilled".

2. Imaginative repetition. In my Compound Creativity research with the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising), Effie Worldwide and System1 we found the most consistent brands see 4x higher ROI and are 3x more likely to report profit growth. But refreshing the creative platform like this to keep it interesting is key. 

3. Happiness totally nailed this brief using a key creative principle: dramatise the product. Often the best creative brief (alongside "make me famous") is finding the drama and revealing the extreme within the mundane. It ensures brands aren't just talking to current customers, but the 95% who might buy in the future.

4. Media choices provide inescapable boundaries on creativity. I've researched outdoor ad creativity for years with JCDecaux; we found posters with fewer than 7 words, a clear pack shot, and something visually "right-brained" (especially a clear sense of place) that dramatically drove commercial effects, including store visits.

Congrats to anyone involved in this. It's simply epic. I've put it into System1 testing to see if consumers agree.

content:
Lots of chat about earned and owned being MORE important than paid ads. So, wheeling out some old gold from Les Binet, Peter Field and the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising)

Massive caveat: this was published about 10 years ago; a lot has changed, but the field has lacked good practical research in this space since. Do share anything you think is genuinley new and robust below!

Using the IPA databank, Binet & Field showed campaigns using paid online and paid social dramatically drove far more share-of-market changes than unpaid (organic/owned). Paid social is twice as effective as unpaid, according to their data.

Digital media has changed a lot since, including its penetration, and the algorithms have moved from making mates to the Robbie-Williams-Algo ("let me entertain you", you can have that one for free). 

But the accompanying case study dramatically shows just how far off these two mediums are, with 99% of sales for Wall's being driven by paid, and 1% from unpaid.

They conclude that adding owned and earned lifts large business effects (+13% and +26%), so should be viewed as paid multipliers. And when organic appears to have done a huge job, paid has always always been involved.

Other work in this space uses survey-based brand equity stuff, where owned and earned will have such a huge crossover with brand size and equity, so it's just hard to make any serious conclusions from.

I find a lot of questions marketers wrestle with have usually already been approached by Les and Peter, this is from Media in Focus. All their work is available online, recommended reading.

Earlier this year, Ipsos did something nobody in marketing had ever bothered to do.

They tested us.

1200 marketers. Across five countries. Real questions on the fundamentals of the discipline they practise every day. Positioning. Pricing. Brand versus performance. The stuff we all claim to know.

Most failed.

Not junior marketers. Not people from adjacent functions who wandered into marketing by accident. Marketers. With marketing job titles. Failing a test. On marketing.

When Ipsos separated out the marketers who had received formal marketing training, the results flipped. Trained marketers were 5x more likely to pass than untrained ones.

content:
Heineken's half-year results are an impressive read

Cutting costs, holding marketing budget. Volume +0.4% but profit +6.7%.

When a market is flat, there are only so many ways to grow margin. You can cut the company indiscriminately, with marketing usually first into the woodchipper because its value is less tangible and the sales damage rarely appears before next year. Or you can remove structural cost from the business while protecting the brands that allow you to charge more in the first place.
 
Heineken removed around 3,000 roles and expects gross savings of €500m, with cuts across breweries, supply chains, head office and individual markets. This is a serious restructuring, not a couple biscuits in meeting rooms. 
 
Marketing and sales were protected at 10.1% of net revenue (actually slightly higher than before); clearly this is not a business funding profit growth by starving demand. They are aware they must create it.

The results should make most FMCGs jealous. Revenue per hectolitre +2.3%, with price-mix +2.8% and premium brand volume +5.8%. With all of its key brands and 2/3rds of its market taking share.
 
A half-year report cannot prove that marketing caused this price and profit gains, because price-mix also reflects portfolio, channel and geography. And you'd actually expect them to reap the benefits of this over years, not months. But it does look very much like the result of making their business more efficient while driving actual desire for their brands. Which is what a lot of businesses claim they are doing, while really cutting marketing.

In my 'Creative Dividend' research with Effie Worldwide & System1, we found that reducing price sensitivity is the rarest business outcome, reported by only 5% of campaigns. Yet highly emotional ad campaigns were 178% more likely to achieve it. When strong creative was supported with enough media, campaigns were three times more likely to report reduced price sensitivity. Proper advertising clearly can impact a brand's ability to charge more and create profit.

Heineken has been ruthless with waste and patient with what creates demand.

author.headline: World’s Third Strongest Man / Senior Brand Writer, Monzo

content:
e.l.f. didn’t start with money. It started with a problem no one else wanted to solve

We recorded this week’s episode in Paris, and somewhere between the café and the microphone, we kept coming back to the same question people ask us.

"It's one thing to have money to launch products, but what if you don't? What if you're starting from scratch?"

So, we answered it.

Building a brand from scratch is really, really hard.

More than 90% of startups fail.

1 in 5 don't survive the first year.

Half don't make it to year five.

More than two-thirds don’t reach a decade.

However, the ones who make it do three things.

NAIL THE PROPOSITION/ Before spending even a penny on advertising, get brutally clear on who you are, what problem you want to solve and why someone should choose you over everyone else.

SURROUND YOURSELF WITH GREATNESS/ Don't hire for where you are, hire for where you want to go. Two levels up. People who believe in the thing so deeply they'll take a pay cut for the upside.

PLAY THE LONG GAME/ It takes, on average, seven years to build an “overnight success.” Seven years of hard graft. In and out of distribution. Starting in a niche nobody's heard of.

The biggest takeaway; constraints don't kill innovation, they create it.

Glamour magazine told e.l.f. they couldn't get coverage without a place to sell, so they built a website.

In 2004, when nobody was selling cosmetics online. The problem became an opportunity which then became the breakthrough.

So often, the thing you end up being successful for is NOT the thing you set out to do. It's the problem you had to solve. Stay curious. Stay open. Embrace the good unintended consequence.

More than money to start, you need a bulletproof proposition, believers who will charge the horizon and the persistence to keep going when the spark hasn't caught fire yet.

content:
Best marketing research I’ve seen this week: Emotional advertising works hardest when a brand is creating relative difference

A new paper in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science analysed ten years of Super Bowl advertising. Comparing ad liking and whether it had a brand-differentiating message (what academics call BDM) to loads of full-funnel data (awareness, brand emotion, consideration & intent, and purchase).

27% of the ads had a BDM, which gave people a reason to see this brand as different from competitors. In practice, this looks like Turkish Airlines saying it "connects more countries than any other airline". The Wendy's Company saying its beef is "fresh, never frozen". Bud Light's "twist-and-reseal" packaging. And Volkswagen Group dramatising German engineering reliability.

As I wrote about in my column last week (https://lnkd.in/dd86fjbQ), the industry has adopted the idea that brand differentiation doesn't really exist, and it isn't that useful in marketing. Which is clearly BS, and this new paper goes a little further to help explain why. 
 
1) A clear differentiating brand message directly improved ad awareness and brand liking.
 
2) Ad emotion (liking) then became more valuable when the ad ALSO had a differentiating message.

3) The differentiating message helped people move further down the funnel, from consideration to purchase intent and from purchase intent to actual purchase.

Don't be mistaken. This is not evidence that rational persuasion is more important than emotion in advertising. It's evidence that many things can cause an emotional response (a clear brand-differentiating idea, the right price, etc.), and emotion works harder when it is used to strategically build around a positioning to create relative difference. That's what causes growth.

I see this all the time in my work at System1. First we check ad fluency: is the brand being recognised in the creative, will it simply build familiarity? Then we understand if it's emotional, and what's driving the emotion. Then we look at the key memories built by the ad, this needs to match the brand's strategy.

Is it consistently putting that distinctive emotion to good work? Consistently building stronger associations around the brand's core positioning and category entry points.

For me, this is the job of proper marketing.

I rarely discuss this because genuinley, about 50-75% of the ads in the world are so dull that that's clearly the first problem to fix. But masterful marketers get their strategic eggs in a row, and then use Fame, Feeling and Fluency to build and refresh a couple of memories over years.

The danger with "differentiation doesn't exist" is we skip strategy and just get on with making distinctive ads. When we need emotional ads, fit to a long-term strategy, to predispose customers and change behaviour over time.

Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

content:
"How does the LinkedIn algorithm work?"

I get asked this more than anything else. And the honest answer is: nobody knows exactly. Not even the people who built it.

But after 4+ years inside LinkedIn and now leading an agency that lives on the platform every day, I've learned enough to separate signal from noise.

So I put together a breakdown of what's actually changed. The old algorithm vs the new one, across multiple factors that matter.

1) Templates are (hopefully) dying. LinkedIn is actively filtering for originality now. The same hook format that worked for 500 creators in 2023/24 is getting suppressed in 2026.

2) Comment quality flipped. It used to be about volume. Now a single thoughtful reply thread does more for your reach than 40 "great post 🔥" comments ever will.

3) Engagement pods are on their way out. The algorithm weighs dwell time, saves, and shares now. Gaming reactions doesn't move the needle like it used to.

4) Topic authority is real. The algo rewards people who stay in their lane and build depth over time.

5) AI slop gets caught fast. If your content reads like it was generated in 30 seconds, it probably gets treated like it was.

6) And the biggest shift of all: follower count no longer equals distribution. Relevance does. Which means a 2k follower account posting something genuinely useful to a specific audience can outperform a 80k follower account posting generic content.

content:
Key moment in marketing history: St-Germain is growing dramatically more than Aperol

You've seen the headlines but this reveals something much bigger about what the drinks industry is now getting wrong: its refusal to build future demand.

Over the past 3 months, St-Germain Elderflower Liqueurs' sales rose 40% in the US, with Aperol -4%. In the UK, St-Germain grew 46%, compared with only 10% for other spritz brands.

For the first time ever, more people are searching “Hugo Spritz” (an elderflower spritz) than “Aperol Spritz,” up +1,300% over 5 years!

But what the headlines are leaving out is how Aperol sold nearly 9 million cases in 2025, with St-Germain selling about 450k cases.

This is important for two reasons:

1) How these two brands have actually grown. With a playbook that theory doesn't really agree with: innovation, free sampling, and targeted experiential to hammer feeling and difference before scaling.

2) Two exceptions in a booze industry on its knees. Showing us why the alcohol category is only going to get worse before it gets better as we sell small, different incubation brands. Cut innovation teams. Dial back events, brand homes and experiences. Reduce and focus marketing spend just on large brands.

In my column this week, I share how these brands have done it, new System1 data showing most booze ads are well branded but struggle to create the emotion to grow future demand, and (cute) pictures of me when I worked on St-Germain and had blonde hair: https://lnkd.in/eE2vwD8U

Booze is struggling right now and this shows us how most businesses have totally dropped exactly what has made these brands successful.

It's a moment to celebrate and be very concerned about this industry. But let me know what you think in the comments.

content:
Motivation gets you started. Consistency keeps you going. 

Anybody can show up when energy is high, enthusiasm is fresh and the goal feels exciting. That’s the easy part.

The real test is what happens when:

The initial excitement fades.

The results are taking longer than expected.

You're tired, uninspired and just don't feel like doing the work.

Winners aren't people who never feel demotivated, they’re people who have learned to separate their actions from their emotions. They show up because they made a commitment to themselves, not because they feel like it in the moment.

Talent gives you a head start but consistency is what wins the race.

When you master the discipline of showing up on the hard days, success stops being a matter of "if" and becomes a matter of "when."

Keep putting in the work, especially when nobody is watching.

content:
AI hasn't made great content less valuable.
 
I actually think It's done the opposite.
 
The easier it becomes to create content... the more valuable originality becomes.
 
That's one of the biggest things we unpack in Part 2 of our conversation with Giulia de Oliveira Camargo on What Just Happened Podcast 

A few moments worth highlighting:
 
→ AI is an amplifier, not a replacement. The best creators don't use it to think for them. They use it to think faster.
 
→ Don't fight your creative rhythm. When you've got momentum, create in batches. Don't force it on the days you don't.
 
→ Humour, personality and genuine perspective are becoming competitive advantages. They're still some of the hardest things for AI to replicate.
 
→ Your credibility matters more than ever. On LinkedIn, authority isn't just about what you post. It's about who you are, what you've done and whether people trust your expertise.
 
One point Giulia made that I really liked: just because everyone can create content now, doesn't mean everyone will create content worth reading.
 
If anything, the bar has gone up.

content:
The quickest way to fail as a leader is to get defensive when you’re given feedback.

This has stuck with me.

I’ve lost count of how many people have told me “feedback is a gift”.

But when they’re given it… they focus on explaining, getting defensive, or ignoring

You’ll never grow if your only focus is being right all the time.

Some of the best leaders I’ve worked with have the same trait: they’re open to feedback. Even if it stings in the moment.

My advice:

1/ Be quick to listen. Slow to respond. 

2/ Be objective. Put yourself in their shoes.

3/ Listen to the words without ego.

4/ This info IS a gift if you’re humble enough to take it.

5/ Learn that being a team player means how the team perceives you is important..

6/ Respect is earned not granted.

The elite want to be coached. If you don’t want to be coached, you’re not elite.

content:
Advertising is an incredibly weak force

People often compare it to gravity, a very weak force that keeps us ... walking and ... on Earth. Unlike magnetism, which can move stuff despite gravity because it's a strong force.

Advertising causes small incremental changes in the chance of behaviour change. However, unlike gravity, advertising can compound into large changes over time.

If you don't believe me, go look at all the research into what happens to brands when they stop advertising. They eventually collapse into nothing. Weak force? Sure. But quite like most things in life, consistent everyday work compounds into what makes the difference.

So if you are stuck in the trap of thinking advertising won't do much, you reach for magnets (discounts, rational targeted ads, pleading for a conversion). The stuff that doesn't compound. You start looking at your ads through the lens of just distinctiveness, recognition and repetition. We must nudge, remind and hope.

But if you believe in the power of advertising to compound into behaviour change. You start to reach for storytelling, emotion, and consistently building around a strategic positioning to create relative difference.

The kind of stuff that over time will get you chosen more, paid more for. And dare I say, chosen more often.

Which is largely what I talked about at WFA's Global Marketer Week. It's like brushing your teeth. You brush today because if you don't, then don't tomorrow, they will fall out in a month. Quite a stretch, but you get the point.

content:
you can now buy your protein bar in a sardine style tin
ridiculous? not necessarily....


first - thanks to Snaxshot who put me on to this brand.
(we are not worthy Andrea Hernández)

packaging a protein bar in a tin is, let's be honest mental.

it's adding so much cost to the product.
it's actually quite inconvenient for the target consumer who probably wants something quick and easy to eat with packaging that they can throw away.
retailers probably hate it.

not to say the packaging isn't absolutely banging though!

but from a practical POV it's all a bit bonkers.

BUT

that's also what makes it such a great example of challenger thinking.

Jacked Granny (what a name!) doesn't use preservatives.

They only have 4 ingredients

They're the antithesis of the David bar which is great macros for terrible ingredients
and the only way they can package that to meet shelf life demands (so they claim) is to put it in a tin, not a wrapper.

As Louis Bedwell smartly pointed out to me - "everyone moans about the middle but challenger thinking is to think outside the box"

This brand is not occupying the middle in any respect.
They are proudly in a different quandrant.

And I'm not sure whether it will get them to $100m but it will certainly help them stand out in a ridiculously overcrowded market and get them out the blocks.

Which is often the most important thing for any brand.

What do you think?
Would you buy a protein bar in a tin that's called Jacked Granny?

(I would!)

content:
Five observations from spending too much time on LinkedIn  😆 

(I don't think content should be engineered for an algorithm. But I do think it's worth paying attention to what resonates)

1) newsy/timely insight + personality is the highest-engagement format going
Take a headline everyone's already seen and add a take only you could write. The news gets you reach. The personality gets you comments.

2) one-liners and short satirical posts are becoming a thing
These are the posts people screenshot and send to colleagues. Low effort, high resonance. (I'm all for it and trying to do more of these)

3) numbered opinion lists work when each item has actual edge
"9 things I'm thinking about LinkedIn right now" works because it's a window into how someone sees things.

"My 30-minute weekly content recipe" gets scrolled past. People follow for perspective, not templates.

4) generic how-to posts are out
If your post could've been written by anyone in your industry, it probably won't be remembered by anyone either.

Your audience isn't following you for a step-by-step guide they could Google. They're following for how you see things.

5) company promotion posts tank unless they're disguised as genuine insight
If it reads like a press release, it performs like one. Lead with the lesson or the story, not the logo.

The pattern across all five: the platform is rewarding people who sound like people.

That used to be a nice-to-have. Now it's the whole game.

content:
On Running's new "Run On Clouds" creative platform is another vote of confidence in their global positioning

I first wrote about this over a year ago, global fitness brands had all reached the same performance-slop positioning conclusion.

They all felt the same. Shouting and pushing you on to achieve greatness.

I'm the world's biggest supporter of consistency. Still, it needs to serve the end goal: emotion (I'd call this 'brand love' but have accepted it's not worth the arguments), familiarity and relative differentiation.

So when everyone's landed in the same place, a new 5-10 year campaign must be started.

adidas went first with "You Got This". 3-4 years in now, you can see the power of this companion, supportive positioning really paying back.

On went even further, it’s not about the numbers. It's about showing up for yourself. If it feels good, that's the win. Supported by their product truth: On's cloud technology makes running a joy.

So I love this new campaign's commitment to that positioning. Positioning only works if it's backed with scale, time and creativity. Positioning doesn't have to be unique, you just need to say louder and in a more interesting way for longer than the competition. But it helps if everyone isn't fighting for the same space.

However, I'm not 100% on the execution. I think this comes across as a little category generic. Which is a shame as their Elmo campaign had its own distinctive creative world that feels a bit lost in this spot.

So I've put it into testing with System1 to see if this makes a broad audience feel something. And whether it engages those not already interested in the brand.

Either way, I think fitness advertising is the most interesting category right now. And On are getting loads right to challenge the big boys.

"It's never been easier to succeed"

I wonder how many people would agree with this comment from Jonathan Kerr (JK)?

It doesn't feel easier that's for sure and yet I agree with him

Here are 5 things I would do today were I starting out on my career

1. GET SOME TRAINING

Let's start here because being trained in something gives you confidence and credibility. When I started in marketing the only training was on-the-job or a very expensive MBA but now you can put yourself through the Mark Ritson MiniMBA for example

2. DO SOME READING

I am always quite surprised at how few books most marketers have read. There are some incredible books out there that will inspire you and give you ideas on how to take on the challenges you will inevitably face. If you prefer listening then find a good podcast.

3. BUILD YOUR NETWORK

You next job is more likely to come from your network than it is from an advert. This is a harsh reality so make it your mission to build up a strong network that you use. With Linkedin it has never been easier to do that!

4. GET A MENTOR

The advice from someone who has been there and done it is invaluable. Find someone who will give you honest advice and push you to dream bigger and climb higher than you thought possible. You'll be surprised at how willing people are to help if you ask.

5. BUILD A PERSONAL BRAND

When I started out your personal brand was basically how polished your CV was. Now you can prove your value every single day on a number of different platforms, even if all you do is share one thing you have learned a day! And who knows you might even end up with a new career like I did on Uncensored CMO

So yes compared to when I started I do think it is easier to succeed than ever before but perhaps the fact it doesn't feel like it is a good thing because it will give you an advantage over others afraid to try

Do you agree?

What other advice would you give?

Australian culture never fails to make you feel something

I go on a lot about making people feel something. But a possibly better framing is the risk of making people nothing.

Adam Morgan, of eatbigfish, has been helping challenger brands grow for decades through the power of (essentially) having a point of view, being interesting, and taking on a challenge (where the damn name comes from!). I recommend his books for more growing like a challenger.

System1 partnered with Adam and the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) to release 'The Cost of Dull'. Which Jon Evans shared at Cannes.

Dull costs US marketers $189 in wasted effectiveness a year.

So this ad might look risky. But the riskiest thing a brand can do is to be dull.

content:
Seven years ago, Jon was unemployed.

Well fired actually if we’re going to be completely honest, and sitting at Cannes with a single 30-minute panel planned for the day.

Then suddenly CNBC walked by looking for CMOs to conduct a video interview. It just so happened that they had heard about the recent firing through Marketing Week.

Immediately they’d found their person to feature.

They took Jon down to the beach and asked “What’s the one thing you feel about Cannes?” Jon had no idea how much his candid response would shape his future.

“The one thing about Cannes is that the customer’s not here and so long as we are celebrating ourselves but not celebrating the customer and the difference we make to their lives, we're missing the point, and we'll cease to exist if we lose the focus on the customer."

The cameraman stopped the recording, poked his head around, and said, "You, sir, are the first uncensored CMO I've spoken to all week."

The podcast was named before it even existed, and here it is 7 years and 279 episodes later.

The themes of this week’s episode are the same things that started it all:

SURPRISE/ Something that is extremely underutilized. Most advertising makes zero difference. We put a price on it. Surprise amplifies emotion by 400%. It's the number one way to get your brand into memory.

FEAR / Why is the work so dull? People are afraid of the breakthrough. Safe work gets a safe response. Brave work gets an unknown one.

STRATEGY / Surprise isn't a stunt. It's a strategy. The dopamine hit declines as you get familiar with an experience. Successful brands repeat surprises, deepening the relationship every time.

Surprise is the most underused tool in business. We've been measuring happiness for 20 years and ignoring it. But surprise is what breaks through the monotone, what gets remembered, and what creates the OMG moment.

What’s one way that you can tie surprise into your strategy? 🤯

content:
If I was a founder with no budget trying to grow my business (again), here's what I'd do:

1. Spend zero on paid ads until you've exhausted LinkedIn. Organic reach is free. Your founder story, your insights, your mistakes - that's content. Post 3-5x a week before you spend a penny on ads.

2. Start finding advisors alongside hiring employees. They’ll bring experience and guidance you can’t afford full time. Those conversations will save you from expensive mistakes you'd make alone. Find people who've done what you're trying to do. Ask specific questions. Do it before you're desperate.

3. You don't need a full-time CFO when you're pre-revenue. Get someone who's done it 10 times before to spend 1-2 days a week getting your finances right. Senior expertise at a fraction of the cost.

4. Track three metrics obsessively, ignore the rest. Pick the numbers that actually matter right now. Revenue, churn, CAC - whatever moves the needle. Solve for them obsessively. Everything else is noise.

5. Build relationships before you need them. Don't wait until you're fundraising to start talking to investors. The founders who move fast have been building those relationships for months.

6. Get comfortable being uncomfortable. If you're not slightly terrified by what you're building, you're playing it too safe.

Most early-stage failure comes from trying to do too much with too little.

Focus. Find the right people early. Move fast on what matters.

Not all role models show you who to become some teach you exactly who to avoid. 

We often talk about mentors who guided us, bosses who believed in us and leaders who lifted us up.

But some of the greatest leadership lessons come from bad behavior.

The manager who took credit for your work taught you the power of giving visibility to others.

The boss who ruled through fear showed you why psychological safety matters.

The leader who made promises they couldn't keep taught you the weight of integrity.

Bad leaders write the best playbooks on what not to do.

Every time someone treats you poorly, cuts corners, or acts out of ego, write it down. 

Use their mistakes as a blueprint for the kind of leader, colleague and human being you refuse to be.

Turn toxic examples into your personal standard of excellence.

content:
Can you build a global technology empire on the back of a 1980s knit vest and a catchy song? 

Take a look at this absolute gem from our archives: a Samsung Electronics TV commercial from 1988. The tagline? "You can't go wrong with Samsung." 

True then. True now. 

At the time, this was a highly deliberate business strategy. In the late 1980s, the European consumer electronics market was dominated by established brands. As an emerging challenger, our biggest hurdle wasn't just selling features — it was earning consumer trust. 

We needed to reassure families that choosing Samsung was a safe, reliable decision. 

Fast forward to today. 

We are no longer just the "safe choice" you "can't go wrong with." Samsung has driven the global standard for TV innovation and has been the world's No. 1 TV brand for 20 consecutive years. 

Three takeaways from our 1988 campaign:
• Meet the market where it is: In 1988, we needed humour and cultural familiarity (suburban comedy and a catchy tune) to humanise a foreign tech brand.
• Consistency builds empires: The trust we earned in those early living rooms laid the foundations for the premium brand we are today.
• Never forget the fun: Great marketing has always been about emotional connection. Even decades later, light-hearted storytelling can still bring a smile.

To my LinkedIn community: What's the most memorable heritage campaign for you?

content:
Warming to a theme here.

We spend way too much time looking for things that “only we can say” 

“Anyone could say that” is the scythe wielded by the hack in the room – and all too often their frantic slashing nicks a vein before they can be ushered out to the hallway where the damage they do can be contained. 

“Only” is used by people who don’t understand advertising, but think that they do because they read a post by someone who read a book by someone who practiced advertising in the 1950s.

The truth is that almost anyone can say almost anything. 

The fact that they haven’t (because they’re too slow or too scared or have some internal hangup about using verbs in strategy) should be the starting gun on us going there, not pause for thought.

Anyone could have said “Just do it”, “Think Different”, “I’m lovin’ it”, “Because you’re worth it”, “The ultimate driving machine”, “You’re in good hands”, “We try harder”, “Can you hear me now”, The real thing”, “Have a break”, “Eat fresh”, “Drivers wanted”, “Zoom Zoom”, “Save money. Live Better”, “Every little helps”, “"You Can't Buy Happy, But You Can Buy Ice Cream" or even “wherever you are”

But anyone didn’t. A specific brand did – and they stuck with it. And I’ll wager that you know where most of those lines came from.

And guess what, not one of them had a competitor that said “us too, we do that, we can say that, we’re going to use exactly the same line, thought, idea and positioning” – despite the fact that in the offices of agencies working for Nike, Apple, McDondalds, L’Oreal, BMW and all of the rest there was a Simon suggesting that that was exactly what would happen.

Do yourself a favor; retire “only” and anyone who insists that it’s the criterion upon which to choose work. You’ll save yourself hours while saving what might just become iconic work.

content:
The biggest mistake marketers are making right now is thinking distinctive is enough, and "differentiation doesn't exist"

The increasingly dogmatic approach to the theory around brand growth is leading us down the garden path, with no help to the practice of actual marketing.

An uber focus on distinctive brand assets, recognition and repetition at the cost of creativity, emotion, fame, culture and relative differentiation is not a practical strategy for growth.

It all sounds very good on paper, but sadly, you can't bash someone over the head with your logo until they choose you.

We must predispose customers to our brands, building useful memories that create a competitive advantage. This isn't possible without distinctiveness, but it doesn't cause it. 

What does cause it is something far more obtuse, difficult to achieve and measure: creativity. The kind of stuff that makes the suits uncomfortable.

And the idea that "no differentiated brands exist" is based on research where people were asked whether a brand is "different". Few people consciously agreed. So it concluded that differentiation doesn't really exist and isn't important.

In reality, brand growth comes from owning a few strategic associations (including category entry points) more than other brands to achieve relative differentiation. No consumer will consciously call that "different", they are unaware of it.

My column this week challenges something I see about 5 times a week. Really great DBAs, in a really shit ad: https://lnkd.in/dd86fjbQ

author.headline: The World’s Best Ads & Why They Work | Chief Growth Officer @ System1 | Marketing Effectiveness

content:
Here's an egg to suck on

We do a very simple thing.

We make whatever we’re tasked to sell a little more memorable.

That’s it. That’s the job. 

Move (X) into a little bit of real estate in an easily accessed part of people’s brains; ensure that it lives there rent free.

There are lots of ways to do this and there is no “right way.”

Jingles, mascots, rhymes, slogans, celebrities, jokes, colors, narrative stories, huge productions, stunts, a logo, a line, endless repetition, characters, a dance, a slap, a mood, a promise.

A squadron of Harrier jets hovering over the white cliffs of Dover, a baby injecting heroin, a Martian laughing, the sea becoming white horses, a wide eyed kid with a Scottish accent saying “and conquered worlds”, an ambassador's reception, a guy in denim shorts twerking, flirting over coffee, a man and a yellow puppet, the view from an airplane window, balls rolling down a hill in San Francisco, you can’t get better than a Kwik Fit Fitter, meerkats with Russian accents, a subservient chicken, FCUK, FCK, the wind as an asshole, a glass and a half, kills all known germs, dead. Sport is war without the killing. Size 14 women in a beauty ad. A piece of silk, artfully cut. 

Work like that is within your reach. 

But you need to let go of your wish list and replace it with three simple questions. 

Will it be noticed?  Will it be remembered? Have we linked our product, inextricably, to that memory?

That’s it.

Not “is it on strategy?”, not “have we included all of the mandatories?”, not “will Nadine hate this?”, not “do we know how to make this?”, not “is this too much?”, not “how do we make it more palatable?”. 

Noticed, remembered, inextricably linked.

And on linked,  no it doesn’t have to be something that nobody else can say. Almost anyone can say almost anything. 

A better question would be “how much would it hurt if a competitor said this before you did?”

But try this. In your next review. Let go of everything other than the need to make it noticed, memorable and inextricably linked.

You’ll probably get nothing at first. You’ve been training your creative teams to churn out work that fulfils the “needs” listed on a spreadsheet. 

But two rounds of “would anybody notice this?” is transformative and gives people permission to do what they’ve always known needs to be done.

Go. Make something striking.

author.name: Richard Cook
author.headline: World’s Third Strongest Man / Senior Brand Writer, Monzo

content:
WARNING: Excess organic content will not cause growth

My post about organic content being oversold got deleted yesterday. But marketers are being conned, not every brand needs an organic strategy.

It's important to challenge it. So I'm resharing again with more thoughts today.

Someone shared the chart below, citing a large brand that claims paid media no longer works for them, so they are going hard on "organic." Ie. Content that has no mechanism to show it to people in a certain channel.

Here's my issue with organic...

1. This graph has no data, source, units, x-axis, cost base or control because there's a genuine lack of public evidence that organic can reliably grow a brand, "organic" is used interchangeably by people depending on what they are selling. Creator campaigns that actually worked, for example, usually had paid media behind them.

2. Evidence linking organic content to business outcomes is painfully thin. Most cases report engagement, clicks or fantasy PR reach figures, rather than incremental customers, revenue or profit.

3. Organic hits a scale ceiling. You might prove it works for your brand. But can you then 10x the results?

4. Organic cannot reliably control reach or frequency. The algorithm decides who sees your content and how often. Paid media lets the brand decide. If you believe repeated exposure matters, explain how you plan it organically.

5. Organic audiences over-index towards people who already know, follow or buy you. Engagement may be an effect of brand strength. Growth usually requires reaching new and light buyers.

6. Millions of brands have grown without organic content, a couple have (truly) without paid advertising. When you look at the P&L's of golden organic-growth brands, there's a load of paid media in there.

7. If you were honest, how much time, focus and cash went into that organic content. Would you have got more scale with paid media? Probably.

Organic has useful roles:

- Earning attention around genuinely big, PR-worthy campaigns, alongside paid media.
• Finding reactive creative ideas, then scaling the winners with paid media. I share a lot of content from brands I admire winning with creativity. 1) they are not the norm 2) they usually then pay to boost this stuff.
• CRM, community and co-creation with existing customers.

Organic has a role. But what are you doing organic INSTEAD of? All brands do not need to do organic content.

Very open to being challenged on this, so please do below. But the number of rooms I've been in recently where people think the job is creating organic content that 10,000 people see once is not great.

content:
I was standing behind a counter at Macy's Herald Square at Christmas trying to sell my new brand.

Everyone around me was giving something away. A faux diamond watch. A duffel bag. The guy next to me was shouting, "cool water, get your cool water!"

And I had nothing.

I'd argued with my sales team at the time, with total conviction, that a gift set would devalue the brand.

No gift set. Not happening. I dug my heels in.

Then I stood at that counter and watched the truth walk right past me. I went back to the office and apologized to everyone.

I had conviction for my belief in brand building. What I didn't have was conviction for the people I served. I had not yet found the center of the Venn diagram.

Jon learned the same lesson a different way. Building a beverage brand in London, he told his team; once a month, we're all van sales drivers for the day.

They moaned, but their motivation skyrocketed, and decision-making back at the head office became ridiculously easy, because they weren't theorizing anymore. They had first-hand experience.

On the latest episode of Uncensored Renegades, we unpack what nobody at the office hands you a manual for. From doing the work, to leading the work, to leading the leaders. Each phase demands a completely different skill set. The skills that made you valuable in phase one can quietly make you a liability in phase three.

Here's where we landed:

PROXIMITY IS POWER/ 
The field is where you go to learn. The office is where you go to put learnings into action. Find the moment of truth in the field. Then get your ass to an office to translate those truths into meaningful actions for the communities you serve.

PRESENCE IS THE NEW CURRENCY/ Managers multitask. Leaders unitask. I once had a boss who answered his phone during my annual performance review. What I heard was; you are not important enough to get all of me. I never want anyone to feel that way.

CLARITY OF COMMUNICATION/ Your job is to move people from confusion to clarity. The best communicators are the best listeners.

The biggest takeaway?

Leadership isn't one job. It's three. And the transition between them is where most people stall. Not everybody wants the next level, and that's okay too.

The real renegade move is knowing which leader you want to be and committing to the daily practice of becoming it.

content:
When your video isn't accessible, it doesn't just become exclusionary. It becomes boring. 

Automatically. To more people than you'd think.

Yep, even your sexy ad with that celeb you just spent literal millions on. 

Think about your own social media feed for a mo. If you're scrolling without audio (because you're on public transport, in bed, fancy a bit of quiet) and you encounter a video that isn't captioned, what do you do?

You scroll. 

In just a couple of seconds, your brain registered that you couldn't understand the message. Decided it wasn't relevant to you. And moved on. 

Same goes for audio. Say you're watching without *watching.* You're concentrating on something else, and the video is background noise. Maybe you're dual screening with the telly, you're chopping some garlic or feeding a baby. 

You can't look at the screen, so what do you do when a video comes on that's just music or trending audio? You don't stop what you're doing to make sure you watch the action. You decide that video isn't relevant to you. 

You scroll. 

You find something where the narrative is audible, even if that's as simple as somebody talking to the camera, or a "come to work with me" edit with a voiceover.

So, making sure your video's message comes across both audibly and visually (with captions) isn't just a must for people with sight or hearing loss. 

It's a way to stop your content from immediately becoming irrelevant. Illegible. Dull. The moment it lands on the feed of somebody who is disabled, or distracted, or has their audio turned down. 

And that must be the majority of us, right?

Banish the threat of dullness by asking yourself:

"If I was looking away, could I still understand this video?"

"If I had my audio turned off, would I still get the message?"

And would you still enjoy it? Would the humour, the emotion, the urgency, still come across?

Of course, there's a lot more to video accessibility, especially when it comes to people who navigate the internet using braille, or those who don't like watching videos and prefer to read instead. 

But audible + visual is a great place to start.

content:
A lot of people have sent me the Pangram Labs study this week.

"41% of long-form LinkedIn posts are AI-generated. Is LinkedIn dead?"

LinkedIn was a third of the sample but accounted for nearly two-thirds of all detected AI content. The detection model is conservative, so the real number is probably higher. For comparison, Reddit was at 4.4%.

I spent four years inside LinkedIn. I have seen every version of "the platform is dying" disscourse. This one is different because it is not about a feature change or an algorithm tweak. It is about whether the content itself can still be trusted.

I'm not going to pretend this is not a real problem.

But here is where I stand. 

There's a concept in economics called Jevons Paradox. In the 1860s, steam engines got more efficient and an economist predicted coal consumption would drop. Instead it exploded. Cheaper energy didn't reduce demand.. it made entirely new uses viable, and total consumption went through the roof.

The same thing is happening with content. AI made creation nearly free, so volume exploded. But that volume isn't evenly distributed. Most of it is generic, competent, forgettable. Which means three things are now true:

1) Sounding polished is table stakes. That used to be enough to stand out. It isn't anymore.
2) Generic content now competes with infinite supply. If your post reads like anyone could've written it, you're in a 'price war' you can't win.
3) A real person with a specific point of view just became significantly harder to replicate.. and significantly more valuable.

I see this every day at Shake Content. The founders, execs, athletes who sound like themselves, who have an actual opinion and aren't afraid to put it on the page, are getting more traction now than they were a year ago. Not less.

When the commodity version of something floods the market, the premium version appreciates. That's just economics.

The 41% isn't a reason to leave LinkedIn. It is the reason your voice matters more than it did six months ago.

content:
The most interesting marketing research I've seen this month

AI beats paid social, but loses to all other channels

A new academic paper (https://lnkd.in/e3YPhqpw) has just been released where they analysed 12 months of first-party data from 1000 ecommerce sites (20bil in revenue). Looking at 50k+ ChatGPT-referred transactions and 164mil transactions from established digital channels.

ChatGPT referrals produced higher conversion rates and revenue per session than paid social, but underperformed every other traditional channel studied.

The paper also finds that the relative performance of LLM referrals is stronger for products that require more complex consideration.

There are some massive caveats here:

- This is an early look at advertising on AI; it will change weekly, but it's a strong signal that it's going to be super good at helping consumers decide and buy with more complex decisions.

- Affiliate marketing completely trashed AI (by 86%). People are far more likely to convert if they've come from somewhere that's usually rather "curated" and full of human content.

- This is obviously only bottom-of-funnel, performance effects. And AI traffic right now is tiny, but an early sign that OpenAI's advertising business will be able to really deliver.

content:
Creativity turns "lots of littles" into a compounding advantage for your brand

But we must move from thinking about impressions to thinking about memory

A brand manager's most important job is looking after the memories and associations of their brand (and categories, if they are REALLY good) in the minds of current and future buyers.

That's what brings the mind, and what the brand brings to mind. Both clearly important, despite the hysteria around this at the moment.

I love this new chart from WPP Media, TikTok and System1's "Creator Effectiveness Playbook" as it clearly lays out the importance of this and how practical the implications are for people actually practicing in marketing.

Looking at how much awareness and recall grew for 600+ social campaigns across 8 markets on TikTok, we can see that (of course, as many have shown before) managing to capture and hold more is useful but:

1. Enough attention is enough, at least on social, but you do see this in other research as well. Advertising is often just refreshing and nudging memories.

2. Distinctiveness matters. Getting brand recognition in the first few seconds of a social asset clearly helps impact memories for your brand.

3. The impact of emotion is massive. Emotion and attention are clearly connected, making people feel something lead to more memory formation, etc. If your brand, strategy, idea, and execution turn a few seconds of attention into feeling, you will dramatically impact brand building.

This is what brand building can look like now. Small incremental memories formed for brands that compound over time to change behaviour.

Creative choices turn lots of littles into a compounding advantage against your competition.

content:
4 years at System1. Here's what I've learned scaling a challenger brand

I was terrified when I left Diageo, although I think I played it pretty cool. The past 4 years have been transformative for me personally. The guy on the left (with cute painted nails, may I add) wouldn't believe how much I've learned or changed.

So, sharing a list of what I've learned as we've scaled System1 by +54%ish and become one of the hottest brands in market research.

1. Partnerships are symbiotic gold

I've worked with some fantastic agencies, media owners, and effectiveness bodies. And some damn amazing people. When you partner, you lose very little, but you usually gain at least double. Find complementary brands that need what you can do, and work your ass off for them.

2. Motivate for the long

Campaigns, teams, contracts, people, etc., should all be working towards things that compound. It must get EASIER every quarter. When making decisions, you need to think about what decisions will become easier after. The longer time horizons you are thinking in, the more useful you are. And conversations quickly become more interesting.

3. Reciprocity

Jon Evans, who hired me (!), says this most weeks. It's especially true in B2B. Be strategically generous. My LinkedIn content is basically me handing out decks, research, and data for free. But I saw this when I used to grow drink brands; free sampling is like wildfire (look at Aperol). Be short-term generous, long-term greedy.

4. Bust your ass hiring right

I can't describe how fulfilling hiring people has been. Such a unique feeling meeting someone, knowing they can do more, and giving it them. That coming back from holiday or something, and they've just smashed it. Spend far too much time hiring. Be an ass about pushing for more and getting it right. And side note, any serious hiring decision I've usually made after a 30minute meeting. When you know, you know.

5. Respect the past enough to challenge it

There's a reason something is going so well. There was an insight, a person, a campaign, or a product. Understanding that enough and looking at what's going on around you will truly allow you to take the magic and scale it into the future. I like to think that in the next few weeks, you'll agree with this, as we launch our first huge AI research tools. One of the funnest things I've ever worked on!

6. Fame

You need someone, something or a team making you famous. Luckily, we have many people at System1 who have always done this (Orlando Wood! And our brill marketing team, Vanessa Chin!) Do that cool thing, post on socials daily, be outrageous, be memorable, be worth talking about. I can't describe how much easier things are when you walk in a room, and people already know you (or are already cheering you on).

Hope that's useful! Big thanks to everyone who works with us, and big thanks to our Exec and board for taking a shot on me (James Gregory!)

content:
LinkedIn's CEO just gave one of the clearest explanations I've seen of what actually works on the platform.

Daniel Shapero told The Times that "the magic equation is insight + personality"

I've been saying this for years. Not because I'm some prophet, but because I spent 4+ year inside LinkedIn watching what actually worked. 

The pattern is always the same: the people who grow are the ones who have something to say and sound like themselves saying it.

Dan made a clear distinction most people miss. Personality is not the same as being personal.

That's where people get stuck. They hear "show more personality" and think they need to share a divorce story or a mental health confession. Then they freeze, because that feels weird, and they're right, it is weird if the only reason you're sharing it is because someone told you vulnerability performs.

Personality is simpler than that. It's the way you explain a concept. The specific example you reach for. The opinion you actually hold instead of the safe version. 

It's the difference between "leadership requires empathy" and telling us about the one meeting where you got it completely wrong and what you changed after.

Shapero put it well: "If you wouldn't share your post in a room of 12 colleagues, you probably shouldn't." That's a good filter. Not because LinkedIn should be sanitised, but because the best content here comes from professional credibility, not personal exposure.

He also called out generic AI content directly. No personality, no insight, limited distribution. Which tracks with everything we're seeing at Shake Content. The algorithm is getting better at rewarding the stuff that sounds like a specific human wrote it.

The formula isn't new. But hearing the CEO say it out loud might finally get some people to stop writing like a company page and start writing like themselves.

Listen, we’ve got to talk about this…  🙂‍↔️🎙️👋🚫 ad

Black Friday and Christmas are fast approaching and brands, I hate to break it to you but no one wants to be gifted another boring tote bag slapped with your logo on it. 

At best? They’re used occasionally for the mid-week fridge top up shop. 
At worst? They’re hiding behind some cobwebs at the bottom of someone's wardrobe, donated to a charity shop where it’ll live out the rest of its days or immediately thrown out. 

If you want to stay off the naughty list this year, the gift has to actually be giftable. Think about what your creators, and attendees at events will actually use. It’s probably as simple as a discount code, or being able to try your product for free. 

(Examples: I’ve been gifted a camera by Canva as part of The Canva World Tour campaign, and newly launched lipglosses at a Ole Henriksen x Cult Beauty event. They make sense.) 

But if you have gifted BORINGGG 😴tote bags in the past, don’t fear! You can still get on Annie-Mai’s nice list… By giving customers and fans the influencer treatment. 

Here's what would actually earn you a spot on the nice list: giving customers and fans the influencer treatment, not just influencers. 
→ Bold Bean Co don’t just send their product to influencers, they send them to the people closest to them too like their mum, or their daughters at university. 
→ Refy has taken customers on trips to Mexico and Spain. 
→ Hair Syrup took fans to watch Ariana Grande in their box at the 02. 

And that's the kind of gifting and experiences people remember, screenshot, and talk about – way more than a tote bag ever will. 

👋 But there’s a catch: you can’t sleigh gifting campaigns like that if you’re planning them last minute. A report by Modash found that 6 in 10 creators feel like brands reach out too late for holiday campaigns and when you're rushing, you don't get a thoughtful gift or the influencer treatment, you get whatever you can get from the stockroom. Tote bags, probably.

When a loyal person stops caring, it’s not a mood, it’s a commitment. 

Loyal employees are the backbone of any team. They are the ones who put in the extra effort, advocate for the culture and stay through the tough seasons because they genuinely care about the mission.

But loyalty isn't infinite. It’s a bank account.

Every broken promise, ignored piece of feedback, and act of disrespect is a withdrawal. And once that account hits zero, something dangerous happens:
They don't get angry. They don't make a scene. They just go quiet.

The day a loyal person stops fighting to make things better is the day they've mentally checked out. And once you lose their heart, no pay raise or counteroffer will bring it back.

Don't mistake patience for weakness and don't take commitment for granted.

Leaders: value your most loyal people before you have to learn how much it costs to replace them.

content:
Nobody cares how talented you are if they dread working with you.


Talent is table stakes.


Most people misdiagnose why their career plateaus. 


They look at output. Output is rarely the problem.


The problem is friction. 
If working with you costs more energy than it creates, people route around you. 


Quietly. No feedback, no announcement - you just stop being part of the plan.


This applies to managers even more. 


Your behaviour is the system your team operates in. 


If someone feels anxious on a Sunday night, that’s not their flaw. 


That’s a signal about the environment. And you built the environment.


I’ve created that friction myself. 


A message that read colder than intended. 


The fix wasn’t complicated: notice, adjust, repeat. Self-awareness compounds like anything else.


One clarification, because it’s often misunderstood: low friction doesn’t mean soft. 


The most direct people are usually the easiest to work with.

content:
You can teach someone how to do a job but you can’t teach them how to care. 

We spend weeks scanning resumes, checking certifications and vetting past company logos. But we often overlook the single most important trait: character.

A "brilliant jerk" with a flawless CV and a toxic attitude will destroy your team's morale faster than any technical skill gap ever could.

Skills can be taught. Processes can be learned. Software can be mastered.

But you cannot train:

Humility
Empathy
Curiosity
A collaborative spirit

When you hire someone with the right attitude, they will close the skill gap in record time because they are actually hungry to learn. But when you hire someone with the wrong attitude, no amount of training will fix the cultural damage they bring with them.

Build a team of hungry, humble and human-centric people. The rest will follow.

Hire for who they are, not just what they can do.

THE PARALYSIS OF PERFECTION

This comment from Adobe CMO Lara Hood Balazs really struck a nerve with me

As someone who is a closet perfectionist - just ask Kerry Collinge about Uncensored Pantones - I can sometimes struggle to do something because it doesn’t feel perfect

Is the decision you are making a one-way door you can’t go back through or is it a two-way door you can

content:
Two years before Kory ever worked at e.l.f., she saw Tarang Amin speak at a CEO summit. 🗣️

She took eight pages of notes, leaned over to her boss at the time and whispered: "At the end of this guy's talk, I'm going to give him my résumé."

Her boss whispered back: "Do me a favor, give him mine too."

That's the power of a leader who makes you see the future while they're talking about the present.

We sat down with Tarang Amin, CEO of e.l.f. Beauty at Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity for a live episode of Uncensored Renegades. 29 consecutive quarters of growth. A culture built on ownership, transparency, and long-term thinking. Here's what stayed with us.

OWNERSHIP IS NOT A BUZZWORD/ When every employee is granted equity and becomes a shareholder, the word "ownership" is no longer aspirational, it becomes the fuel to put your best foot forward for yourself and your teammates. People protect what they own. They build like the future is theirs, because it is.

GROWTH AND HUMANITY ARE NOT OPPOSING FORCES/ Most companies treat culture as the cost of growth. e.l.f. treats it as the cause. You can scale at an extraordinary pace without leaving your people behind, but only if you decide, early and often, that the people come first.

CONFLICT IS A FEATURE, NOT A FLAW/ Healthy conflict should be encouraged across all levels and teams throughout an organization. It’s the result of working with smart people who care. The job of a leader isn't to eliminate conflict. It's to make it safe enough to be useful.

The biggest takeaway from this conversation?

Leadership is communication.

Every week Tarang writes a personal email to our employees and partners alike. For over six years, 325 weeks and counting. Not memos or decks. Updates on our business strategy alongside news of his 35th wedding anniversary and his father’s 90th birthday celebration.

Anyone can respond, and many do. Every. Single. Week.

That's what Kory felt in that conference room over seven years ago. Not a strategy. Not a pitch. A leader making the future feel present.

That's the kind of leader people hand their resume to.

content:
They don’t want your talent. They want your inability to say "no." 

Toxic bosses don't target people-pleasers because they value their dedication. They target them because they know they can exploit their boundaries.

They look for the individuals who will:
Work through weekends without a peep. 

Accept unrealistic deadlines with a forced smile.

Stay quiet when boundaries are crossed, just to keep the peace.

To a bad leader, a chronic people-pleaser isn't just a "good team player" they are a free pass to overwork, overstep and underappreciate without facing any pushback.

If you are a natural helper, your empathy and work ethic are your superpowers. But in a toxic environment, they are vulnerabilities.

Start setting boundaries. A healthy workplace will respect you for them. A toxic boss will only be angry that they can't use you anymore.

Protect your peace. Your career shouldn't cost you your sanity.

content:
The best World Cup ad I've seen this week

With 4 clear principles of ad effectiveness for brand building

1) Mass reach - this campaign is for anyone who would possibly place a bet on the World Cup online this season. It's made to attract attention and entertain to build salience for Paddy Power around football. This is mass reach for penetration in action.

2) Truly understand your audience - following the same principles, in System1 testing (https://lnkd.in/eSJi7Xs8) for people open to placing a bet online, this scores 5.9 Stars in our testing, maxing out our long-term emotion score! But for a broad audience, this also lands in the top 1% of all betting ads. It will do an excellent job at actually growing the category.

3) Dramastise the creative tension - the team at BBH London manage this by finding that tension between the UK and US, and dramatising. Obsecuring it. Stretching it into absurdity. This is a key creative principle that the best agencies apply.

4) Make them feel something - it doesn't even mention betting or the specific act of placing a bet. It puts on a show to entertain and build memories. This is simply what the best brand-building campaigns do: not try to persuade people.

Congrats to anyone involved in this. It's a tricky category. But this is a clear demonstration of marketing effectiveness all marketers can learn from.

content:
If an investor zones out during your pitch, that’s the most useful information you could have got out of the meeting.

Fundraising can be rough.

In an ideal world, investors owe pitching founders the courtesy of hearing the full pitch and giving honest feedback. It’s what I’ve always tried to do.

But having also been on the fundraising end of things as a founder, the blunt truth is that the responsibility still sits with us to hold people’s attention.

I saw it back when I was doing stand up.
I’ve seen it as a founder pitching.

You’ve got to bomb on stage a couple of times and test the material in a ‘low risk’ environment before assuming it will land with the people you really want at your table.

Practice the pitch.
Ideally to people who don’t care.
Try it on your team.
Then try it on your family.
Test it out at events.

There’s an art to getting people to care.

If you nail that, you’re much less likely to lose investors mid-pitch.

But if they are zoning out - that’s your signal to seriously up your game (or maybe it’s just their fifth meeting of the day and it’s 29 degrees outside. You choose)

content:
At some unknown point, some unknown person decided that personality and professionalism were incompatible.

And the advertising agencies of the world leapt on the thought – buying gray carpets, moving people to souless offices with identical open plan schemes, adopting the language and vernacular of LinkedIn for internal communications, and AI written, jargon filled nonsense for external comms.

We convinced ourselves that people didn’t have time for an interesting or quirky idea and tried to get a half dozen messages into the first 5 seconds, so that people would hear them before they skipped.

And it showed in the work

“At 60 miles per hour the loudest thing you can hear is the ticking of the electric clock” became  “Drive. Luxury.”

We became obsessed with the idea that looking, sounding & behaving like our clients would make our clients like us more. 

With the thought that a hail of bullet points was the way to sell an idea – as though you could list your way to love.

We censored ourselves, expelled the people who provided the friction needed to make the oyster and congratulated ourselves on the ruthless efficiency of it all – as the industry crumbled. 

Dullards with the artistic soul of a lobotomized Excel spreadsheet now sit atop almost every department. 

“Gurus” with a templated way of approaching every problem and presenting every solution now pay their mortgages with money taken from young people looking at ways to negotiate the machine.

We smugly parrot the line “Ai will never replace human creativity” while doing all that we can to turn our people into machines.

We have replaced trust with endless reviews. Thinking with orthodoxy. Ideas with content.

We are the bland.

An army of the undead, walking in well-drilled unison towards the cliff edge.

And it makes me rather sad.

If you’re a neurodiverse founder, this works in your favour. It can make you a better leader of your team and a more effective storyteller for your business.

Too many business meetings are wasted on jargon.

You get to set the standard for communication:

Encouraging the team to ask more ‘obvious’ questions
Asking more people “and what’s your take on that?”
Prompting the team to ask their own follow up Qs

Your job as a leader isn’t to look like the smartest in the room.

It's to strip away the noise so everyone can actually execute.

Simplify everything.

WHY DISTINCTIVE BRAND ASSETS MATTER

This is one of the topics that Mark Ritson and Byron Sharp were passionately in agreement over when we spoke on Uncensored CMO

Byron uses the phrase 'a brand that looks like itself' to define what he means and as Mark explains you want to be recognisable when your customer is thinking about buying the category

There are 3 really important things to consider here

👉 Firstly your customers tends to buy a lot less frequently that you think they do. 

When I worked on Lucozade I discovered that an enormous about of my sales came from people who bought less than once a year. That was a shocking discovery and emphasised the importance of being easily recognised

👉 Secondly marketers are bad judges of their own distinctive assets

One of my favourite Ehrenberg-Bass Institute studies looked into how recognisable and how unique marketers thought their own distinctive assets were. The gap between the marketers and the customer was huge showing just how important it is to research what they actually recognise

👉 Thirdly Distinctive Brand Assets are built over decades

Before changing your design every year consider that most strong brands have been built through consistently applying their distinctive brand assets in all their packaging, point of sale and media

Consistency and discipline matter a lot
