Unreasonable hospitality isn't a luxury.

It's sometimes a $10 decision that someone makes to actually pay attention.

The surprising power of giving people more than they expected.

Most people do their job. A few people notice you.

A hotel housekeeper noticed that Kory kept rearranging her toiletries. So she brought a makeup organizer, organized everything in order, and left a handwritten note that said at the top, "We noticed."

Two words. Infinite signal.

Jon had a personal driver Jean-Pierre, who was within 2 minutes. Every hour. Every day. And every time he said thank you he would immediately respond, "You are welcome."

Here's the lesson:

GIVE PEOPLE MORE THAN THEY EXPECTED/ The gesture doesn't have to be expensive. It has to be thoughtful. Notice the person, not just the task. The ripple effect of one small act of care outlasts the moment by miles.

TRUST IS THE ONLY CURRENCY THAT COMPOUNDS/ We talked about the creator economy this week. Brands keep making the same mistake: turning creators into spokespeople. The moment the audience senses a script, trust breaks.

Real collaboration lifts both sides to higher ground neither could reach alone. Find the intersection point. That's where the magic is.

STOP WAITING FOR THE AI CONVERSATION TO END/ It already has. The question isn't "should we use AI?" It's "what can we do now that we couldn't do before?" That's a much more interesting place to start.

And the biggest takeaway from a week in Cannes?

The real power wasn't the creative. It was the connections.

Phones down. Long lunches. New friends. The World Cup reminded the entire world that community still wins.

Let's get back to basics. Stop and smell the tuberose.

content:
LinkedIn is testing suggested feeds.

I've had a few people ask me about this since my last update. "What does it mean? Can we do anything about it?"

Short answer: yes. Here's what I'm thinking.

How it works: LinkedIn looks at the topics you follow, posts you engage with, and content you spend time reading. Then it surfaces posts — and creators — that match those interests. Even if you don't follow them.

They tried something like this before and it didnt work. But with posts up 14% and video up 30% YoY, they have more content to work with now.

If this rolls out, discoverability changes. Your content won't just reach followers,  it will (hopefully) get surfaced to strangers based on topic and engagement quality.

Here's how to position for it:

𝟭) 𝗢𝘄𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰 (𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗼𝗿𝘆)
Topic-based feeds reward specificity. If LinkedIn's algorithm can't figure out what you're "about," you won't get categorized. Pick a topic that's likely to have its own feed (AI, leadership, marketing, sales, career growth) and stay in your lane. There may also be event-based feeds (like Cannes, the World Cup or major conferences), so timely content tied to big moments could get a boost too.

𝟮) 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗲-𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁
Suggested feeds will likely weight saves and shares over likes. Frameworks, how-tos, contrarian takes with substance.. content people bookmark to revisit.

𝟯) 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗵𝘁𝗮𝗴𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆
If feeds are topic-based, hashtags may matter more for categorization. 2-3 specific ones. Not 10 generic ones.

𝟰) 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗼
Video is surging. Suggested feeds may prioritise it to keep users on-platform longer. Worth experimenting if you're comfortable on camera.

𝟱) 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗼𝘂𝘁-𝗼𝗳-𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵
LinkedIn's new analytics show in-network vs out-of-network views. High out-of-network % = the algorithm is working for you.

To be clear: this is still in testing. Nothing is final, and it might not even roll out. But these are good habits regardless of what LinkedIn does next.

The creators who are ready will benefit most.

Practical (no bs) fundraising advice from a startup founder who has raised $23M in funding over the last four years:

→ Before you do anything else, build the narrative

What are you building

Why does it matter

Why now

Why you

→ Walk it through out loud.

Things that read well on paper don't always land when you're saying them to someone in-person.

You need to hear yourself say it. 

Thats how you will feel where it flows and where it dies.

→ Test it on people who'll be HONEST with you.

Go to your business minded friends, other founders, anyone who'll push back. 

Your objective isn’t to impress them. 

You need to find the gaps before an investor does.

→ Start pitching to investors.

Seek out investors in networking events, intros, wherever you can get in front of them. 

Don't wait until you feel ready (you’ll never feel ready)

Get in front of people and emphasise hard on what's working.

→ What to have before you go:

✅ Pitch skeleton 

✅ High level forecasts (they won't be accurate but you need them)

✅ Strong competitor analysis (know who's out there)

✅ Early traction (even your advisors count)

✅With AI at your disposal, the "I need a prototype to raise" excuse is gone. 

The pitch will get better every time you do it.  

That’s just how it works.

Twix keeps on delivering

1. It's emotional AND distinctive, my research with Effie Worldwide and Mark Ritson showed that campaigns that manage to do both see 4x the chance of reporting incremental profit.

2. It's lent into the most powerful marketing tool: time. This campaign has been running for years; we saw in the Effie data that campaigns that are emotional and distinctive AND run for over 3 years are 7.5x more likely to report profit growth.

3. 29% of viewers actually found this funny, double the UK average. It's rare that advertising actually delivers this. Humour opens us up to new ideas and brands.

4. It will build salience, not just awareness. 28% of viewers built memories for "chocolate." Sounds obvious but most ads don't do this, we must anchor our brand equity around the category.

A lot happened in the last few weeks. Here's what's changing on LinkedIn (and what it means for you)

𝟭) 𝗡𝗲𝘄 "r𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵" 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰
LinkedIn now shows whether your posts are reaching new audiences or just your existing followers. Your analytics will split performance between in-network and out-of-network views.

Why this matters: You can finally see if your content is actually growing your audience... or just preaching to the choir.

𝟮) 𝗦𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴
LinkedIn is testing topic-focused feeds recommended based on what you engage with. Think: curated feeds for your industry, trending news, specific interests.

They tested something similar last year and it didn't stick. But with posts up 14% and video up 30% YoY, they have more content to surface. This could be their next attempt at expanding how we consume content beyond the main feed.

𝟯) 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 (𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲'𝘀 𝗯𝗶𝗴)

What this tells me: LinkedIn is making it easier to tap into partner networks. Company pages notoriously get less reach than personal profiles - this is a workaround. Great for product launches, team wins, brand partnerships.

Currently testing, broader rollout coming in the next few months.

𝟰) 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
LinkedIn is expanding its "connected apps" feature. You can now showcase verifiable skills from 15+ platforms including HubSpot, Fiverr, Beehiiv, Buffer, and more - with Adobe, GitHub Copilot, Zapier, and others coming soon.

The twist: these aren't self-reported. The apps generate descriptions based on your actual usage. Top users get a "Top User" badge.

What this means: Your profile becomes a portfolio of verified capabilities, not just claims. With demand for AI skills doubling YoY, this could become a real differentiator.

My biggest TAKEAWAY: LinkedIn is getting more sophisticated about content distribution.

Reach metrics. Suggested feeds. Collaborative posts. Verified skills.

They're building infrastructure for creators and brands to grow more intentionally - while giving users more control over what they see.

The platform is maturing. And the people paying attention will benefit most.

WHY THE 95:5 RULE BEATS THEM ALL

This has to be one of the most important rules of marketing ever created

I had the chance to ask Byron Sharp from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute how the 95:5 rule originated

He said John Dawes was struggling to explain the 'negative binomial distribution in B2B' and casually said that only 5% of people are in market at any one time

Splitting the G vs Setting the table

Moretti can't believe their luck

Splitting the G, where you drink enough Guinness to half the logo on the glass, has surely done wonderful things for sales.

Mainly because if you gulp past the foam at the top, you actually avoid the nitrogen, which is bitter. Making it a far more pleasant pint.

This came about as a happy accident, born from brand equity. If people care about your brand enough, and know what you look like and stand for. Then you'll find it popping up in "culture."

I've never seen an agency manage actually to manufacture something so brilliant.

Now we are starting to see people take to social to "set the table" for The HEINEKEN Company's Birra Moretti.

Admittedly, this looks like nailing half a pint of the stuff. And there's no creamy head to gulp past. So it's a LITTLE more random.

But let's see if this actually goes anywhere. Will this catch on? Do Brits need to find a new hobby? Is there an evil mastermind behind all of this, and is it Schooner Scorer? Who knows.

content:
15 years later. With different data. We've shown the same: engagement rate is NOT brand growth. But is engagement really "useless"?

This is one of the things TikTok's Sarah van den Eertwegh, WPP's Joshua Gornell and I will be really diving into in our webinar on Wednesday (open to all: https://lnkd.in/eYKeFTn8)

Here's my thinking:

1. Nielsen showed 15years ago that Click Through Rate doesn't have a significant relationship with brand lift outcomes.

2. Now, we see the same relationship on TikTok with a modern, huge dataset. There's no significant relationship between a campaign's overall engagement rate and the Brand Awareness and Ad Recall it generates.

3. However, not all engagement is equal. We found that the comments-to-likes ratio has a small but significant relationship. So, deep engagement can help us decide that week a little. But creative quality (how well branded and emotional ads are) explain Brand Memory lift 5x better!

4. So is engagement rate useless? No. In our new Creator Effectiveness Playbook, I share that 1) it's still a useful signal of what the platform algorithms like and if users have found the content engaging and 2) within a campaign, mid-flight, that week, it could be a useful guide to refining a campaign. But we cannot treat this as an outcome, just an output that we treat properly.

However, the data is clear, ending a campaign and reporting on general engagement rate as success. Or having this as your overall campaign objective clearly is not best practice.

If you are interested in this sort of world-leading, nuanced, practical insight. Join us tomorrow to hear more!

Congrats to the team for unlocking these huge insights: TikTok TikTok for Business System1 WPP Media Services WPP Beth Marchant Josh Fruttiger

9 things I'm thinking about LinkedIn right now.

1) Talk about one thing. The people who grow fastest on LinkedIn are the ones who become synonymous with a topic. Not five topics. One.

2) Industry influence > influencer status. Being known by 500 decision-makers in your space beats being known by 50,000 random people. 

3) Newsjacking works if you bring it back to you. Commenting on news without linking it to your expertise just makes you look like everyone else chasing clicks.

4) Commenting is the most underrated growth strategy. I've watched people build real relationships and pipeline from comments alone. Most people skip it.

5) Storytelling wins when you make it about the reader. The story is the vehicle. The reader's takeaway is the destination.

6) Visibility compounds. Opportunities find the most seen, not the most skilled. I've seen this play out dozens of times with clients.

7) Personal experience beats generic advice every time. "Here's what worked for me" outperforms "Here's what you should do" almost always.

8) Share your wins. Even when it feels awkward. Especially when it feels awkward. If you won't promote yourself, who will?

9) Send the DM. Worst case: silence. Best case: career-changing. I've had both. The upside is always worth it.

That's where my head is at right now. What would you add?

LinkedIn is drifting further into marketing stunts, cheering on organic content and awards stuff. So I cracked open System1's Competitive Edge database of every UK and US TV ad tested with millions of consumers to see what sort of advertising is actually moving the dial at the moment.

Yano, the stuff with millions of spend. billions of high-attention impressions. And the ad is actually distinctive and emotional. What I call an "Excess Share of Creativity" in market.

VCCP's new work for Carlsberg Britvic's Tango stood out, top of the pile.

1. This is more than a strap line, its a repeatable, ownable creative framing that compounds memories over time. A Fluent Device like this makes advertising more emotional and distinct with each use, and it grows fame (people talking about your brand). The fact that this full line hasn't been used since 2002, yet everyone still loves it, speaks volumes.

The same positioning and creative platform have been used, but the execution has been refreshed for 2026. In my research, "Compound Creativity," we showed that similarly consistent brands report 4x more Large Brand Effects. Consistency is how brands grow.

3. Despite it being so short, it lands in the top 20% of emotional response and 91% of people recognise the brand. All due to this compound effect, but because they've leaned into showmanship. content:
Founders need to spend more time scrolling social media.
There I said it - but hear me out on why....



This isn't a point of view I love holding because it goes against all the healthy narratives around positive mental health and good habits.

But…

If you’re a founder or marketer in a consumer-facing brand, you need to be spending a LOT of time on Instagram and TikTok.

Doesn’t sound that counterintuitive?

Not at face value. 

But if I had a pound for every founder I’ve heard say something like “I don’t use social media at all, it’s a waste of time, leave that to the social person,” I’d be a few hundred quid up.

It’s almost become a badge of honour.

But the truth is, for all its ills (and I hate a lot about it too), social media is where culture lives, is created and moves. 

It’s where creativity is on constant display, where freak flags fly and new ideas collide.

By refusing to be on social media, lots of founders (and more marketers than feels right) are giving themselves a competitive disadvantage. 

They’re reducing exposure to the culture they’re trying to insert their brand into. 

They’re ignoring what their customers are consuming. 

And they’re limiting themselves to less interesting inputs, which leads to less interesting outputs.

So am I saying doom scroll every day?

Not exactly. But some aimless scrolling helps when you’re trying to build a brand of the culture. It gives you new ideas to try and unlocks creative blockers.

Just be mindful of what you scroll. Change it up, find new and interesting things that push you out of your comfort zone, don’t get complacent.

So there you go. I’m a stooge for Zuck, advocating for his toxic platform. I’m sorry.

But until culture moves somewhere else, I can’t shift this uncomfortable belief.

Let me know if you agree or disagree 👇

content:
3 WAYS TO LAND A C-SUITE ROLE

Interviewing the World's most successful CMO's and founders on Uncensored CMO naturally means I get asked how to get a C-suite role

In my experience it has very little to do with functional expertise - although that is probably a given

If I was starting out I would focus on these 3 things

(1) A BOSS WHO BACKS YOU

It's easy to obsess about the brand and role but the one thing you should really be obsessed about is who you work for. Your boss can make more of an impact on your career than anyone else

Do they believe in you even more than you believe in yourself?
Are they willing to push you even before you are ready? 
Will they provide aircover when things go wrong? 
Are they promoting you in rooms you aren't in? 
Are they coaching you to replace them?

I will forever be grateful to the bosses that did that for me and I try my best to be that boss to people who work for me

(2) GO SMALL TO GO BIG

This might sound counter-intuitive but the fastest way to gain experience is to take a step down. Find a smaller brand, business or team and you will quickly be given way more responsibility and a chance to prove yourself

I did this a few times in my career and once you get over the hit to the ego you quickly realise the freedom you gain can accelerate your career massively

(3) BECOME A LEADER

The greatest lesson I learnt is that success on the C-Suite isn't really anything to do with functional competence but how good a leader you become. In my largest role I had over 100 people in my team so success was determined by my ability to be a leader of leaders.

You also quickly discover in a C-suite role that your success is based on your ability to manage multiple stakeholders and influence across the entire company

Having made it how to do you succeed?

Because every conversation with someone smarter than you is an opportunity to compress years of learning into minutes.

content:
7 tips to excel in a marketing career

I get asked "What advice do you have for young people just starting in marketing" a lot. So I've given it proper thought.

I won't pretend I had a grand strategy to get to the C-suite before 30.

But I've thought about the big wins in my career so far, from growing successful challenger brands to helping run huge consumer brands, and now scaling System1 and leading huge partnerships, campaigns, and research.

This stuff stands out as big unlocks.

1. Every person & meeting matters

The people I'm working with now to do crazy impactful things were often random chance meetings, or I worked with them once while we weren't super senior. Treat everyone like you would want to be treated. Like they could be your CEO one day.

(Jeez, I hope people think I do this. I try 😂)

2. Today could be the day it all changes

There have been 2-3 days when I felt momentum lurch forward. I never saw it coming, but that presentation, meeting, or launch could be the spark that catches. You'll never see it coming. Often the days you think are big and important aren't.

3. Compound effort

To be ready for those moments, I've reaslised it's really just the culmination of hundreds of little things (meetings, projects, ideas, people) that compound over time to create what you think is luck but it really isn't.

4. Be weird

If you aren't weird, you're normal, and you'll end up doing normal things. Sounds rude, but it's true. Don't be weird for weird's sake, be you. But following what everyone is doing is obviously the road to average.

5. Follow the crumbs

If you feel that tickle, follow it. Read, search, research, play. The most interesting stuff I've worked on came about through taking time to explore. AI massively helps with this.

6. Go to the gym

Not the actual gym (although that helps). But there are largely 2 types of marketers, one that understands the theory and best practice, and one that wings it. You want to be part of the former. The difference is training.

The single best thing I did to level up and get serious was genuinley Mark Ritson's MiniMBA in Marketing. Anyone I've met who's done it agrees.

7. It's not brain surgery

I studied and trained first as a doctor when I was younger. People get so damn worried about things in marketing. Don't, it will wear you out.

Equally, it's really not that complicated. Marketing is influencing for (commercial) gain. If you're in a room where people are pretending it's more complicated than that, try leaving that room.

Hope that is useful to at least one person. If you read this and you have a tip, please share it below!

Oh and a bonus one: there's a handful of mentors that gave me a shot before I was ready, find those people. Work for them. Pay them back. They turn into the most beautiful relationships.

content:
Culture isn’t a buzzword.  

It’s how it feels to be you in your company on a random Tuesday.

Culture = behavior, not slogans

If your values are the words on the wall, culture is what people actually do when the pressure is on.

Values are what you believe, culture is how you behave. 

And since you can’t live what you haven’t named, the first job of any leader is to clearly codify the ethos:

“In this team, how do we show up in conflict, in teamwork, in accountability?”

If you’re in a position to shape culture, start here:

CODIFY YOUR ETHOS
Be bullet proof on your vision, mission, values, purpose, cultural norms. 

Write down the behaviors that matter in plain language.  

Think: “We say the hard thing with care,” “We own mistakes in the open,” “We debate ideas, not people.”

Communicate it with clarity and consistency.

HIRE AND PROMOTE FOR IT
Don’t just hire for skills. Hire for frequency.  

Ask: “Does this person’s natural way of operating enhance the environment we’re building?”

Hire people who contribute to the culture, not detract from it.

MODEL AND PROTECT IT
The things you let slide are just as powerful as the things you celebrate. Every behavior you quietly tolerate becomes the new standard.

If you’re not the boss… you still have a choice

Pay attention to how leaders act, not what they say.  

Ask in interviews: “What behaviors get celebrated here?”

If the culture and your ethos don’t match, it doesn’t mean you’re broken.  

It might just mean you’re in the wrong room.

In this weeks Uncensored Renegades, we go deep on fear-based vs. love-based cultures, cultural contagion, and one question every leader should be asking their teams:  

“What do you need to see differently from us in order to set you up to succeed?”

Find a company whose culture aligns with yours.  

That intersection point—between who you are and how they operate is where the magic happens.

content:
Finally, someone's as committed to consistency as I am

Byron Sharp and Mark Ritson doubled down on consistency on the main stage at Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity this year

It caused quite the stir. It's one of the key principles of marketing effectiveness over the past decade. And, as I shared in my column last week, marketers are ready for the next decade of effectiveness learnings.

What is consistency? How do we plan it? How do we use imagionative repetition to refresh, to move on without moving anything off?

"Compound Creativity" is worth revisiting, and I'll be sharing more from that research with System1, IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) and Effie Worldwide again over the coming weeks.

It's a holistic view on creative consistency that I've now worked with hundreds of the world's biggest brands to help implement, exploring how different types of consistency do different things.

Les Binet, sarah carter and I shared it at Cannes last year - Les and Sarah each brought their own special magic...

1. Consistent Foundations - depending on which category, market, or region you're in, people call this different things, "roots" or "cohesion". A key theme leaving Cannes this year.

A brand consistently sticking to its essence, with the output often an enduring Creative Platform/Idea, Positioning and Agency-Client Relationship.  In Compound Creativity, we found brands with more consistent Creative Foundations are 5.4x more likely to report large gains in awareness and 7x more likely to report differentiation gains.

sarah carter likens this to the 3 Ms. Monet, Marmite and Marge. How artists, the Simpsons and Marmite have never stuck to the same execution but they've consistently delivered what they are known and loved for.

2. Culture of Consistency - putting ideas to work. Mark Ritson often talks to this point heavily, wear out doesn't really exist. "Let your cakes bake for longer." And we must consistently put our work in more places and channels.

But Les Binet has extended this thinking further recently with "Go Big or Go Home" showing the need for big ideas in more places, with a campaign's budget being 9x better at explaining budget compared to ROI.

In Compound Creativity, we've found that brands with a higher culture of consistency are 6x more likely to report large profit growth.

3. Consistent Execution - Often what Byron and Jenni at EBI talk most about, repeating the same look and feel (inc. distinctive brand assets) again and again over time, to increase uniqueness recognition. Ie distictinvess.

I think this is the most obvious type of consistency that many talk about, but what this research shows is that all three types matter. The most consistent brands report 2.2x more very large brand effects in the IPA databank.

The research and lots of videos on this are now free here: https://lnkd.in/ekBjYSGQ

content:
Clients don’t want boring.

But, fuck, account people are convinced that they do.

Three times in the last month I’ve had an account team take a proposal that they said they loved and butcher it by trying to make it “client friendly”

The language got more corporate, boxes were added, bullet points were liberally sprayed around, jargon found its way through the cracks and into every sentence - until the proposal we had read like a legal document that needed to be signed before Grandma could be unplugged.

Two of those teams apologized saying “we just have to make it a little more boring, because it has to go to the client for approval”

Obviously the shrift that was given to these teams made Kylie look tall – but the idea that an agency would deliberately seek to present “a more boring” option genuinely worried me. 

Who told account people that clients wanted “boring” from their agencies?

Not the client, I can assure you. 

We’re in the engagement business. 

And that has to extend to the way we communicate with clients.

So having the rules of a workshop be “no biting, no gouging, lots of fighting” or opening with Prince on Sesame Street, or having a part of the meeting be Flintstones themed (“Yabba, Dabba, Don’t”) or telling the truth about the product, or admitting that you’re primarily bought by assholes, or admitting that one of the ideas you presented last time was an absolute dog, but that it taught you something is all good. 

Nobody got fired for presenting something interesting. Or for presenting in an interesting way. And if they did it wasn’t a firing, it was a lucky escape.

No, you can’t make it “more boring” for the client.

content:
I've analyzed over 100 of my own LinkedIn posts.

Looked at what performed. What flopped. What drove actual conversations.

Here are 10 content types/patterns that consistently work. Not formats like 'video' or 'carousel'... Something more specific and useful. 

ps: you might want to save this for future reference 😉 

𝟭. "Breaking News" commentary
Spot something happening in your industry. Add your take before anyone else does. Speed + opinion = reach.

𝟮. Cultural moment hijacking
A viral moment happens. You connect it to your world. My Jaguar/Nothing post did 18x engagement because I extracted a marketing lesson from a brand beef.

𝟯. Personal stories with business punchlines
I wrote about a school trip with my 4-year-old. Turned it into a funny B2B sales lessons. Relatable setup, unexpected payoff.

𝟰. "The thing nobody's talking about"
Algorithm changes. Platform shifts. Industry blind spots. Position yourself as the person who decodes what others miss.

𝟱. Sports-to-business bridge content
(Or whatever your passion is.) Take an iconic moment from your world and extract a lesson that non-experts still get.

𝟲. Industry job listing analysis
Find a job posting that signals where an industry is heading. Dissect it. 
(s/o to Noah Greenberg who is the best at this)

𝟳. Contrarian platform takes
Acknowledge what everyone hates about LinkedIn. Then flip it. "LinkedIn is cringe... and that's fine" energy.

𝟴. Milestone posts with a unique twist
Skip the generic "grateful for 10k followers" post. Subvert expectations. My "28,000 followers, here are 28,000 lessons" post worked because it was self-aware.

𝟵. Visual trend spotting
Catch a UX change or new feature early. Be first. Explain the implications.

𝟭𝟬. Creator economy shifts
Spot when traditional companies adopt creator strategies. Explain the shift, not just the news. (I called it "creatorfication" and people remembered it.)

main takeaway:

These aren't templates to copy. They're starting points.

You can take "Sports-to-Business Bridge" and make it "Music-to-Leadership" or "Parenting-to-Product Management."

The framework stays. The context becomes yours.

The best content sounds like something only you could write. These 10 types just help you find where your experience meets your audience's curiosity.

content:
As a travelling gambler aboard a train bound for nowhere wisely advised

“You've got to know when to hold 'em. 
Know when to fold 'em.
Know when to walk away. 
And know when to run”

The key is in the knowing. 
And that's not easy.

But there are things that you can look for.

"Does the work you're being asked to do align with your values?"
Are you being asked to do things that you fundamentally disagree with?

"Are you being fairly paid?"
There's no greater barometer of what a company thinks of you than what they pay you

"Are you being heard?"
Are your ideas fairly considered? Does your voice matter to the company?

"Does the company share your ambition for the work?"
Never work with people less ambitious than you are

"Are you prepared to make lifestyle changes in order to get out of there?"
Are you prepared to make personal sacrifices in return for an exit?

"Is your issue with a person or with a culture?"
Never leave because of a toxic person, do leave if the agency won't / can't deal with them

And as a very wise woman once said to me

"Do you need to change everything, or do you just need a nap?"

Which is probably the best life advice I can pass on to anyone

content:
The Instagram algorithm doesn't hate you, you just haven’t updated your strategy in the last three years !! 👀🎙️👋🚨

Remember: over a decade ago, Instagram didn’t have Explore, Reels or Stories. You posted your content, your followers saw it in a chronological feed, and reach was follower-led. 

But this is no longer how the platform operates, and it hasn’t been that way for a *long* time. 

Reach hasn’t disappeared but instead, it’s been redistributed across multiple surfaces designed to show content to non-followers via: Reels, Explore, Suggested and Search. 

There’s two things to remember, each of these surfaces have different algorithms, and you’re competing with more content than ever. 

Making reach and engagement far more competitive, and hard to achieve. A post can resonate with your audience but struggle to reach beyond that if your content isn’t easily understood, categorised, and surfaced to the right users. 

In practice, this means formats now play different roles within the ecosystem:

→ Reels + Carousels = best for reaching new audiences
→ Carousels + Static Images + Stories = best for engaging current followers 
→ Lives + Channels = best for nurturing your most loyal fans 

The shift is less about the algorithm “constantly changing” and more about Instagram evolving into a multi-surface discovery platform rather than a single feed.

Beyond this, social SEO is becoming increasingly important as Instagram deprioritises hashtags (you can now only use five in your posts) and the search experience continues to be improved – with your Instagram content now surfacing in search engines, and blue search suggestions in comments. 

(📌 Speaking of Social SEO, I created a free workbook alllllll about it: https://lnkd.in/dTpsc-Pu) 

I’ve created a couple of cheat sheets that explains what Instagram thinks helps reach vs. what I think helps reach, make sure to screenshot or save for later !! I  would LOVE to hear your takes in the comments 👋🙂‍↕️💬

P.S. You can see how your content is performing with non-followers by clicking on your individual post insights, where it then breaks down the percentage of people who viewed your post by: feed, stories, profile, explore and search.

Just got back to the UK, looking at a notebook that's definitely seen better days.  

Cannes is a beautiful whirlwind, and sometimes you need a little distance to find the real signal.   

Here are the 3 biggest reality checks from the Palais - the stuff that felt most human, honest and useful for my audience: 

1. The creator economy isn't coming - it's already here. 

Never before have this many creators landed on the streets of Cannes. 

What used to be a fringe conversation at this festival is now front and centre.
 If you needed proof that the industry has shifted, just look at who's walking the Croisette this year. 

2. Relationships and networking should be taught in school.
We spend years learning theory and almost no time learning how to build real connections. Yet in this industry and honestly, in most your network is often the difference between a good idea and one that actually goes somewhere. 

3. Taste and humanity will be the only moat in an AI-first world. As AI lowers the barrier to producing content, what won't be commoditised is judgment - knowing what's actually good, what resonates, what feels true. 
That's a distinctly human skill, and it's about to become the most valuable one in the room. 

Another odd, yet insightful thing I noticed? "We should do something" is probably the most popular way to end most conversations. 

You hear it on the terrace, in the Palais, and definitely while waiting for an Uber.
It's the industry's way of sharing a spark of inspiration before life gets busy again.  

But for the creators who showed up to actually build, that phrase is the start of a real bridge. 

Cannes Lions isn't about fitting into an exclusive club. It's about realising that if you've got a perspective that adds value, you already belong in the room - even if you're still navigating the fancy dinners and the endless networking. 

I'm heading back to the grind feeling sharper and admittedly a bit exhausted, but ready to actually do something with all that inspiration. If you were there, I hope you found your spark.   If you weren't, see you next year!

content:
Twice in two days I've been reminded of one of the most important lessons every challenger brand NEEDS to learn....

 
Fish where the fish are.
 
Or, to put it another way - meet your customer where they are.
 
One example of this came up in a conversation with 🌍 Adam Joe Parker 🌊, CMO of OceanSaver. 

Whilst most eco brands are in the business of making eco mainstream, Ocean Saver are trying to make mainstream eco.
 
It's nuanced but makes perfect sense. 

Because if you're selling everyday goods (that happen to be eco) like dishwasher and laundry tablets, it's a lot easier to meet your customers where they already are...

- i.e. in the dishwasher aisle in Tesco with a product that feels familiar (category cues, pack size etc.) 

than trying to convince people to change their buying habits by, for example asking them to buy their dishwasher tabs online.

The other instance was with a brand trying to get people to engage with content they desperately wanted to make. 

The content wasn't bad and it was very in line with their mission but it also wasn't the sort of content their target demo were desperately seeking out.
 
So we reframed to ask 

- how can you still stay true to the core brand purpose, but meet the audience where they already are - i.e. in different niches, formats, styles. 

How can we make the brand purpose work within content formats that their target audience actually are seeking out already?
 
Simple reframe, powerful results.

I see lots of brands trying to push water uphill but there's no prizes for playing the game on hard mode - so be sure to ask yourself whether you're really meeting your customer where they already are.

- Being honest with what I didn’t know. People can tell when you’re bluffing

You want to find the right ones.

When you remember it’s a two way street and that it has to work for YOU as well, it feels a lot less brutal.

One of the best things about Cannes Lions is watching very successful people completely lose their composure.
A CMO spots their favourite musician.
A founder bumps into a creator they've followed for years.
A CEO suddenly wants a selfie.
It turns out that no matter how impressive someone's job title is, we're all fans of something.
I've certainly been guilty of it this week.
That's why Spotify Advertising focus on fandom is so interesting.
Marketers spend a lot of time talking about audiences, impressions and reach. But audiences don't recommend things to their friends. Fans do.
Fans don't queue for hours because they have high brand awareness.
They do it because they care.
And when people care, they participate. They share. They bring other people with them.
That's what I've enjoyed about Spotify Beach this week. A reminder that behind every audience segment is a real person who's passionate about something.

content:
I went on a school trip with my 4-year-old this week.

As the designated dad.

5 things it taught me about B2B sales  😆 (bear with me)

𝟭. 𝗦𝗻𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗻𝗲𝗴𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹.
You think sales is tough? Try explaining why one kid gets the blue wrapper and another gets red. 

𝟮. 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗴𝗵𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂.
One kid held my hand for 20 minutes. Best friends. Then she saw a butterfly and I never existed. Sound familiar?

𝟯. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸.
I thought I was in charge. Turns out it was the teacher. She controlled the schedule, the bathroom breaks, and whether we got ice cream. I had zero authority.

𝟰. 𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.
I tried to get everyone excited about the next activity right after lunch. 15 kids. Full stomachs. Zero interest. Read the room before you pitch.

𝟱. "𝗠𝗮𝘆𝗯𝗲" 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱.
I said 'maybe ice cream' once. Once. The fallout lasted 45 minutes. In sales, vague commitments create very specific problems.

Next time someone tells me  sales is complex, I'm sending them on a field trip.

Better ROI than most conferences I've been to.

content:
People talk about work/life balance. 

But for a lot of founders, the fun is in doing the work.

I've worked most weekends for most of my career. At least one day. Usually both.

And as a founder, this schedule suits me.

I'm not going to pretend there isn't privilege in being able to do this (no dependents, a very understanding partner).

But I love and am obsessed with the work we’re doing.

I’m committed to my company and my team.

I want to use this one life to build something with meaning.

There's a difference between grinding because you feel trapped and working because you're genuinely pulled towards it.

The first burns you out.

The second drives you forward.

When you love what you're building, logging on for a few hours on a Sunday doesn't feel like sacrifice.

It feels like progress.

Find work that pulls you in - not work you have to push yourself through.

The most dangerous bullies don’t work in school hallways.

Not because it strengthens teams.

They interrupt.

They belittle.

They humiliate.

They intimidate.

Real leaders do the opposite.

They hold people accountable without disrespecting them.

They create environments where people grow instead of shrink.

The strongest person in the room isn’t the one who makes everyone uncomfortable.

It’s the one who makes everyone better.

Your title may earn respect.

But how you treat people determines whether you deserve it.

'What metrics should I track on LinkedIn?'

I get asked this a lot. And the answer is always: it depends.

Impressions? Engagement rate? Follower growth?

Sure, they all matter to some degree. But there's one metric I think is massively underrated:

Who is actually seeing your content?

Here's a snapshot from one of our clients (shared with permission):

5% Founder
4% Managing Directors
3% CEOs
2% Owner
2% Board Members

This is who's reading his posts. Every week.

Not random eyeballs. Decision-makers.

This is what we optimise for at Shake Content.

We don't focus on personal brand for the sake of personal brand. We focus on business outcomes.

→ Are the right people seeing you?
→ Are they engaging?
→ Is it leading to conversations?

For this client, it has. More inbound. More pipeline. More closed deals.

Vanity metrics are easy to chase. But reaching the people who can actually buy from you? That's a different game.

If your content isn't getting in front of the right audience, we should talk.

content:
Your best post won't be the one you spent 3 hours on.

My friend David Walsh (CEO of Limelight) asked me about the biggest mistake I see people make on LinkedIn.

My answer: treating every post like it's a book.

You write something. Sleep on it. Edit it. Sleep on it again. Ask three friends. Delete it. Start over.

Meanwhile, someone else just posted a half-baked thought that outperformed your masterpiece.

The truth is:
→ High effort ≠ high performance
→ Your quick takes often hit harder than your polished essays
→ Social media is a long-term game | consistency beats perfection

Stop waiting until it's perfect. Start posting until you find your rhythm.

Thanks David for having me on 🙏

content:
We are filtering out incredible talent because of unrealistic checklist expectations. 

Look at most job descriptions today. They require 5 years of experience for an entry-level role, mastery of three different software ecosystems and a hyper-specific background. We’ve turned hiring into a data-matching exercise instead of a human one.

But here is the reality: 90% of jobs can be taught.

You can teach someone how to use a CRM. You can teach them your internal processes. You can teach them how to analyse your specific datasets.

What you cannot teach is curiosity, work ethic, integrity, and a willingness to learn.

Stop looking for the perfect resume on paper and start looking for the right drive. 

Give people a freaking chance, they might just surprise you.

Don’t let a bad experience rewrite who you are. 

We’ve all been there. You go above and beyond for a client, only to get taken advantage of. You support a colleague, only to be left out of the credit. You stay loyal to a company, only to see corporate politics win the day.

Keep doing the right thing. The right people will eventually notice.

A lot of leaders mistake a loyal employee's compliance for happiness. But often, it's just the final stage before they walk out the door.

The dangerous thing about losing your most loyal people isn't that they suddenly start causing drama. It’s that they stop. When a passionate employee goes quiet, stops pushing back and just nods along, they haven't become "easy to manage" they’ve checked out.

Take care of the people who care about your business before it's too late.

content:
Not sure why no one's explained this to me before

B2B marketers have a content problem

I worked for very large FMCGs as a B2C marketer for years, then made the leap over to B2B marketing at System1 - helping other marketers make their marketing better.

People overstate the difference between B2C and B2B, it's all behaviour change. But one clear thing that's different (and I've struggled with) is the volume of genuinley interesting content you need to reach people.

The go-to is webinars and events; I do these a lot. Then they usually sit on YouTube, or if I'm lucky, I'll try to clip these into something for socials.

That's the B2B Content Iceberg, 80% of our best content is hidden.

After working with Riverside this week, I truly believe this is an easy thing for AI to help with. I recorded one bit of content, and they have this magic button (literally called "Magic Clips") that turns the 10min video into social clips and written posts, ranks them all for quality, and the top 5 are actually worth sharing (check that out yourself here: https://lnkd.in/etEJys2Q)

content:
Jeremy Clarkson's first Hawkstone TV ad is the best beer ad of 2026 so far

But there are two clear next steps for the brand.

System1 tests every single beer ad that goes on TV with millions of people (and a shed load privately for marketers that work directly with us). All to understand what people feel and think, to predict and explain how they will convert demand and grow brands.

This new campaign (launched right before the England match > and their first Hawkstone ad to not get banned!) just landed in the top 3% of beer ads we've ever tested for long-term creative effectiveness.

There are a few reasons that make this so impressive:

1. You can't claim this is just a lucky execution and ignore the wider strategy the team has around this brand, now the fastest growing beer in the UK. Clarkson's Farm, the Farmers Choir winning Britain's Got Talent, all the PR stunts. It's a masterclass in narrative and fame.

2. This is a challenger brand with low brand equity. It's incredibly hard to get people to care about ads in this situation. Yet these scores are similar to what we see for Guinness, which has been doing this for centuries.

3. Some people hate Jeremy (he brilliantly balances the line of too far to get reach, and that comes at a cost), yet our research with a nationally representative group of people barely picks that up due to T&P's use of showmanship. It's a world-class example of the use of character, humour, storytelling and more to capture broad attention. Even if you don't know the brand, or like Jeremy.

4. This is a genuinely elite lesson in proper positioning. "Farming" is one of the top memories the ad evokes. The category is owned by global giants. Guinness has cut through with "Irish, Hardwork, Soul." They are cutting through with "British Craft, Local, Farming, Worth It."

You see all this playing out where the ad actually scores FULL MARKS with 35-54yo. 5.9 Star Rating. Incredible.

But the testing reveals two clear next steps for the brand. One, only 75% of people linked the ad to Hawkstone. The famous characters and the wider brand really steal the show. And two, you see about 5% of the audience have a unique, visceral negative reaction to Kaleb.

If this is going to become one of the next category leaders, the job now is to slowly grow Hawkstone equity beyond Jeremy's gang and the Amazon show. A very interesting strategic challenge.

I've made the full research free for you to see for yourself here: https://lnkd.in/e7Kve4wF

Congrats Johnny Hornby and the team. This will become a global marekting case study that will teach the next generation of marketers, I'm sure.

content:
Exposure to failure as a founder is crucial if you want to grow. 

I was in major debt before selling my first company.

I also invested and went on to the board of a company that failed. 

I’ve failed and lost so many battles.

These failures taught me more than any success ever could.

When you've been through it - really been through it - you start to see patterns others miss.

You recognise when someone's about to make a mistake you made three years ago.

You understand why that "perfect" hire isn't actually perfect.

You know when to push through and when to step back.

The founders I meet who've never failed:
They're often the most fragile.

One setback and they spiral. One rejection and they question everything. 

Their over-identification with success means failure becomes devastating.

The ones who've been knocked down before:
- They get back up faster.
- They're calmer in chaos.
- They know how to survive.

Failure doesn't just teach you what not to do.

It teaches you who you actually are when things fall apart.

And that's the person you need to be when you're building something real.

If you're going through it right now - good.

You're becoming the founder you need to be for what comes next.

content:
Challenger brands - if you don't understand incrementality, you're not getting listed...



I'm sorry to break it to you but you're just not that special.

Most buyers don't want to list small challenger brands.

Think about it.

Why would they want to give up valuable, finite shelf space to a brand

> who's rate of sale will be slow
> has an increased chance of wastage
> has very little brand awareness

You can talk about being better.
You can show off your Great Taste Awards.
You can extol the virtues of being a B Corp.

But the real deal breaker is this 👇 

👉 Is your brand different enough that it can drive an incremental purchase from a shopper?
👉 Can it help bring in new shoppers to grow their category?
👉 Can it grow overall revenue, rather than just reallocate it from one product to another?

Because ultimately  - buyers care MOSTLY about 💰 .

3 examples of brands that drove incrementality in their categories:

🍺 BrewDog - before craft beer was mainstream, listing Punk IPA as single bottles grew the overall category because shoppers didn't stop loading up their trolley with a slab of Heineken. They just added 2 bottles of Punk too, thereby increasing their spend.

🍦 Pops - alcoholic ice lollies. If I’m shopping for a tub of vanilla ice cream, I’m still going to buy my vanilla ice cream. But when a Pimm’s Calippo catches my eye, I might just toss a pack of them into my basket too for some extra fun.

🧃 Moju - Yes I want my bottle of innocent OJ. But you know what? I think I’ll also pick up a tidy little shot of ginger juice whilst I’m at it. Boom!

So remember - if you’re looking for those grocery listings:

> think incremental
> ask how your brand is growing the category
> don’t focus on being better, be different

What are some other examples of great incremental products or brands?

According to Reid Hoffman, working for a start up means having zero work life balance. I work at least one day every weekend. Most weekends it’s both days.

But assuming this HAS to be the case for EVERYONE working at a startup is outdated. 

If you’re the founder, this should be a baseline expectation. 

For the first 36 months you’re in business, work/life balance doesn’t exist AT ALL.

But expecting the same of your team isn’t fair unless they have the real upside! That means either:

Giving them equity, or
Paying them a higher salary

You can’t expect a team to all ‘be in this together’ when you’re growing a startup if you’re not giving them serious upside and opportunity.

That’s a recipe for burnout and resentment.

Incentivise your team. Sell them on the vision. Bring them into the process of the build. Give them a great outcome for doing so.

content:
ai could never have come up with this campaign.
it’s just too damn human…



I LOVE this campaign.
It’s there head to head with Pip & Nut for my favourite of 2026.

One of the main jobs of marketing is to connect with people on an emotional level.

Being human is a HUGE part of that.
Some brands do it brilliantly (exhibit A: innocent replying to every single tweet!)

Most don’t do it at all.

This campaign absolutely HITS US PARENTS SQUARE IN THE CHEST.

Which is why I was so convinced it wasn’t ai generated.

Because ai couldn’t have the sort of human insight that comes up with a line as good as “Nobody warned you about the sheets. The blood, the sweat, the tears - literal ones - soaked into everything you own”.

This is raw human experience. I’ve seen it firsthand (albeit as a man not truly experienced it).

OR how about “The baby is fine, how are you?”

The whole campaign rejects the stereotypical focus on baby, on comfort, on absorption, on soft baby bums. And instead focuses on the absolute hero that is mum. On the reality of having a baby. It's messy, it's hard, it's life-changing, it's imperfect.

I was so convinced ai couldn’t come up with this I messaged the founder Rima Suppan to check.

She confirmed my hunch: "Morgan and I came up with the cqmpaign headline on a train ride home on a Friday afternoon as she was in her final week of work before having her own newborn - and then our brilliant marketing and brand team refined the campaign and came up with the narrative, the why, the tag lines, we did a photoshoot in a studio and a location house.”

Ask yourself: if you’d briefed into Claude - create me an ad campaign for a scale up challenger nappy brand, do you think you’d have created imagery, copy and a big idea as good as this?

I doubt it! (I actually tried it, it didn’t).

So next time you’re thinking about how to market yor brand - whether it’s billboards, flyposters or just a Meta ad with £10 spend behind it, remember to bring your human self.

content:
Learning to recharge properly was one of the best things I did for myself. Especially as a founder diagnosed with ADHD.

High energy is my default.

I can hold a room for hours. Full conviction, completely switched on, genuinely loving every second of it.

I can do this for months/years in a row.

Then sometimes - you hit a wall. 

Just completely wiped in a way that's hard to explain if you haven't felt it.

Without having awareness of where you are, and how far you are from that wall, you can find yourself at disaster.

And then pushing through that wall really hurts you in the long run.

What actually helps me:

- Identify your ‘flow state’ hours. Protect them

- Be the founder who goes to bed early (!!)

- Prioritise good-quality sleep

- Minimise back to back travel where possible

- Fuel better - don’t borrow from tomorrow to get through today.

Running high as a founder means planning the recharge too. 

When you build that, everything else falls into place.

content:
🚨🎙️👋🗞️ Governments banning social media is all well and good, but here’s a few things nobody seems to want to talk about: 

→ Third spaces for teens are virtually non-existent. We’ve defunded the places where young people used to hang out (like youth clubs) and now we’re surprised they find community online. 
→ Tolerance for teens in existing third spaces has quietly decreased over the years: coffee shops, libraries, parks or going to the pub with your family. 
→ Banning mainstream platforms doesn’t make teens go offline, and it has the potential for them to go down a more extreme pipeline to find community. For example: there are active, easily accessible anonymous communities out there (like incel forums) that are very good at luring in isolated young people and giving them somewhere to belong. 
→ LGBTQ+ teens rely on social media for building safe connections, especially those without supportive families or local communities. Social media platforms are where they find safety, identity, and other people like them. 
→ Researchers at Frontiers in Developmental Psychology published a review this year saying there is little direct evidence bans actually improve teen wellbeing. We’ve been here before with TV and video games. 

Australia banned social media for under-16s in December 2025. A Molly Rose Foundation survey of over 1,000 teenagers found that more than 60% of 12-15 year-olds who had accounts before the ban still have access to at least one platform. And that in a majority of cases platforms have failed to identify and remove under-16 accounts, meaning that most children haven’t had to proactively use workarounds.

What needs to happen instead: 

→ As Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said, we need to focus on making social media less addictive such as removing features like autoplay, infinite scroll, and algorithms that bombard children with harmful material. 
→ We need to reinvest in actual physical spaces for young people, fund youth services, build digital literacy into education. 
→ Social media is a symptom of a youth mental health crisis (which was a crisis even a decade ago) so we need to treat the crisis with more funding for community mental health services, early intervention and school counselling. 

Banning social media is putting a plaster over the real issues to make everyone feel like we’re actually doing something about the youth mental health crisis.

CEO.

1️⃣ Understanding a complex product problem

Five things equally competing for your attention = perfection !

10 minutes on this problem
15 on that one
25 on the next.

That's just how my brain loves to work.

It took me years to stop fighting it and even longer to find a setting that suited it.

Who knew all I had to do was build that environment myself.

TRY BEING AN ANGELS ADVOCATE

People wanting to look smart in a meeting try and spot the flaw in an idea that no-one else has seen by playing the 'Devil's Advocate'

However when it comes to the early stages of a creative idea when it's not fully formed that can easily kill it off

Often the desire comes from not want to take a risk or feeling uncomfortable so people would rather find ways not to do it

But as Greg Hahn says here

"Try playing the Angel's Advocate and find ways it could work"

This puts people in the right mindset to see how the idea could work and making it even better rather than killing it before it's had time to grow

It also motivates the creative team to present the really bold ideas rather than pitching for safety in a bid to get approval

At System1 we adopted a similar approach called EBI (even better if) where in meetings rather than say what was wrong with something we reframed that into what would make it better. It worked really well.

This week rather than being a Devil's Advocate try playing the Angel's Advocate and see what happens

content:
Top marketers are all having this realisation right now

Profit must be the goal. Not revenue for revenue's sake.

Meg Whitman speaking far too much sense via Fortune  

If you look a bit closer at the accepted wisdom I'm marketing, including the push for new customer penetration, most of it is based on market share and revenue.

When I worked brand side, and now most of my clients, all the key metrics we chase in marketing are revenue-based.

The easiest way to generate revenue is to offer 50% off.

The easiest way to boost revenue Return On Investment is to stop spending on marketing, the ROI jumps to infinity.

It's a terminal issue in marketing that we must address. In my research with System1 and the past decade of advertising campaigns submitted to Effie Worldwide across the US and Europe.

77% reported incremental revenue. Only 9% reported incremental profit.

It partly comes down to a lack of marketing training. The role of marketing is hard when we are trying to do the real job: influence long-term behavior that stacks up and compounds in our brand's favour.

This is a far harder job than simply being easy to buy, and being recognisable and distinctive.

It requires creativity, proper positioning, relative differentiation, emotion, innovation close to consumer needs, and disruptive ideas worth paying attention to and sharing. And a key understanding of culture and how to insert our brands into it.

I've played softball on a lot of this so far. But I genuinley don't think most of the (dogmatic) marketing thinking most use addresses any of this, and doesn't grow brands. It just holds brands at their current size, at best.

Working on some new, unique, huge datasets at the moment to share more on this soon.

WHY SUCCESSFUL LEADERS WORKOUT

Without going full-on Stephen Bartlett on you there is good evidence for why working out and exercising regularly actually helps you be more successful in business

Here is a stat that Kory Marchisotto dropped on the latest episode of Uncensored Renegades

"there is a 22% productivity gain on days you exercise"

"I am too busy NOT to do a workout"

Think about when you last had clarity on a business problem, last felt that extra bit energy to complete a task, last felt like you had a balance in your day, last felt like you were unstoppable? Chances are you had done your workout that day.

content:
Your need to be liked is a toxic leader's greatest weapon.

It sounds harsh, but it’s a reality we don’t talk about enough in the corporate world.

Toxic bosses don’t just look for high performers. They look for specific psychological profiles.

Toxic bosses love to hire people pleasers.

Why? Because a people pleaser is a dream for an micromanager or an abuser of power:

They rarely say "no," even when their plate is overflowing.

They take blame for things that aren't their fault just to keep the peace.

They over-index on validation, meaning a toxic boss can control them using breadcrumbs of praise.

They internalise stress instead of pushing back against unrealistic demands.

If you are a natural people pleaser, you have to be incredibly careful during the interview process.

Your empathy and desire to do a good job are beautiful traits, but in the wrong environment, they will be exploited until you burn out.

Protect your boundaries. Learn the power of a polite but firm "no."

A great leader wants a partner who can challenge them, not a door mat they can walk over.

Another day, another fake update COMING TRUE as LinkedIn announces a B2B Creator Marketplace 👋👀🎙️😝

This week, LinkedIn announced a Creator Marketplace to help brands find + partner with creators at scale !! 

And it makes it so so much easier for creators to land brand partnerships on the platform too, as once you opt-in, you can: 

→ Get discovered by leading brands as your profile + content will be put directly in front of them 
→  Showcase your best work
→ Choose how brands get in touch with you, and approve how your sponsored content is used 

The move isn't *that* surprising. We’ve watched the B2B creator economy explode over the last few years, brands are desperate to tap into it, and even The New York Times is discussing if LinkedIn is in its “post-cringe era.” 

And LinkedIn's own data from earlier this year speaks for itself: 

→ 82% of buyers say B2B creator content influences them, and nearly 80% engage with it monthly.
→ 59% of buyers discover new brands through creator content, and almost half of buyers say they visited a vendor’s website after engaging with creator content.

content:
I've had thousands of conversations with founders about LinkedIn. The same 8 excuses come up every time.

1. "I don't have time for LinkedIn"
You have time. You don't have conviction. The founders posting consistently aren't less busy than you.

2. "LinkedIn is cringe."
It can be. It doesn't have to be. And the cringe you hate? It's still driving pipeline.

3. "I don't want to become one of those LinkedIn people."
You're not resisting LinkedIn. You're resisting a caricature of it. Buyers are researching you right now... what are they finding?

4. "I don't know what to say."
You know exactly what to say. You say it on sales calls, in board meetings, to your team. You just haven't written it down yet.

5. "Followers don't equal revenue."
Correct. But visibility does. The question isn't how many followers but whether the right 50 people trust you. 

6. "I don't want to look self-promotional."
Sharing what you know isn't self-promotion. And if you wont promote yourself, who will?

7. "Our marketing team handles content."
Your marketing team can't replicate your credibility. Buyers want to hear from the founder (not the brand account)

8. "I'll start when I have more to say."
You'll never feel ready. The founders who "have something to say" just started before they felt like it.

The fear of looking cringe is costing you more than the cringe itself.

That difficult colleague isn't always just "difficult."

They might be dealing with a personal crisis you know absolutely nothing about.

In the corporate world, we’re taught to leave our personal lives at the door. But reality doesn't work that way.

Behind the:

 Delayed email response

 Brief tone in a meeting

 Missed deadline

 Lack of focus

...there is often a human being carrying a weight they can't talk about.

A sick family member. A mental health struggle. Financial stress. Heartbreak.

We are so quick to judge people by their output, but we rarely stop to consider their input.

You seriously have no idea what people are dealing with in their personal lives.

Leadership isn’t just about driving KPIs. It’s about managing people with empathy.

Before you react with frustration today, take a breath. Give someone the benefit of the doubt.

So just be nice. It’s that simple.

content:
For a platform so full of “hot takes”, LinkedIn is surprisingly lacking in warmth.

I talk to my friends and they’re brimming with enthusiasm for the performances in Tip Toe, for the batshit brilliance of Madonna’s Vagina Lasers, ready to talk about The Chrisophers – or the Kylie documentary. About a book they’re reading or a person they’re not sure if they’re stalking or dating.

The conversations are full of energy and opinion. They’re candid and sometimes crude, they’re an excuse to share ourselves with each other, to fill the air with a little more love, a lot more noise and evidence that we are here for each other.

And then I come to LinkedIn and find my wall filled with near identical comments, on near identical topics, from near identical people.

And the message is almost always “I don’t like it.”

There’s no diversity of topic or opinion – just an algorithmic invitation to shout past each other as the engagement meter spins. 

Ferrari, Jaguar, Nike, Burberry, any logo that has changed at all. 

People hate them all. 
People think that the people in charge are idiots. 
People know what should have been done instead. 

And then the next and the next and the next.

We are white goods plugged into an engagement farm.
Cold and cynical and snide. Offering the empty white noise of the opinion d’jour served just as you’d expect it.

There's a real world full of joy and despair and hurt and fear and Madonna's vagina lasers (did I mention them?) out there - but here on LinkedIn it’s all hate for logos, launches and any new font, with a side order of 18 lessons we can learn from your brave battle with kidney stones and 2484 takes on a Ferrari design

They hung him from a fucking lamp-post. And lasers shot out of people’s butts, and Iain McKellen is going to die and so is David Attenborough and who else do we have? Judy Dench won’t be far behind, surely? And there are genocides. And hate crimes. And people feeling that now is the time to say the ugliest things. And the hate we see online turning into the violence we see on our streets and in our politics. And damn, how had I missed just how gay He-Man was? 

And I wish my friends could be as funny and engaged and opinionated and beautiful online as they can when we head out for a sunset on a boat, or swim out to a platform for a picnic, or just send voicemails asking whether they really “had to cut him out of the chastity cage?” or whether that was just a rhetorical flourish.

But this isn't the place. Here we are slaves to a machine that rewards us for sounding like machines

Anyone wanna talk Tip Toe?

That’s the real ADHD unlock.

I love this Festival, but let’s be real: if you’re heading out there, you aren’t there for "deals." 

You’re there for the human connections that make the deals happen six months from now. 

To survive the week without losing your mind (or dignity), here is my unofficial guide:

The Palais is the Anchor: I spend my mornings here. It’s where the "mental software" gets updated, and honestly, it has the best air-con. If you aren't in the rooms hearing how the big ideas were actually built, you’re just on an expensive holiday.


The 40% Rule: I leave nearly half my day unscripted. Some of the most important people I know, I met while waiting in line for a coffee or sharing a bench because my feet gave out. Leave room for the "unplanned" - that's usually where the best conversations live.


Don’t "Pitch," just Chat: Nobody wants an elevator pitch in 34°C heat while they're looking for a napkin. Just be a person. Ask people what they’ve seen that actually inspired them. The best partnerships start with a normal conversation, not a slide deck that nobody can see because of the sun glare anyway.


The Essentials: Two battery packs (rotate them like shifts), a reusable water bottle, and shoes you can actually walk 15k steps in. 

Save the fashion moments for the evening; daytime is for the grind. If your shoes hurt by noon, the day is already over.

content:
Sunday used to be the most STRESSFUL day of my week.


Until…  last Sunday happened without me. 

Perplexity Computer took over. The orchestrator I didn't know I needed.

Here's the thing. Sunday decides the week.


Get it wrong and Monday's already lost. By Wednesday, you're barely surviving.


Same cycle, every week, for as long as I can remember.


But this week, I did something different. I decided to watch the Arsenal game.


Five minutes before kick-off, I sat down and looked at what was waiting for me.


The deck was half-done. The brief hadn't been touched since Thursday. 

I still had 1:1s to book, a New York flight to confirm, a posting schedule living in my head, and Tuesday's call notes I knew to action.


Clients, creators, a pitch, a team waiting on me by 9am Monday.


So I typed one line: "Get me ready for Monday."


Left the laptop. Watched the game.


One prompt, and it broke the week into tasks and ran them in parallel.


Sub-agents working through my inbox, my calendar, my docs, one off chasing the flight.


Different models for different jobs - Claude reasoning through what mattered, Gemini doing the deeper research - all running at the same time, in the background, without me.


And because it plugged straight into Gmail, Calendar, and Drive, it wasn't guessing. 

It was working inside my actual world, like a teammate who already knew the brief.


At Full-time, I was back on the laptop.


Inbox drafted and prioritised - two things flagged, the rest handled.

Calendar blocked around New York, 1:1s in. Flight sorted. Deck pulled together, brief drafted, posting schedule written.

A quick review. And… Send 


That's what an orchestrator does. Holds all the parts so you don't have to.


Sundays used to be the most chaotic day of my week. Now they're the most productive and I'm barely there for it. 

Autopilot, in the best way.

Perplexity Computer helped me own my Sunday.
What will YOU do with it?

Putting yourself in the room allows you to learn.

content:
Why the empty chair on stage?

Last week at SXSW London the one and only Adam Morgan and I went on stage with a rather provocative POV

"why you will ignore everything heard today"

We have all been to conferences like this full of great data and inspirational stories and then left without making a change

As Adam said in his introduction

"we are living in a golden age of marketing thinking. But not a golden age of marketing doing"

There are many reasons we unpacked during our talk including what I learnt via the very revealing Confessions of a CMO research done in partnership with John Harris and Gabriel Cohen last year but one factor required an empty chair on stage

Adam came up with this idea when interviewing Lucinda Barlow the International CMO of Uber suggesting that the empty chair as a metaphor for the missing customer could also be used to represent when fear was in the seat

This really struck me because I am convinced that fear is often the single biggest factor that stands between what we know to be true and actually doing it

To make the point we added an empty chair on stage and asked the audience what they would do if fear wasn't in the seat

As an aside this is why I find Rory Sutherland so engaging because he really doesn't fear what anyone else might think

Surely it's time to switch from marketing knowing to marketing doing and banish that seat for good

Thanks to SxSw for having us and thanks to Kerry Collinge and Anna Cairns for setting us up and pushing the topic to ensure it wasn't dull

content:
Static ABM makes no sense in a moving market.

Your buyer changes.

Your category changes.

Your competitors change.

Your target accounts change.

But somehow the account list stays the same.

That is the bit I find strange.

Most teams put a lot of energy into building the list.

Far less energy into keeping it alive.

So the GTM motion becomes a snapshot.

Useful when it was created.

Less useful every week after.

The better way is to make account prioritisation responsive.

Here is the ZoomInfo GTM Studio workflow I’d test:

1. Build the account universe using firmographic and intent filters.

2. Score accounts against ICP fit.

3. Assign tiers automatically based on score thresholds.

4. Push those tier changes into Salesforce.

5. Sync updated audiences to LinkedIn.

6. Alert sales and marketing when an account moves into a priority segment.

That turns ABM from a spreadsheet into a system.

The list is not just “built.”

It is listening.

It changes when the market changes.

That is the difference between campaign planning and GTM orchestration.

One is static.

The other reacts.

How often does your ABM list actually change based on live signals?

content:
2019: Founded Connectd.
2026: Team of 120. 12,000 founders supported. Close to 60,000 connections made.

Here’s how I built a business despite often walking into rooms where nobody knew what the word ‘fractional’ meant: 

1. Understand other people’s POV first
Speaking to people and getting to know THEIR business makes explaining yours much, much easier. Make sure you understand their experience and context first, before jumping in with yours.

2. Put yourself in their story
Not everyone understands the word ‘fractional’. But the founder who just told you they’re struggling to expand in the US? You now get to explain how you can connect them to the CFO who has done this for businesses 10x over - and they don’t even have to hire someone full-time.

3. Appreciate your early adopters
Even better than you explaining what you do is having someone else vouch for it. Being in early rooms alongside the people who had found their COO/Head of Marketing/etc through us, and hearing them vouch for the business did more for trust-building than I ever could.

That’s how you start to grow a business that sits in a non-traditional space, or that not everyone understands yet.

It all comes back to people ;)

content:
Founder-led content used to be enough.

It's not anymore.

The companies winning on LinkedIn right now don't have one voice. They have three. Sometimes five.

I've watched this shift happen in real time. One of our clients went from a single founder posting to three internal voices. The metrics went up. But more importantly: more inbound leads. More offline pull. More pipeline.

Here's what we helped them mapped out:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗘𝗢 → Long-term vision, hiring principles, raw company strategy

𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁/𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 → Future builds, system bugs, technical frameworks

𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 → Humor, relatable customer pain points, product-led templates

Each voice has a lane. Each lane builds trust with a different audience.

The founder still matters. But they're no longer carrying the entire brand alone.

This is exactly what we're helping some of the fastest-growing companies build at Shake Content.

Not (only) more content... but better distribution of who's creating it.

The companies that figure this out now will own their category in 12 months.

We work with a handful of B2B companies on exactly this. If you're doing £1M+ ARR and thinking about scaling your LinkedIn presence beyond just the founder..  send me a message.

content:
The 9-to-5 isn’t just outdated. It’s a relic.

We are trying to solve 2026 burnout with 1950s corporate structures. And let’s be entirely real, it’s failing miserably.

Tobi Oluwole is spot on. The world has shifted, human expectations have evolved, yet too many legacy companies are still desperately clinging to rigid, decades-old frameworks because they are terrified of letting go of control.

They think "flexibility" means letting people wear jeans on Friday or log off at 4:30 PM before a long weekend.

Huge mistake. That’s not flexibility; that’s a marketing gimmick.

True flexibility is about absolute autonomy and radical trust. It means:

Ditching the surveillance culture: Trusting your adults to manage their own time and work where they are most productive, without tracking their keystrokes.

Respecting the off-switch: Creating non-negotiable boundaries between professional output and personal life. No midnight Slack messages. No weekend emails.

Humanising the workload: Dynamically scaling back targets during high-stress periods and offering mental health days with absolutely zero questions asked.

Life-stage inclusivity: Customising structures to support caregiving responsibilities, side projects, and continuous learning.

You cannot build a high-performance culture on top of a broken foundation. When you treat people like cogs in a machine, they will give you machine-like effort. But when you genuinely support their mental well-being and give them ownership of their life, everyone wins, the individual, the team, and the bottom line.

Stop managing by attendance. Start leading by impact.

The future of work is fluid, empathetic, and human-centric. Adapt your workplace, or watch your best talent leave for someone who will.

P.S. What does real flexibility look like in your world? Drop your thoughts below.

The World Cup is the most democratic sporting competition in the world and adidas has positioned themselves as the ultimate challenger in our own backyard

Here is why I love it

THE CASTING

Not Beckham or even Messi but Timothee Chalamat for the very reason he is recognisable but not a footballer. He is every one of us who loves the game and wants a piece of the action.

3 IS THE MAGIC NUMBER

The action is 3 against 3. The perfect metaphor for the 3 stripes of adidas on every trainer. It's the kind of branding you discover rather than have pushed in your face. It means something.

THE STUFF OF LEGEND

This is a real story and despite the star studded cast they are playing in support of the legend. When people talk about brands being in culture this is what they should be referring to.

IN OUR BACKYARD

This wasn't set in a huge stadium with massive crowds as most World Cup ad tend to do. This was in our own backyard which tells you exactly who adidas see themselves being for. The positioning vs Nike is spot on.

AI PUT TO GOOD USE

So much AI still feels pointless and fake but here it's been used to bring to life a young 'buzzcut' Beckham. It's the second-take you do when seeing if it's actually him and how they managed to de-age him.

DIRECTION

Last but not least the direction is pure class. I worked with SMUGGLER when they were less well known on a film for Lucozade Sport that won a Cannes Lion for film craft. This is their trademark craft and director Mark Molloy has nailed it.

Massive credit to LOLA who were the creative agency behind this work I think they have created their own legend with this film

Well played adidas.
