An office bully is just a schoolyard insecure kid who managed to get a budget.

Let's stop calling it "tough management" or "demanding leadership." Call it what it is: a playground power trip in a tailored suit.

Too many adults are hiding behind titles and corner offices, using their authority to belittle people and turn boardrooms into battlegrounds. They crush spirits because it’s easier to project their own toxic insecurities onto the team than it is to look in the mirror and do the inner work.

They think dominance equals respect. Huge mistake.

A title might give you authority, but it will never buy you loyalty. True strength doesn’t come from making everyone else feel small just so you can feel tall.

Weak leaders dominate: They use fear, manipulation, and control to force compliance.

Real leaders elevate: They use their influence to lift as they climb, ensuring people leave better than they arrived.

The real flex in corporate culture isn't how many people you can control. It's how many people you can empower.

If you are leading through intimidation, you aren't a visionary, you are a bottleneck. Get a grip on your own unsolved insecurities before you project them onto your culture.

Leave the playground behind. Build trust, earn respect and start acting like the leader your team deserves.

🚨👋📌🎙️ SOCIAL MEDIA UPDATE YOU NEED TO KNOW: LinkedIn has added a NEW metrics in analytics called "In and Out of Network" — here's what you need to know! 

→ You’ll see a percentage breakdown of who has seen your content and whether they’re in your network or not.
→ In-network reach: the % of impressions that come from those who are connected with you, or following you on LinkedIn.
→ Out-of-network reach: the % of impressions that come from those who aren’t connected with you, or following you.

👋 Why You Should Care: Understanding whether your content hits your existing network or pushes beyond it gives you *such* an invaluable diagnostic tool. You can now see exactly if you have a discovery problem or a conversion problem because if you have a high non-follower reach but it's not converting into anything (follows, connections, leads, whatever your goal is) then your profile and positioning is needs assessing. And if you're only reaching your current followers? Your current content strategy resonating enough. 

Beyond this, though, I think it really signals the shift that LinkedIn is making in the creator economy. It's moving further away from *just* being the place that people look to find a new role. 

(Love love love this new metric Sam Corrao Clanon, thank you for listening to the people 🙂‍↕️)

Kindness isn’t a management tactic. It’s a leadership superpower.

We’ve been conditioned to think that powerful leadership means asserting dominance, exposing weaknesses, and driving people through fear.

That’s not strength. That’s insecurity wrapped in a suit.

Real leaders don't use their influence to crush people's confidence just to prove a point. They use their weight to uplift, support, and lend their strength to others. Because in a world obsessed with raw execution, people will always deliver their best work when they feel valued, not attacked.

When you trade criticism for compassion, the entire game changes:

You unlock innovation: When people feel safe to fail, they actually dare to try new things.

You build unbreakable trust: Loan your strength by saying, "I’ve got your back while you figure this out," instead of "You're not good enough yet."

You amplify the wins: Celebrate breakthroughs loudly and treat setbacks as learning moments, not death sentences.

Kindness isn't soft. It’s the ultimate competitive advantage. It builds resilient cultures, drives sustainable results and creates a legacy that outlasts any quarterly target.

Stop reminding people of their flaws to make yourself feel bigger. Lift your team up, protect their energy, and be the leader who builds people up instead of breaking them down.

content:
You cannot expect a flower to bloom if you keep watering it with poison.

A toxic culture will ALWAYS break down a good person. It doesn’t matter how strong they are, how resilient they are, or how much they believe in the mission. Eventually, the environment wins.

As a leader, you have to stay sharp. You need to catch the warning signs before the foundation completely rots out from under you.

Pizza parties and corporate swag won’t fix a broken culture. People see right through it.

If you want to know if your culture is slipping, look for these fractures:
The Hypocrisy: Leaders who talk about "values" on LinkedIn but act completely different behind closed doors.

The Hollow Purpose: A flashy mission statement on the office wall that never actually informs a single business decision.

The Echo Chamber: Asking your team for feedback just to check a box, while completely ignoring their suggestions.

The Blind Eye: Letting toxic high-performers slide because they hit their targets. You are actively licensing behavior that destroys your team's morale.

The Lazy Hire: Rushing to fill seats based purely on CV technical skills while completely ignoring cultural alignment.

Culture isn't a policy you print out and stuff in a drawer. It’s not a mandate you force from the top down.

Culture is an organic ecosystem. It’s built on shared respect, open communication, and psychological safety. When times get tough, it should be the absolute last thing you sacrifice not the first thing you cut to save a quick buck.

Stop trying to manufacture a vibe with perks. Fix the foundation, protect your people, and build an environment where they can actually thrive.

💡 Rob Dance

→ Bot-generated comments that just restate the post

The platform is rewarding real people with real expertise who show up consistently.

Generic content is (hopefully) getting buried. Original thinking is getting amplified.

2026: Working almost every weekend. Happiest I’ve ever been.

Each role you take on teaches you something new about the experience of building a business. You’re always learning.

My first company taught me how to be scrappy to grow
My second business is teaching me how to step back to scale
My own investments are teaching me how to be a better founder to my investors

all of it has made me the (non typical) founder I am today.

→ treat everyone like you have something to learn from them.
→ treat your network like your prized possession.
→ learn fast. take feedback. Be humble

content:
Did you miss our panel chat: "When brands get it wrong: inclusivity, backlash and social trust,"  at SocialDay ®'s Social Media Fest? Don't fret. 

Here's a wee summary of what I chatted about. Animatedly. 🥲 

> A key part of making your campaigns inclusive is making them accessible.
> Inclusivity requires careful thought. Have you involved the right people? Can your brand speak authoritatively for that community? Sometimes, it's better to exercise restraint if you're not sure.
> Accessibility is different. The biggest mistake you can make here is *not* acting.
> That's because 89% of disabled people have faced challenges with digital accessibility, making them feel frustrated, disappointed and angry (Source: Agile Brand Guide).
> I dunno about you, but I've worked from a lot of campaign, marketing and business briefs. And none of them ask to make the audience feel this way!
> The counterpoint to this is accessibility. As my wonderful pal Holly Tuke says: "Accessibility is a love note. It says 'we want you here, too.'"
> So on the one hand, you have inaction. Anger, frustration, disappointment. On the other, you have accessibility. Making people feel acknowledged, welcomed, even loved.
> And it isn't only disabled people who benefit when your content is accessible.
> Accessibility can be situational. Have you ever watched content with the volume down, because you're on public transport, in bed or just fancy a bit of peace?
> If that's the case, you're one of the 80% of people who use captions (or you might call them subtitles) even though you don't have hearing loss or you aren't deaf (Source: Ofcom).
> By not making your content accessible you're not only forcing disabled people to scroll past your content, but a huge portion of your audience. 
> So, when it comes to inclusivity, by all means tread carefully.
> But with accessibility, something is better than nothing. Trying is better than nothing. Give it a go, and see what happens.

(And remember, I'm here if you want a lil bit of guidance or training).

content:
If you’re the smartest person in the room, you’re in the wrong room. And if you built that room, you’re in serious trouble.

The rule sounds incredibly simple: Hire people who are better than you, different from you, and then get out of their way so you can learn from them.
Yet, so many leaders flat-out refuse to do it. Why?

Because of ego.

Let’s stop wrapping it up in corporate jargon and call it what it is. Leaders don’t skip out on top talent because of "alignment." They do it because of insecurity.

They are terrified of being challenged. They want the comfort zone of a team that nods along, the control of being the ultimate bottleneck, and the safety of being the most capable person in the building.

But ego-driven leadership is a slow death for a business.

When you hire people who are smarter and think differently than you, everything changes:

You destroy blind spots: Different backgrounds bring perspectives you physically cannot see.

You fast-track innovation: Humility opens the door to fresh ideas; arrogance shuts it.

You build true scale: A powerhouse team allows you to focus on the horizon, not the day-to-day fires.

The ultimate goal of any great leader isn't to become indispensable. It is to make your daily responsibilities redundant.

Build a team that forces you to level up. Empower them, learn from them, and watch how fast your culture multiplies.

Drop the ego. Fire yourself from the micro-management, and hire your future.

content:
KPIs don't have feelings. But the people delivering them do.

We’ve been conditioned to track everything. Inefficiencies, revenue targets, quarterly performance, burn rates. We live in the dashboards.

But when was the last time you paused, looked a team member in the eye, and asked:

"How are you actually doing?"

We need to stop pretending that leadership is about corner offices and metrics. It’s not. It’s about people. Real, complex human beings.

Right now, someone on your team is delivering incredible results while silently breaking inside. They are the ones smiling on Zoom calls, hitting their targets, and then crying in private. They are battling anxiety, grief or burnout and still showing up for you every single day.

You will never find these struggles on a performance chart. But they impact your business more than you think.

There is a massive misconception in the corporate world that empathy is "soft."

It’s not. Leading with kindness in a world that worships pure execution is the bravest thing a leader can do. Anyone can manage by fear and control. It takes real courage to lead with compassion.

My challenge to every leader reading this today:

Be the one who notices. Look past the metrics to see the human.

Be the one who checks in. Don’t wait for a crisis to show you care.

Be the one who builds psychological safety. Kindness isn’t a perk; it’s the foundation.

You have no idea what silent battles your team is fighting behind closed doors today.

Choose to be a leader who protects people, not just profits.

content:
The best speaking advice I've ever been given. Everyone in my team agrees it's a game-changer.

Treat it like karaoke.

I'm serious.

Karaoke has nothing to do with you knowing the words or even being able to sing. People want to see you having a good time. That's literally it.

They have no idea what you were "meant to say". Or if that animation was meant to work. Or even if that video was meant to have sound.

No one gives a shit. If you're having a great time, so are they.

Once you think like this, speaking is a dream, and carrying notes makes zero sense. You know your topic and what you want to get across, everyone's giving you their time. It's a treat - enjoy it.

It's a hill I'll die on. I've seen Beth Marchant, Amy Houlihan & Josh Fruttiger all adopt this, and the crowds go wild.

When speakers really mess up, it's because they clearly get flustered or annoyed that they messed up. Truly, no one in the crowd gives a shit. Crack on!

And the best part of this advice is you don't have to do anything. Next time you need to speak, you'll think of this, and everything will just go better.

content:
8 years ago I sold my first company. I thought it was the peak of my career. It wasn’t.

After dropping out of university to build a business, I’d spent years learning how to pitch, building a product based on the feedback of our early and most loyal customers at the forefront of what we were building. We raised just under $1m in funding but truthfully, behind the scenes I was fighting to keep myself afloat.

I learned so much about building a business, but I had no tools for taking care of my own health.

The aftermath of that exit left me exhausted.

When I started Connectd I was committed to helping more founders get it right the first time.

I myself had to learn and unlearn some things:

→ how to work with my (ADHD) brain
→ when to step back and let the team run things
→ how to recognise the people I can rely on
→ when to be honest that I didn’t know something

Now, we’re an $18M ARR business with a headcount of over 100 people. I’m proud to say that we have an amazing leadership team, and incredible people working in the business to support more startups.

It’s crazy now to look back at over eight years of being an ‘exited founder’.

I wouldn’t change a thing. I feel like the best is yet to come. Which is why it’s so important to build a company where you’re excited for the journey as well as the outcome.

content:
The quietest exits are always the loudest.

You didn’t lose your top talent today. You lost them six months ago when you ignored their feedback, promised a promotion that never came and gave the spotlight to a toxic high-performer because "they hit their numbers."

Loyalty isn't a permanent state of mind. It’s a daily subscription that leaders have to renew.

But too many leaders operate on a dangerous assumption: "They love it here. They’ll never leave."

Huge mistake.

Loyal people don’t wake up one morning and decide to quit. It’s a slow, agonising burn. It’s the death of a thousand cuts.

If you want to save your culture, you need to spot the shift before the resignation letter hits your desk. Look closely:

The Silence: The person who used to challenge ideas in meetings is now just nodding along.

The Disengagement: The culture champion who used to organise the team socials is now clocking out at exactly 5:01 PM.

The Isolation: The ultimate team player who suddenly pulls back and works strictly solo.

By the time they hand in their notice, they’ve already mentally moved on. No sudden pay rise or fancy new title will bring them back because you can't buy back self-respect.

Every missed "thank you" chips away at trust. Every ignored boundary weakens the relationship.

Leadership isn't about managing headcount; it’s about protecting heart count. Value the people who hold your culture together.

Before they realise they deserve better. 

💡 Justin Wright

content:
WHY YOU SHOULD SPOT THE COUNTER TREND

Loved this point from Rory Sutherland that every trend has a counter trend and we spot them because we disproportionately notice things we weren't expecting

My youngest daughter seems a great example of this as she once asked for a 'clickety keyboard' to use with her Apple Mac so she could hear herself typing and the juxtaposition with the slick apple computer really stood out

Likewise when it comes to TV she would much rather watch Friends than the latest Netflix series mainly because nobody has a mobile phone and they all seem to be having so much fun

I feel like this about AI. We may be automating so much of our jobs away but surely that will create a counter trend for things that are real and in real life

A bit like the trends we seen in consumer goods

Vinyl records vs digital 
Polaroid cameras for weddings
Dumb phones rather than smart ones
Clean food rather than processed
Craft beer over massed produced

Perhaps a good business plan would be to do the exact opposite of what the trend report tells you to do?

What demand is being created as a counter to the trend?

content:
First Jaguar. Now Ferrari.

Their new luxury electric car has got the internet enraged again with the share price taking a 8% hit.

Jaguar's first electric car caused the largest uproar in car history. Too pink, weird and fashion. Not acknowledging the past enough.

Now, Ferrari has launched the Luce, a four-day €550k EV, a large step from the brand's past, and similar noise is already online.

Too blue. Too big. Too five-seat. Too electric. Too not-Ferrari.

This will split marketing in half again.

On Jaguar, Rory Sutherland (behavioural science icon) argued that in a disrupted, all-electric automotive landscape, the past doesn't guarantee future success.

Mark Ritson (legendary marketing professor) argued that for Jaguar to be a true luxury brand, it needed to respect and leverage its rich DNA. And they should've refreshed, not rebranded.

Brand managers have struggled with this for decades. Keeping what makes the brand distinctive, while refreshing it for the modern day.

My take? We can't plan off online noise. The most viral stuff is quickly dwarfed by any paid media plans. How this new car makes Ferrari’s future customers feel will determine if this is a flop or a win.

What do you think? A necessary gamble? Or a heritage luxury brand ruined overnight?

HOW TO MAKE A CREATOR PARTNERSHIP WORK

Killer chart here from some System1 research with the team at TikTok for Business looking at how to create brand awareness

Take out for me here is

🚀 Challengers x Creators - huge opportunity for challenger brands to partner with creators especially if they can brand early

🚀 Category Leaders - all forms of content respond well to early branding presumably as the brand is more well known

🚀 Uplift largest on leaders - brand early with creators sees a 2.2x uplift for challengers and a 3.3x uplift for leaders

The key question is how to brand earlier?

One of my favourite insights from the report was that you don't just add a logo. In fact that was very low in terms of driving brand awarness.

Instead us sonic devices, jingles and use the logo in context (via the product)

The key for me is

👉 Use creators to engage their own audience with your message

👉 Make the content entertaining to capture their attention

👉 Brand in a natural rather than forced way to gain brand awarenes

Kudos to Andrew Tindall and Josh Fruttiger for the work with TikTok that uncovered these insights

You can get the full report over at the System1 group website - its well worth it!

A great story here from Rory Sutherland about an insurance company dealing with complaints about the length of time claims take to process

The company was about to spend a large amount of money speeding up the claims process until someone asked a question

What was the actual length of time an average claim takes? 

The answer was 2 weeks

Write and tell everyone that claims take 4 weeks

If you're a brand working with supermarkets, please please please understand this one basic principle....

➝ IS whether you can bring in new shoppers to their category 

➝ IS whether you can help them tick a box that makes them look good to their bosses

➝ IS whether you have enough brand awareness to make sure your product actually moves off the shelf 

➝ IS whether you have a budget to put into activating in-store, be that sampling, POS, media or promo fees.

content:
OFF CAMPUS, HEATED RIVALRY + THE SUMMER I TURNED PRETTY ALL TOOK OVER THE INTERNET, HERE’S WHY 👀🎙️🔗📌

Of course, niche communities like BookTok are a huge reason that these shows get the greenlight in the first place. Amazon renewed Off Campus for a second season before the first season even aired because the pre-built demand both online and offline was already there. 

But getting a show made + launched is only half the battle (!!) and the actual driving force behind the massive success of these shows post-launch? 

Clippers, and fan edits 👋

(Clippers turn long-form content and edit them into highly engaging social-first snippets.) 

They’re doing the heavy-lifting that actually pulls people from doomscrolling, and onto the streaming apps to watch these shows. 

And the streaming studios are taking notes, completely flipping their marketing strategy to replicate this. Instead of the usual “streaming now” slop, they’re posting fan edits. They’re completely immersed in the community, so it doesn’t feel cringe, out of place or like they’re trying too hard because it’s only when they’ve stopped the scroll that users realise it wasn’t a fan that made the video, but the streaming platform. 

The hierarchy of discovery looks like this:

→ Niche communities validate the demand to get projects built. 
→ Clippers and fan edits are the driving force post-launch.
→ Entertainment networks have a clipping strategy (in-house, and externally) to blend naturally into the community feeds. 
→ Rinse + repeat. 

But you don't need a hollywood budget to do the same. Use TikTok as your playground, and try to replicate the strategy: 

→ Experiment with episodic cuts: Break your content into a repeatable multi-part series with clear hooks. Giving your concepts a serial structure gives people a genuine reason to follow along for the next part.
→ Edit ruthlessly: Watch how fan accounts cut down long videos. They cut out the fluff, start right in the middle of the high-emotion action, and drop the value instantly, 
→ Optimise for search: Format your titles, text overlays, and captions based on what people are actually typing. 
→ Research: What are your audience asking for the most in your comment section? What are people talking about in your industry? What can you bring to life for them?

Try it for a month, and see what results you can get (!!) 

Would loooove to hear your thoughts on the rise of clippers (because no doubt studios are already low-key hiring them) and WHAT DO YOU THINK OF OFF CAMPUS? 🤪💬🚨✨

At The Calling Nils Leonard said something that has really stuck with me

Speed is something we don't talk about enough

In this episode of Uncensored Renegades Kory Marchisotto and I discuss why speed matters and how to create the conditions for it to happen

🚀 Setting a stretching goal that creates a sense of urgency

🚀 Training for speed by building the muscle memory of how to do it

🚀 Eliminating the blocks that slow you down like sign off proceedures

🚀 Trusting in a team that have the experience to deliver repeatedly

🚀 Deciding what you won't do to create the capacity for what you do do

content:
What if 8,000 followers could outperform 80,000?

Not in impressions.. but in influence.

I was asked to contribute to a Net Influencer piece on B2B creator vetting. 30 experts. One question: how do you actually evaluate who has real influence?

My take: the standard metrics were built for B2C.

Follower count, engagement rate, audience demographics - these tell you who follows a creator. Not who listens when it matters.

Here's what I actually look for:

→ 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘆. Are decision-makers engaging with substance? Or is it mostly "great post! 🙌" from other creators and job seekers? A cybersecurity creator with 8,000 followers whose comments come from actual CISOs beats one with 80,000 getting applause from career coaches.

→ 𝗔𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁. Does the creator talk about enterprise sales while their commenters are mostly coaches and consultants? That's a mismatch. The audience should reflect the buyer you're trying to reach.

→ 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗽𝘂𝗹𝗹. Does their content translate to speaking invites, podcast appearances, "I saw your post" conversations at industry events? If influence stays purely digital, it may be surface-level.

This is exactly what we think about at Shake Content when helping founders build their presence.

The real question isn't how many people see you.

It's whether the right people act on what you say.

content:
WHY RYANAIR TELL YOU HOW BAD THEY ARE

I was at K:SYD this week in Sydney doing a talk about the surprising power of giving customers more than they expect

You might naturally assume this means setting a high expectation in advance and then beating it

However Ryanair takes a different approach

Instead as Rory Sutherland points out they terrify you so much with fines for bags being overweight, threats of charging you for the toilets or roasting you if you make a complaint that when you actually fly with them you think it's a rather good experience

This aligns to a theory I recently discovered called 'reward prediction error' by a neuroscientist Wolfran Schultz who discovered that the dopamine hit we get isn't the experience itself but the variance (error) with our anticipation of the event

So you can either try and give people a positive surprise OR as Ryanair do you can just set the expectation very low

Intrigued by this I analysed 13,000 Adverts on the System1 to find out the main 'reasons for surprise' and by far the greatest driver of both positive or negative surprise was how the brand experience lived up to expectation

This episode of Uncensored CMO was recorded with Rory and Tom Goodwin on a Sunday afternoon in Miami after lunch

3. Attention-bait videos with vague 'business wisdom'

content:
13 weird and lovely things I learned at SocialDay ®'s Social Media Fest yesterday.

1. The best place to meet new people is in the bathroom, while they're trying to hand-dry a coffee stain off their boob before presenting to a huge room full of people. It makes an impression.

2. Queue up early for the free ice cream.

3. If you're going to do a panel talk, make sure you have the best beside you: like the one and only Laura Perry, Aisha Jefferson and Angela Balakrishnan. We each brought something so different to the discussion, and Laura chaired it wonderfully. The audience was clearly so engaged and asked some brilliant questions, which I reckon is testament to us all!

4. Mel Barfield is everything you'd expect and more. We went from 0 to huge hugs and planning a conference exclusively focused on reading vintage tweets in 1 minute flat.

5. Grab people's lanyards and add them on LinkedIn on the spot. #Networking.

6. Social media and comms folk are so curious about accessibility and keen to learn more (this was a lovely learning for me after the panel talk.)

7. Catching up with old faces nourishes the soul, especially when they are smashing their new role/life as hard as Laura Perry.

8. There's free candy floss. Lucy Hall was very consistent with this messaging. 

9. A brilliant social media learning from Isobel Keane: don't just talk to your creators when you need them. Be there for them in their big life moments too. Like sending them a ton of baked beans when they have a baby, because who has time to prep anything else? Genius.

10. Another fab tip from the same panel from Tasha G. - don't just look for creators in your industry, be on the lookout for creators starting *series* which fit your niche. Very clever.

11. Nothing is better than a free lunch, especially when it's buddha bowls, tacos and toasties.

12. Not social media related, but Marcus Foley said something that will stick with me for writing my novel: alongside every scene in Psycho, Hitchcock outlined exactly what he wanted his audience to feel in that moment. Alf doing audience-first before it was cool.

13. Next time, go to both days because it's a blast and there were so many folks I didn't catch, cc. Annie-Mai Hodge Katie Murphy Nimisha Mistry

content:
I initially dismissed innocent's new dessert smoothie range as a desperate ploy to reverse stalling growth, but actually I think it's probably cleverer than that.
As per, I've been over-analysing it 😄


For the record, I think they look pretty banging (and remind me a bit of their OG Thickies - IYKYK).

The desperate read goes like this: YoY volumes are flat, innocent aren't growing the category like they used to, so dessert smoothies are a stretch for growth.

I think it's the opposite. 

It's a great example of innovating close to the core (as ex-innocent legend Giles Brook likes to call it).

Breakfast, innocent's traditional home, is flat. 
Afternoon snacking is up 13%. 
Evening snacking is up 14%.

And GLP-1 adoption is sky-rocketing, meaning a big chunk of people are trading unhealthy snacks for something sweet but healthier.

When you look at "A Bit Like Lemon Pie" and "Blueberry Muffin-ish" through that lens, the picture becomes a lot clearer.

Close enough to the core liquid. Serving a different occasion. Tapping a bigger market?

Will this play work?

I am definitely going to be taste testing them all in the name of research!

You are wishing away the best part.

Right now, you're looking at the chaos, the pressure and the sleepless nights and you're calling it suffering. You’re waiting for the day you can finally "arrive."

But look closer.

There is a version of you ten years from now who has the stability, the title and the recognition you are currently stressing over.

They miss the hunger.

They’d trade a piece of their comfort just to feel that raw, electric feeling of wanting something so badly it keeps them awake. 

They miss the days when they had everything to prove and nothing to lose.

You think you’ll only be happy when you finally "make it."

But the "making it" is happening right now.
It’s in the messy middle. The pivot. The becoming.

Stop treating your present like a waiting room for your future. If you don't learn how to exist in the climb, you won't know what to do when you reach the top anyway.

Be here. Move accordingly.

content:
It’s fucking awful out there.

Good people have lost good jobs. Rates for freelance are through the floor. Recruiters have nothing to offer people but their best Casper impression and everybody is just hoping that they’re not on the next excel spreadsheet list of “salaries we can save”

The world is being battered, upended, pillaged by opportunists. We’re close to real recession, we’re in a deep trust recession and nobody really believes that anyone is coming to save them.

Most of the people I know are in a half crouch, barricaded in against the storm, hoping to get through it alive and able to get back onto their feet.

The fear is palpable – and you feel it in the work. At a time where things feel broken the work feels timid. It feels as though it’s a product of the moment, not a response to it.

It doesn’t try to lift people, it doesn’t harness anger, it doesn’t seek to be refuge from the storm, or to be a thing of beauty amongst the ugliness. It just feels small, and scared and not a little sad.

Nobody seems to be raising their heads and saying  “what about a killer joke?” Or “what about giving a voice to the anger.” Or even “what about admitting just how shit things feel right now?”

Give me punk, or disco or absurdity. Give me anarchy or art. Give me something, please. 

And I know that it’s hard. When things feel like this it’s not easy to be the person with their hand up saying “let’s go again, this could be better” – but that’s what we need right now - if we’re going to get to work that responds to the current malaise, rather than adding to the general sense of pointlessness out there.

Ever struggled with presentations? try doing this

These are the 20 things I do every single time.

1. Never use notes
2. Tell a joke early on
3. Talk in statements
4. Practice a lot. Then forget it.
5. Address one person in the room
6. Know exactly who is in the room.
7. Tell a story to really make a point.
8. Go to the loo right before. Twice.
9. Eat properly to avoid getting the shakes.
10. Request your favourite track as a walk-on.
11. PowerPoint is wallpaper. You are the show.
12. Pose a question that the next slide answers.
13. Speak. At. Two. Thirds. Of. Your. Usual. Pace.
14. Modulate. High energy. Pause. Quiet reflection.
15. Admit mistakes. The audience will like you more.
16. Eliminate the unpredictables. Clicker, Builds, Mic.
17. Never under any circumstances read from a slide.
18. Use 'next slide mode' so you know what's coming.
19. Ask the audience to give a standing ovation to the organiser.
20. Remember the audience never knew what you forgot to say.

What have I missed?

Was any of that useful?

Quitting is cheap.

It’s always on the table. It’s the easiest thing you can do when the early hype dies down, the setbacks hit and the wins feel too small to matter.

But before you walk away, look back.

Think about Day 1.

Think about the risks you took just to get to the starting line.

The quiet late nights. The work you put in when absolutely nobody was watching.

That wasn’t for nothing.

The pattern is always the same:

People don't usually quit because they can't do the work. They quit because they confuse the discomfort of growth with the sign of failure.

It gets heavy right before it gets good. 

That’s not a red light; that’s the process.

Instead of looking at how much mountain is left, look at the ground you've already conquered. Your past self would have broken fingers to be in the position you are sitting in right now.

You don't need to map out the next ten miles.

Just take the next step. Move accordingly.

content:
Comfort is a slow poison.

It’s easy to choose what feels good right now and completely ignore the most important question:

"And then what?"

We’ve all been there. You feel the tug. You know you’re playing small. You know you don’t belong in the room you’re sitting in anymore.

But the moment you think about leaving, the panic kicks in. So you stall. You settle. You numb the feeling.

Growth is painful. Change is painful.

But nothing hurts worse than staying stuck where you don’t belong.

Stop looking at the immediate friction of making a move. Start looking at the long-term cost of staying exactly where you are.
Before you make a decision today, ask yourself:

• Will this serve me a year from now?

• What is avoiding this conversation actually costing me?

content:
WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THINGS GO BADLY WRONG?

Imagine being in charge of communication for US Airways when flight 1549 makes an emergency landing in the Hudson saving all 155 passengers and crew

That's just one of the challenging crisis that Jim Olson my guest on Uncensored CMO has had to navigate throughout his career

In fact he has written all this down in his new book 'Tailwind' which is a gripping account of some highly publicised moments of crisis combined with some deeply personal ones too like his own battle with cancer

Having had a few in my own career one lesson that resonated a lot with me was not jumping to conclusions about the cause in a bid to sound like you have it all under control

I have twice had to deal with a major incident and in both cases the initial conclusions drawn about the root cause were wildly wrong. In the pressure to find a solution we jumped to incorrect conclusions. In order for real lessons to be learnt it is important to keep all options open and ensure blame isn't assigned. How and when you communicate is therefore critical.

Jim has a simple framework for managing a crisis inspired by his flying days

✈️ Aviate - take control of the plane and stabilise the situation

🧭 Navigate - set the right course to the safest destination

🎙️ Communicate - let people know only after you are navigating

If you have ever faced a major crisis or perhaps more importantly if you havent yet then I really recommend checking this out

Apart from all that Jim has some very inspiring life advice given everything he has been through

I have wanted to do this episode of Uncensored Renegades for some time to find out how the e.l.f has Kory Marchisotto and the team over at E.L.F. BEAUTY managed to pull off 28 consecutive quarters of growth 🚀

Your greatest competition should be ... YOU

How does that work in practice?

By adopting a 'relentless restlessness' to improve things and asking yourself every single time 'how could I have done that better'

I know she does that a lot

I recently sent her a screen shot of Renegades at No.7 in the marketing charts and the message that came straight back was this 

'Nice. Now tell me how we get to 5, then 3, then 1'

I immediately sent back 5 things we should do.

Knowing what to do is actually not that hard but asking yourself the question every time requires intentionality and habit

What I like about this framing is that you can do nothing about your competition but you can do a huge amount about how you react and the constant improvement creates a compounding effect.

Growth is hard and in this episode we unlock some of the secrets to not just achieving it but making it repeatable.

If you’re a creator on the fence, I get the skepticism. I was right there with you.

There is a difference between being a founder vs being a CEO. I made the switch a few years back. The biggest shift isn’t a title change on LinkedIn, or how you sign off your emails, and it doesn’t come when you hit a certain revenue target. 

It’s what your days look like.

In May 2021, we were 5 months into building Connectd.

🕓5am – 7:30am → Emails, Slack, admin, deep work

🕗8am – 6pm → Meetings with team, customers, partners

🕕6pm – 11pm → More emails, more Slack, more work

18-hour days. Every day. 

For over 300 days straight.

Now it’s May 2026.

I’m 5 years and 5 months in.

Still busy, just differently.

🕚Most of my focused work happens before 11am

🕐Calls and meetings are compressed between 11–6pm

⏳ I’ve got space for thinking, not just reacting.

I’ve learned that the job evolves.

In the early days, sacrifice is the signal.

Now? 

Clarity and calm are what help my team win.

You don’t stop grinding

but the shape of the work should change with the stage you’re at.

AN ADVERT WORTH MORE?

World Cup fever is about to create a deluge of blockbuster advertising, in particular from Beer brands, but this one from Stella has set a high early bar - an advertising moment worth more perhaps?

The best Ads are always a simple idea brilliantly executed 

🍺 The idea - "for moments worth more" is a clear brand idea that positions Stella as a premium brand. The fact Stella survives the drama of a goal while all other beer is left on the floor makes the point

🍺 One scene unfolds - using a single scene that slowly unfolds rather than the fast cuts we usually see. This is proof a single scene can provide the magic as Orlando Wood proves in his legendary book Look Out.

🍺 Capturing the emotion - is there a better pub scene that when your team scores and everyone celebrates at once? It's pure System1 thinking tapping into the emotion of the game and the moment of celebration.

🍺 Beckham plays his role to perfection - In this ad he plays his role perfectly at the centre of play but in service of the team. He is starting to build up a strong association with Stella which will compound over time.

🍺 The music creates intensity - the music choice is so good and has a powerful effect on lifting the emotion of the audience. The intensity score of 1.81 vs an average of 1.38 shows the impact.

🍺 Peak end rule - how you feel at the end of an experience tends to dictate how you feel overall and Stella use that really well here leave the audience on a high

The results are impressive ranking at No.59 out of 2548 Beer Ads in the US

Everyone told me fundraising would be brutal. For me it was the part I loved.

I get why that might sound unusual. So let me explain

I did stand-up comedy for 18 months so getting in front of a room and holding attention.. that part never scared me.

Pitching has always felt very natural.

Connectd has now raised $23M. A lot of that came down to figuring out early that my pitching style didn’t have to look like everyone else's. 

Some investors weren't for it but the right ones absolutely were.

Two things I made non-negotiable going into every pitch:

- Knowing my numbers 100% - this gives you huge confidence

- Being honest with what I didn’t know. People can tell when you’re bluffing

You're not trying to impress every investor in the room. 

You want to find the right ones.

When you remember it’s a two way street and that it has to work for YOU as well, it feels a lot less brutal.

content:
The butterfly is a lie if you aren’t willing to melt.

Most people are terrified of change. They’re even more paralysed by the idea of starting over. So, they choose a slow death staying exactly where they are, suffocating in a life that no longer fits.

But here is the cold, hard truth about building anything worth having:
The caterpillar doesn’t negotiate with the cocoon.

It doesn't ask for a "pivot" or a "soft transition." It surrenders. It allows its entire structure to be dismantled because it understands a fundamental law of growth:

Transformation isn’t additive. You don't become new by stacking more onto the old.

Transformation is subtractive. You become new by letting go of what you used to be.

That failed startup? It wasn't a waste of time. That relationship that crumbled? It wasn't a mistake. The version of you that didn't make it to the finish line? That person had to die.

Everyone wants the wings. Everyone wants the flight. But nobody wants to talk about the part where you turn into liquid goo inside a dark shell.

If you are feeling the walls close in, or if your current world feels like it's collapsing, stop fighting the friction.

The discomfort you’re trying so hard to avoid?

That’s not the obstacle. That’s the process.

content:
LinkedIn is changing but most brands haven't noticed.

For years, this platform was downstream. Trends started on TikTok, Twitter, Instagram → eventually landed here → got a 'professional' spin.

That's over.

LinkedIn is now upstream. Culture is being made here, not imported.

NBA players are getting asked at press conferences if they'll post on LinkedIn. Netflix is creating bespoke trailers specifically for this platform. Creators are launching original scripted shows that only work because of the LinkedIn context.

This is a different game now.

We unpacked this on part 1 of episode 4 of What Just Happened. Here's what stood out:

𝟭) 𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝘂𝗻𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱" 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹
Even "boring" industries can stand out by being fun and personality-driven. Your audience wants to be entertained. They're scrolling the same feed as everyone else.

𝟮) 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗯𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘁
You need a founder or team member willing to show up on camera. Personality marketing beats production value.

𝟯) 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸
Being boring leads to irrelevance. The brands staying quiet are losing ground to the ones showing up consistently.

𝟰) 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹
People are choosing vendors based on what they see in their feed. By the time they reach out, they've already made up their mind.

𝟱) 𝗔𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁𝘀, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝘀
Put your engineers, your operators, your subject matter experts in front of the camera. Authenticity beats polish.

The brands, founders, and experts winning on LinkedIn right now aren't importing playbooks from other platforms.

They're writing new ones.

STOP flexing being *sold out & fully booked* on social media

(Respectfully, your audience DOESN’T care) 

Now I’m all for a *shameless* bit of self promotion 

BUT I’ve worked in social media for 7 years

& if you asked me my NUMBER 1 rule for socials???

It’s creating from your *audience’s* perspective, ask yourself:

→ how does this effect me???
→ what’s in it for me??
→ why should I care?

(people are *inherently* selfish, it’s not personal)

Being sold out is great news… for YOU!!!

BUT business wins ≠ customer wins 

because what’s *actually* in it for your audience if you’re sold out or fully booked??

missing out? more expensive resale? wasting time & ££ on an alternative?

You can still flex AND answer “what’s in it for me?” by adding:

📅 a save the date for your next release
💓 alternative ways to get involved 
🎟️ waitlist details 

because your content may be *about* you 
 
BUT your content is *for* your AUDIENCE x

content:
You’re not tired from the work. You’re tired from the weight.

Most burnout isn't from working too hard. It’s from carrying too much.

We leak energy by doing three things without realising it:

1.	Holding onto what already ended.

2.	Resenting where we are right now.

3.	Fearing what hasn’t happened yet.

That combination doesn't just drain your head, it drains your body.

Mike Leber breaks it down simply:

"Happiness is found in three things: letting go of what was, enjoying what is, and having faith in what will be."

So, how do you actually live it?

• Release the chapter that’s closed. Stop re-reading the pages you've already turned.

• Find one thing worth appreciating today. 

Presence is the only place where peace lives.

• Trust the future. What’s coming doesn't need to be controlled by you yet.

None of this is easy, but it’s a lot simpler than we make it.

Burnout rarely comes from the workload; it comes from the mental baggage we add to it. 

True rest isn’t just a nap, it’s the act of letting go.

Unplugged Cabins (one of my top 3 brands out there right now!) absolutely NAILED the hardest thing to do with this social campaign.....


One things brand love to do - insert themselves into every cultural moment. The marathon is one such moment in the year but honestly, most do it badly - it feels forced and irrelevant.
 
The team at Unplugged (led by the brilliant Grace Hawkins Taylor) did what they always do best - they went back to their brand's purpose to find an angle that fit the moment.
 
This campaign was built around a simple but profound idea (as all the best are).
 
Addressing that feeling a lot of people share:

- that the online running community has the potential to be a disheartening space: lots of narratives around having the best kit, the best tech, achieving a PB, sub 3 bros!
 
- instead of actually focusing on the joy of having an amazing, present experience in nature where you felt proud simply because you went on the run in the first place, or because you wanted some fresh air or to explore a new area.

This clear POV is so coherent with their brand & product that it allows them to tap into the cultural moment in a way that's authentic rather than just adding a bunch more unnecessary noise.

And the people liked it if the number of likes is anything to go by.

Love to see brand strategy feed into social like this, top work team 👏 and a shout out to the very talented Lucy Robb who I believe ideated the campaign.

content:
Good strategy is tall. Really tall. 

With its feet on the ground and its head in the clouds, simultaneously.

And it’s exciting. 

You’re offering people the opportunity to explore new areas, to fish in unfished lakes, to hack their way through uncharted jungle, carving their own path towards a destination that has always seemed out of reach.

It’s an invitation to go somewhere new. To try something new. To blow up the status quo and replace it with something more thrilling. 

A great brief is a walk to the cliff edge, with a note that says “the water is deep enough, wanna be the first to jump?”

It should feel exhilarating.

Or terrifying.

Fantastic strategy has the worst account people making calls to your boss and sending out e-mails to express their concerns and cover their asses.

But fuck them - if it has creative people saying “fucking hell” followed by “let’s give it a go”

Brilliant strategy will resist the box, the template, the deck. It will live in an anecdote, or in a picture or in a work of art that says it all. 

It’s often a joke. Or the set up to one.

It cuts the brake lines, puts a brick on the accelerator, then hands the wheel to the creative team (a good planner stays in the car, in the navigator seat. A bad one jumps from the moving car.)

If you’re not excited to brief it, to share it, to throw it as a signpost and a challenge to people who will get it, bring life to it, stretch it… then it’s probably not good. 

All of this I believe to be true. 

Whilst acknowledging that most strategy and most strategists are about as exciting as sex with a Belgian in an airport hotel – in Canberra.

Funny old world, isn’t it?

You can now sort comments to show only replies from verified members.

LinkedIn has 100M+ verified profiles (out of 1.2B+ total). The platform is clearly pushing verification harder.

What this signals: If you're not verified yet, your comments may start getting buried in high-volume threads. Verification is free - might be worth doing now.

𝟯) 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝗽 𝟭𝟰% 𝗬𝗼𝗬
More people are posting. More knowledge-sharing. More competition for attention.

Paid video grew almost 30% YoY. Creators are clearly leaning in.

The bar for standing out keeps rising. Generic content gets lost faster than ever.

𝟰) 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗲𝗱𝗜𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝘂𝗽 𝟭𝟮% 𝗶𝗻 𝗤𝟭
B2B marketing and AI-powered recruiter tools are driving growth. Their AI hiring tools alone hit $450M annualized revenue.

What this tells me: LinkedIn is doubling down on being the B2B platform. If you're selling to businesses, this is where the money is flowing.

𝟱) 𝗠𝗼𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝘃𝘀 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗸𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁

📱 Mobile is optimised for 'what's happening now' - recent posts, short-form content, real-time stuff
💻 Desktop is optimised for relevance - older high-engagement posts, longer reads

My new approach: phone for engagement (comments, DMs, quick replies), desktop for strategy (writing, research, analytics).

Match the task to the tool.

My biggest TAKEAWAY: LinkedIn is rewarding authenticity, trust signals, and intentionality more than ever.

content:
I have always been big on tracking my sleep, recovery, stress levels.. had data on everything. But couldn’t figure out what was draining me.

it's never one big moment is it..?

it just creeps up on you.

Because when you're building from scratch the business becomes everything. 

First thing you think about in the morning, last thing on your mind when you close your eyes.

Your mood lives and dies by how it's going.

(at least it did for me)

The people around me were getting what was left over. Things I used to love getting pushed to later. The version of me outside of work kept getting smaller without me really noticing.

For a founder with ADHD that happens FAST.

The hyperfocus, the all or nothing wiring, the borderline obsession with whatever you're building.. it doesn't stay at your desk.

When I stopped and actually looked at it I asked myself:

if this thing that consumes me was suddenly gone…what then?

Who would I even be without it?

That's not a comfortable thought to sit with.

I try to be much more deliberate about it now. Making sure the business isn't the only thing that gets my time and energy.

I make it a point every day that there's still something left over.

Being aware of it has helped me some.

…and that’s probably the most important place you can start from.

content:
LinkedIn's algorithm hasn't simply changed, the entire job of this platform has shifted. The old rules don't matter anymore.

It's a massively positive move.

I'm a very consistent poster. I've posted about once a day, every day, about advertising/marketing/effectiveness for about 3 years. Favikon's has ranked me the No 1 LinkedIn influencer in marketing for years now. I haven't changed anything - yet this past month everything's gone BOOM.

Why? The new update has clearly moved from recency, virality, and (finally) engagement hacks. To professional relevance, insider knowledge, authenticity, and usefulness.

Key things to be aware of:

1. "Don't include a link in posts" is useless advice. The 4 viral posts you can see below all had at least 1 link in them. If it makes the post better, include it!

2. Yes, video is important, but Socialinsider analysed 1.3 million posts and found that text-only posts saw double the engagement growth vs videos. Again, if it's useful, relevant and authentic...POST IT! 2 of the viral posts below weren't videos.

3. There has never been a link between follower count and post reach, otherwise you'd see the below data slowly growing as I moved from 50k followers to 120k. You have to, you guessed it, share useful, relevant, and authentic content.

4. You can't game the system anymore. I'm so bored of the terrible "comment to agree" posts going viral, LinkedIn came out last month and said they now use AI to actively flag this and limit these posts!

5. There's a decoupling between engagement and reach. LinkedIn is actively deciding itself what is good content and boosting it. I had a post with 100 likes reach 250k people the other day. This is freeing, share good stuff and it doesn't even have to be popular.

I think these are massively positive moves for LinkedIn - 1.5mil people read my stuff last week, 4k decided to follow.

Now is the time to share content and grow your network! But don't get bogged down in the old rules.

content:
Social-first distinctive brand assets 🤳🏻

Here's how to grow brand awareness with short-form ads

In our research, The Long and the Short (Form) of It, we took over 1,000 paid short-form video ads, tested them with 85k TikTok users with System1's tech, and matched them to TikTok's separate Brand Lift data.

A 50-page modern creative effectiveness playbook for brand growth on social fell out (avail here: https://lnkd.in/exijWN8a) but this is my favourite finding.

Certain types of DBA used in the first 2sec show different general impacts in the brand lift data, some dramatically shifting more awareness growth.

This is not as simple as some DBAs being more unique or famous; the type of DBA itself interacts with attention and skipping, driven by the heuristics people have learned online.

We are launching more research on this at Cannes this year, which will reconfirm much of this using different data.

Here's the most interesting parts:

1. Editing a logo into the first part of a social ad causes more skipping and usually has a detrimental effect on awareness.

2. Building the product or logo into the creative itself is far more powerful.

3. The power of sound cannot be ignored. Social flipped to sound on years ago. Use it!

Thanks to our brilliant partners at TikTok for Business for their partnership and data unlocking these industry learnings!

content:
Fast decisions have built everything I have. They've also cost me more than I'd like to admit. 

ADHD founders don't do slow decisions. The brain moves fast, commits even faster and figures out the details later.

In the early stages of building that's genuinely an edge. You move before others have finished deliberating. A lot of good things have come from that.

But not all of them.

Partnerships that looked good in the moment. Choices made after a massive day of meetings that could have waited - and benefitted from a night of sleeping on it.

Those ones definitely cost me.

What I've figured out:

- Reversible decision? Move quick 
Most decisions are more reversible than they feel.

- Involves people? Slow it down
Your instinctive read on others is sharp but it can always use a second look.

- 4PM decision? Better to sleep on it.
Your brain after 3PM is not the same as at 10AM.

The fast decision making is not going anywhere.

just gotta know when to pump the brakes.

TOP 5 INSIGHTS FROM THE WORLD'S GREATEST MARKETERS

The Think with Google team recently asked me to tell them the Top 5 insights I have gathered from interviewing over 250 of the world's best marketers for Uncensored CMO

It was really fun to think about what my top 5 would be and why

As someone who struggles to write and prefers to talk (podcast host) I love how well Alice Cooke has captured my tone of voice here

This is a summary but please do check out the full article

1. Maintain a “humble curiosity”

They are obsessed with how the world works and why humans make the decisions they do. The top tier of marketing leadership never stops asking “Why?” even when they’re at the top of the mountain

2. What got you here won’t get you there

By the time you become a CMO, you aren’t really ‘doing’ marketing anymore. You’re a leader. I found that out pretty quickly in my first CMO role — I spent less than 10% of my time on actual marketing.

3. “Restaurant smart” vs. “corporate smart”

Will Guidara differentiates between “corporate smart” (focussing on uniformity, efficiency, and scale) and “restaurant smart” (where the best-paid person in the building is on the floor, obsessed with the customer).

4. The power of compounding (and strategic laziness)

Great CMOs have the bravery to practice “strategic laziness,” a term I stole from author & CEO of the Marketing Society, Sophie Devonshire⚡️. It means deciding what not to do. It’s the ability to sacrifice short-term KPIs to win the long-term war of brand health.

5. Greatness is in the agency of others

As Scott Galloway famously said, “Greatness is in the agency of others.” To scale, you must be brutally honest about what you’re rubbish at. I hire people who love the technical tasks I find draining, or just can’t do well

content:
If I was responsible for thinking about how to get a B2B FS brand delivering stand-out marketing in 2026, here’s what I think I’d do. But first, an ugly truth about our beloved digital marketing and the business website.

Most B2B financial services marketing in 2026 is competing in the same three places:
LinkedIn feeds
Email inboxes
Search (and increasingly LLM) results

All three are a bamboozling mess of low wattage AI garbage, vanity reporting metrics and your competitors. Unless you’re prepared to be bold or weird or genuinely very different, they are dirty and crowded sandboxes to be playing in.

Dumping all your resources into them makes you look cheap when you really want to look like the real deal. You don’t have to look premium or luxe, but honestly no-one wants their bank or payment partner etc. to feel cheap.

So what to do, what to do. WELL.

I’d go forwards by going ‘backwards’. The two most overlooked channels I see in b2b marketing in general - but especially FS - area events and direct mail.
For years we’ve maligned these channels as legacy tactics — expensive, slow, hard to measure. Meanwhile, digital channels were supposed to scale infinitely and deliver clear and supremely measurable results. But scaling and measuring stuff that everyone wants to ignore is, to use a brilliant Yiddish word, facacta.

Every CFO, CIO, CTO, etc. is hit with dozens of sponsored posts and nurture emails every week. Boooo. Very few receive something physical. Even fewer experience something memorable. That creates an unusual opportunity.

A well-designed physical mailer can cut through 500 digital messages.
A thoughtful event activation can create more real sales conversations than months of digital lead generation.

The key difference is intent. When someone attends an event, they have chosen to be there. When someone opens a physical package on their desk, the interaction is focused and uninterrupted.

Good events and killer direct mailers don’t behave like legacy channels anymore. Get them right and they’re a sort of attention arbitrage. Stand out by showing up in unusual places.

This doesn’t mean abandoning digital marketing, but it does mean recognising things many marketers have forgotten: just because a channel is measurable doesn’t mean it is effective, and just because a channel is ‘old’ doesn’t mean it has stopped working.

If you want to find out how to do something real in a sloppy world - DM me. We’ll run a free workshop with you and your team, and show up with a bunch of ideas and bad (good) film references.

content:
What incredible creativity from IKEA - turning the iconic bag into a new creative device

This goes beyond simply using the blue bag as a distinctive brand asset but turns it into a Fluent Device - a distinctive, creative device that a brand owns and can use repeatably to tell stories, create drama, and consistently create more and more memories and emotion.

One of the many benefits of a Fluent Device is that it can span time and space. Campaigns and media channels. This can work in OOH, social, or digital.

It can be refreshed repeatedly to share new executions without changing the entire idea. Even stretched into new cultural moments (not just summer but NYE, the World Cup, etc.)

This allows it to wear in. Allowing you to stretch the idea further each time, across lower-attention media channels. Where the consistently actually becomes a creative gift, not a constraint.

I'm not sure if this is global work, but I genuinely think whoever worked on this at NoA | Åkestam Holst has produced gold that can serve IKEA for years.

It's a strategy winner as well. IKEA can use this to grow salience for most occasions. Pick a Category Entry Point: dinner with friends, cosy night in, moving house. The ideas then simply present themselves.

If you want to learn more about the Fluent Device, where it came from (Orlando Wood!), and how you can apply them to make advertising more effective, there's a few pages sharing all this with System1 and Effie Worldwide data in this: https://lnkd.in/exppdWEk

author.headline: CCO at Shake Content | Ex LinkedIn | Turning executive expertise into content that drives pipeline

content:
I’m often told that advertising leads culture. 

Usually by people making banners that tell me that the DFS sale is still ongoing and that I can get a huge discount on something if I just click now. 

By the same people who say “let’s create a movement” when briefing on a new, thicker bleach.

My argument has always been that advertising very (very) rarely leads culture, but that it almost always narrows it.

Advertising says “this is what people want, this is what sells, this is what people aspire to” and then fills our screens and our lives with the narrowest slice of human experience – thin, white, young, beautiful, wealthy, well adjusted. 

And when that looks too narrow it asks the thin, white, young, beautiful, city dwelling people inside the agency to cast some new skin tones – but to fit them into traditional roles. We can have an Asian mom now, as long as she’s identical in attitude and behavior to the mom we’ve been showing for years. We may even stretch to gay dads, so long as the teeth gleam, the suburbia shines and the kid is a loveable moppet.

Advertising doesn’t try to create culture, it tries to shape the mainstream. 

Advertising spends its money telling us what’s aspirational, what we should chase, how we should feel. It is an attempt to shape mainstream behaviour, backed by close to a trillion dollars of spend

And then there’s the fact that for decades advertising was gatekeeping the content that it interrupted. Linear TV felt the cold breath of advertisers on their shoulders when they started to look at more complex plots, at more complex characters at more difficult relationships. Would they pull the money? “The sponsors” and their taste in content shaped what we saw on screen. There was no AIDS on TV, because advertisers didn't want to stand next to it. 

Advertising doesn’t lead culture. It filters it and then presents it to a mainstream audience as acceptable culture. It creates a consensus as to what culture is acceptable – and justifies it as being the culture that is inherently commercial.

Maybe not your ad. But as a whole, as a mass, as an industry, as a trillion dollars going into shaping behavior.

So no, you’re not leading culture. You’re narrowing it.

One of my favourite Uber campaigns is back. 3 reasons this is awesome.

1. Compound creativity in action. They launched "You're almost there" last year in airports. Instead of doing what many marketers do (get bored with their own work), they've doubled down on this. Stretching the same insight further, keeping the positioning and strategy the same, refreshing the execution to achieve imagionative repetition. My Compound Creativity research with the IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising), System1 and Effie Worldwide shows you can 4x your campaign ROI by being more consistent like this!

2. Building a new Fluent Device. A fluent device is a specific type of distinctive brand asset. Sure, it triggers the brand and links it to key associations, but it also carries drama and emotion. Previously, we've seen many brand-character or scenario-fluent devices, but this is much rarer. I'm not sure I've seen it before. It's turning a product feature (the Uber journey line) into an ownable creative device to tell a story. It's creative AF. Check out Orlando Wood's book "Lemon" or his course Advertising Principles Explained - a.p.e to learn more about the Fluent Device, and its power to build brand.

3. Outdoor perfection. You might think out-of-home advertising sucks because there are serious creative restrictions. Over three years, System1 and JCDecaux explored how creativity in outdoor leads to brand growth. Beth Marchant and I published all the findings in "Double Take", a rather large playbook for OOH creativity, which makes this case of simplicity but selective strong branding and showmanship. Age 51 - Started my own business. You are not too old.

Age 43 - Started a podcast as a side hustle. Success can come from anywhere

Age 42 - Got fired twice in the same year. S**t happens. Use it as fuel.

Age 40 - Left Private Equity with nothing. Ran out of money. Forced to get a "big job"

Age 37 - Left very comfortable job, invested all my savings in a PE backed business to make serious money. Didn't. Learnt a lot.

Age 34 - Failed at a high-performance selection so created my own perfect role and secured £6m in funding. Hugely successful.

Age 30 - Rejoined the company I left in a much higher position because my mentor was hiring. Pick your boss not the brand.

Age 27 - Failed to land my dream job internally so left in frustration. Sometimes fail is the fuel you need.

Age 24 - Rejected by the Grad scheme so I made my own one up and landed a promotion a year before the Grads did. Didn't wait for permission.

Age 22 - With a finance degree and a desire to get into market I found a job as a 'market analyst'. Sometimes you have to compromise to get there.

Age 20 - Got a job at a prestigious bank after attending some mock interviews and they mixed me up for a real candidate. Doubled my salary overnight. Put yourself in the way of luck.

My lessons

1. You are never too old
2. Always be learning
3. Just take the leap
4. You will figure it out

Thanks to Amelia Sordell who's brilliant post inspired me to write a similar one

content:
The hardest thing I've had to unlearn as a second-time founder is the word ‘yes’.

new opportunity? Yes!!

Interesting idea? Bring it on! 

meeting with someone I've never met and no agenda? SURE!

My ADHD brain treats everything new like it's the most important thing that's ever happened.

The novelty feels urgent because the possibility feels so real. And before I've actually thought about it…i've already committed.

For years I thought this was all about ambition.

Took me a while to understand it was just my brain chasing the next thing before it had finished the current one.

The cost of that is VERY real.

Scattered energy, half finished things, saying yes to stuff that pulled me away from the work that actually needed me.

I'm better at it now (still a work in progress)

I’ll still say yes to opportunity, or meeting new people. But it comes with an extra sense-check of ‘what’s the cost of this yes’ that it didn’t use to.

author.headline: CEO @ Connectd | Connecting Founders & Fractional Leaders | Creator of ‘Founder’ Newsletter | Featured in BBC, Forbes & The Telegraph

content:
Comfort is a slow-motion trap. 

Most people aren’t constrained by talent. 

They’re constrained by the conclusions they’ve quietly accepted about themselves.

I’ve seen it everywhere:

• Teams staying in roles that no longer stretch them.

• Founders repeating models that no longer scale.

• Brands chasing audiences that have already moved on.

Waiting feels "reasonable," but it has a higher cost than moving.

The real constraint isn't the space you're in, it's the narrative you've grown used to believing.

Stop treating your current situation as fixed. Growth doesn’t require a leap; it requires a series of uncomfortable steps taken consistently.

Skills can be taught. Attitude? That’s DNA. 

I’ve learned this the hard way: Skills alone won’t get you to the finish line. You can have the sharpest technical ability in the world, but if you don't bring the energy, you’re just a passenger.

Victoria Repa is spot on: Hire for attitude. Train for skill.

I’d take someone with raw potential and a hunger to grow over a "technically perfect" hire with zero ego-check any day.
What am I actually looking for? It’s three things:

Curiosity over Compliance: Are they asking the right questions, or just waiting for their turn to speak?

Growth Mindset: Can they adapt? Have they pushed themselves outside their comfort zone?

The "We" Mentality: Do they understand that the whole is always greater than the sum of its parts?
Hiring for attitude isn't "settling" it's strategic. 

Stop looking for the perfect resume. Start looking for the person ready to join the journey.

I’m going out on a limb here but as a founder you should WANT to work long hours.

You should want to pull a 12 hour shift.

I think that if your work doesn’t motivate you to want to do that, you’re not building the right thing.

Now that I've got your attention I'll caveat this by saying it works both ways.

Founders who take an afternoon off aren’t lazy.

Those working weekends aren't the pinnacle of productivity.

And working around the clock doesn't mean you have an unhealthy obsession with what you're building.

The reality is that a lot of us work day and night because we genuinely love what we do. We see a direct reward from the extra hours so they feel more like an opportunity than a chore.

That's the founder feeling. That's what it's supposed to feel like.

If it doesn't feel like that right now then it has nothing to do with productivity. It sounds like a purpose problem.

And that's worth paying attention to.

I used to be afraid of admitting that I was ambitious. After all, I dropped out of college, I didn’t go to university, and my mum helped me get my first “proper” job in my late teens. 

Factor in growing up in a society that teaches and conditions women to make themselves as small as possible – figuratively, and literally. 

It was the perfect recipe for putting my ambition in a box, and throwing away the key. 

I kept myself small, comfortable and quiet (read: especially as the little girl who was always told that she was “shy”, “introverted” + could “speak up more in class”) 

And the data proves that the world is still trying to keep women from finding the key: 

→ The Promotion Gap: Women are 18% less likely to be promoted than their male counterparts. Not because of performance, but because our ambition is read as "too much" while theirs is "leadership potential." 
→ The Motherhood Tax: Becoming a mother costs women an average of 4% in lost earnings per child, while men's salaries actually increase after having children and dubbed the "fatherhood bonus." In fact, it takes an average of ten years for a woman’s career trajectory to even begin recovering from the birth of her first child.
→ The Representation Gap: Despite outpacing men in educational achievement, women still hold fewer than 30% of senior leadership roles globally. 

The system isn't broken; it was built this way. We are told that if we've made it into the room, we should just be grateful to be in the room. We’re expected to treat our presence like a gift we haven't quite earned, rather than a result of our own potential.

But I’m done being grateful for a seat at a table that was designed to keep me quiet.

Owning your ambition is a refusal to let a statistical bias dictate your ceiling. Whether you’re a dropout, a mother, or the girl who was always told she was "too quiet" in school: your hunger is allowed to take up space.

The best Tesco ad ever made. Purpose but not dull. Here's the data to prove it.

Tesco's new ad from BBH London is truly brilliant.

System1 tests every UK and US TV ad with millions of people to build our Competitive Edge database, filled with ads and our predictions of how they will perform based on emotional and distinctiveness data.

We've researched 600+ Tesco ads over the past decade. This is the highest-scoring non-Christmas ad we've seen. 5.3 Stars! Massive brand recognition, and a super high "Spike Rating", predicting short-term sales.

I've made the full report free (https://lnkd.in/ez_igZ2Z) but here's my thoughts on what works: 

1. Purpose but not dull. There's a growing narrative that purpose (a brand 
claiming to do something not just for profit) doesn't belong in marketing. This is a great example of why that narrative is BS. Giving 1mil school kids free fruit and veg generates a huge emotional response in the ad, key for long-term brand growth.

2. Right-brained goodness. Character, story, humour, a clear sense of place. Orlando Wood and I have shown across various datasets (including IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising), Effie Worldwide and TikTok) that these "showmanship" features attract and hold broad attention, and lead to more business growth. This has them in spades.

3. The brand is the idea. The brand and "product" (i.e., Tesco) are baked into the idea. You can't explain the ad without understanding what Tesco is. This is the acid test for true distinctive modern advertising.

Ads with such a super high emotional and distinctive response have a 7.5x chance they'll report profit growth in the Effie awards databank. We expect good things from this campaign!

Kill the Bias: Diversity isn’t a quota; it’s a competitive advantage.

90% of jobs can be taught. You can't teach hunger. You can't teach curiosity.

Give people a freaking chance.

author.name: Andrew Tindall
author.headline: The World’s Best Ads & Why They Work | Chief Growth Officer @ System1 | Marketing Effectiveness

content:
Ever feel like Sisyphus?

Not the King of Corinth betraying divine secrets bit. 
The boulder pushing bit.

Agency myth would tell you that they’re Sisyphus, that good work is the boulder, that the client is the hill in Tartarus and that the holding company is Zeus - responsible for everything being futile anyway .

In this version all that agencies want is to get great work out. They push and shove and sweat and struggle and fail because they’re cursed at every step by clients, by ownership, by structure. They’re caught in an infinite loop of futility and none of it is their fault.

Which is bullshit. But convenient bullshit.

Ask any really good creative person where the impediment to getting great work out lies and they’ll tell you that it’s the constant fight against the mediocrity and desire for the easy option in their own office.

Creative people don’t fear stupid reactions in the client presentation, they’re most wary of the amount of fear in the room when they have internal creative reviews. They're scared of the team wondering whether this might challenge the client, upset the Prozac nation status of our meetings with them, whether this is something they know how to do, whether this will take too long and, often, that they don't really understand what the fuck they're looking at

When you spend your life fighting fear & cowardice in your own agency, fighting the people who want it easy, who want it Thursday, who want it to look like everything else, who want it sold without questions, who want it in the template, who want it in a box, who want it gift wrapped - you realise that actually it’s your colleagues who are hill… and that a good number of them are standing on the boulder too

I get into trouble, quite often, for expressing my belief that the job of everyone in the agency is to be in service of the work. And that that means being in service of the creative teams.

The argument against me is that it's a point of view in which the creative teams are more important than others in the agency and that it doesn't acknowledge that "ideas can come from anywhere."

I say - they are more important. And ideas tend to come from them

My belief is that when the work looks good we should all get behind it and push – not throw obstacles and impediments in front of it and ask the creative teams to zig zag their way up the hill, along a path you’ve created in order to preserve the daisies.

I genuinely don’t understand how creative teams are still standing in the current environment. Because it feels, to me, as though they’re being asked not only to push the stone up the hill, but to navigate landmines that need not be there.

Not where you work or where I work, naturally (we're hill free zones). 
But in too many places, across too many clients, in too many geographies.

So my plea is – when you see good work get behind it and start pushing.

content:
The most important thing I’ve learned in the last 6 months as CCO of Shake Content

Has nothing to do with content strategy, posting frequency, or going viral.

It’s this: The conversation changes completely depending on who made the first move.

I still do outreach. It’s part of the job. Reaching out, crafting messages, following up.. it all works to a degree. But it always starts from the same place. You are interrupting someone who wasn’t thinking about you 30 seconds ago. 

And even when that turns into a call, you’re slightly behind from the start. You are speaking to someone who hasn’t spent any time with your thinking, hasn’t built any familiarity with what you do, and doesn’t yet have a strong reason to trust you. So a lot of the conversation is spent explaining, positioning, and trying to earn that trust on the spot.

Compare that to when someone comes to you.

By the time they reach out, they’ve already done a surprising amount of the work. They’ve seen your content, understood how you think, and formed a view on whether you understand their world. 

And you can feel this right away.

The questions are different. The tone is different. The dynamic is different. 

You are no longer trying to convince someone to listen to you.  That’s the part I hadn’t fully appreciated until I saw both sides play out consistently.

Content, when it’s done well, isn’t just a marketing channel. It’s a system that runs in the background of your business. It introduces you, explains your thinking, answers questions. 

More importantly... it builds trust (long before you ever get on a call). And the beauty about content and ideas is that they don't sleep. 

If you're still relying entirely on outreach, you're not doing anything wrong. But you are leaving leverage on the table.

Content is how you change who makes the first move.
