Kindness isn’t a strategy. It’s a way of life. 

Too many people in power think fear drives results.

Newsflash: Fear doesn't create greatness. It creates silence, resentment and high turnover.

If your team is afraid to speak up, they aren’t underperforming, they’re surviving you.

Real Leadership vs. "Babysitting":

• Real Leaders: Create safe spaces. If people can’t fail in front of you, they’ll never grow with you.

• Babysitters: Move the goalposts and critique without care.

Kindness isn't weakness. It’s the ultimate strength. It builds the trust that makes teams go to war for each other.

Your job isn't to feel important. It's to make your team feel capable.

THE SURPRISING POWER OF SONIC ASSETS

In marketing we get so obsessed about the font size and logo and tend to forget what actually makes our brand memorable

Of all the charts I got to see at System1 - and believe me I got to see a lot - this is one of my favourite

It's from a huge study with TikTok to understand which brand assets help drive brand awareness in social media

The most effective asset might surprise you!

🎶 Sonic Assets 🎶 

Distinctive sounds have such a big impact on our ability to recall brands. Just think McDonalds, Intel or Netflix. You don't have to see them to know they are advertising. A beat or two is all that's needed.

Last week I hosted my first ever event Uncensored CMO The Calling and every guest was welcomed on stage with a live guitarist playing the intro music to the podcast (based on the Sex Pistols 'God Save the Queen'). That has become a sonic asset for the podcast and triggers instant emotion for the brand.

The other striking thing about this research is the logo

Show it in context rather than in isolation. 

The trick appears simple.

Open with your product in context supported by a distinctive sonic asset associated with your brand and you have a (sonic) BOOM!!! 

If you want to know more this is from a study called The Long and Short (form) of it which is packed with clear and actionable advice for brand building in social media.

content:
Most founder advice doesn’t go beyond the exit. I got mine at 26 and had no idea what to do with myself. Nothing really prepares you for that bit.

So here's what I wish someone had told me before I got there.

- Figure out your purpose before you chase the number, not after. 
The exit doesn't hand you one and if you don't know what drives you beyond the business, the money just makes that question louder.

- Quit treating sleep, relationships and health as negotiable. You will get to the other side and realise what you gave up. (and some of it you really don't get back.)

- Ask yourself what YOU actually want from the exit instead of what sounds good. So many founders never answered that honestly before they got there.

- The ego stuff is real but it won't sustain you. Some of what drives us toward the exit is ambition. (and yes a lot of it is ego.)

But neither of those are a plan for what comes next.

I was young, chaotic, and hadn't stopped long enough to look at any of this.

The exit forced those questions. 

I'd rather you ask them now than wait for the same wake up call.

content:
GRACE BEVERLEY'S N0.1 PIECE OF ADVICE

At the end of my interview with Grace Beverley at last weeks Uncensored CMO The Calling I asked her what the single best piece of advice she has ever been given was

It was how to remove the anxiety when making decisions by categorising them into one-way or two-way decisions

One-way decisions can't be undone later whereas two-way decision can be reversed in the future

She said she often agonised over decisions that appeared really important when in fact they could be reversed later (the two-way ones)

Daniel Kahneman once said 

"nothing in live as as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it"

We often put off decisions because they feel much more important than they actually are

Next time simply decide is they are one-way or two-way and place the weight of decision making accordingly

It's a surprisingly simple approach

THE POWER OF BEING IN PERSON

I am convinced that as technology takes over more and more of our lives that the one thing people will be craving more of is being together in real life

This week on Uncensored CMO I talk to Rachel Thornton the Enterprise CMO at Adobe about how AI is changing marketing

The secrets out. We're launching The Creator Effectiveness Playbook

In a couple months, the incredible Eugene Healey and I will step on stage at Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity and launch new guidance on using creators for long-term growth from WPP, TikTok, and System1. 

Last year, we launched 'The Long and the Short (Form) of It', revealing how marketers can use short-form video to create immediate and lasting effects.

We also identified the creator opportunity: the best creator content massively outperforms brand-made stuff.

Effie Worldwide data confirmed this, campaigns with creators see the largest number of brand effects. Then WPP Media and IPA (Institute of Practitioners in Advertising) released the first-ever econometric study of creators, confirming that creators have the highest long-term media multiplier.

So the industry is (rightly) throwing itself at creators, but there are obvious questions that need answering. Why is there no reliable growth in outcomes as we spend more on creators? Why is brand attribution on creator content sitting at 25%? How do we select, brief, and invest in creators to responsibly scale this channel?

The Creator Effectiveness Playbook will answer that. I sat down with Beth Marchant, Amy Houlihan, Josh Fruttiger, Joshua Gornell, Dan Long and Callum Mayfield Smith to review the first headline last week, and I can't quite believe what gold we've got coming.

Some digital media clearly led us down the garden path. Creators are our opportunity to make digital advertising more human and emotional again.

It's a crucial turning point in marketing. AThis will ensure we get it right.

Big thanks to our partners at TikTok for Business - Isobel Sita-Lumsden, Charlotte Skornik, James Eddington

The internet can build your career but only the real world can build YOU.  

I’ve spent most of my life building online. I know the game. I know the rush. But even I’ve had to stop and realise:

The digital world is a room you can’t leave if you aren’t careful.

We’ve reached a point where:

• Scrolling feels like "connection."
• Likes feel like "validation."
• Algorithms dictate our "purpose."

But performance isn't presence.
Somewhere along the way, the internet became the place we live and real life became the place we visit. I didn’t like that realisation.

The Math of the Unplug:

If you are constantly "connected" to everyone, you are rarely "present" with anyone.

I’m stepping back. Not to disappear, but to recalibrate.

The real world doesn’t need a "like" to be real.

content:
You read a lot about young people drinking less than previous generations on-trade. Usually in articles that describe said young people as being a more sober, more sensible, more “Sapphy” generation.

I’m pretty sure than some wag / wanker has already pushed out a LinkedIn post that relabelled Gen Z as Gen Zober. If they haven’t it’s only a matter of time.

What you don’t hear a lot about is alcohol being terrible value vs almost every club drug. Or about people not liking the way it interacts with those club drugs. You almost never read about the fact that it’s a messy high that just doesn’t match the experience that people are out to have – or about how it messes with consent.

I don’t know many planners who are standing in front of their alcohol clients and saying “your product is too sloppy for a night in a club that plays decent music… and it costs about 50% more than a decent supply of the K that does fit.”

There aren’t too many ad people telling Red Bull that their biggest competition on a big night out is Molly (though I’m pretty sure that they know) 

Or a lot of people talking about Chem Sex. About G vs G 'n' T.

They’re certainly not talking about how a heightened sense touch and connection on ecstasy is something that a lot of people out there prefer to the desperate determination to get to penetrative sex on beer. 

And no this isn’t a post about drugs being better than alcohol (alcohol is a drug etc) it’s a post about people not telling the truth.

It’s a post about planners ducking the real conversations and instead pretending that all competition comes from within the category. That all switching comes from within category. And that the world ceases to exist outside of the narrowest field of view. 

This could have been about how vulnerable truck sales are, given the price of gas and how few US truck owners actually need a truck.

It could have been about how vulnerable ad agencies are to technology that works conversationally rather than transactionally. 

It would still have been about the fact that we sit in too many meeting, wearing blinkers when it comes to thinking beyond an assumption about a category and looking at our feet when it comes to calling out the laziness in the room.

By the way… if you do see “Gen Zober” please let me know, I have the number of a euthanasia clinic on speed dial.

content:
Someone came up to me recently and said: 'I love your content. I read everything you post'

I had never seen his name on a single like or comment...

My first instinct? He was just being polite. But he wasn't. 

He was just... 'invisible'

Everyone's panicking about LinkedIn engagement dying.

But I think we are all looking at the wrong numbers.

A new Metricool study (670,000+ posts) just confirmed what I've suspected for a while:

Impressions ↓ 10%
Likes ↓ 13%
Comments ↓ 17%
Shares ↓ 11%

But…
Clicks ↑ 5%
Total engagement ↑ from 12.2% → 13.9%

How?

Invisible interactions 👻 

Clicks on links. Swipes through carousels. Views on videos.

Nobody sees them. They don't show up on your post. Your competitors can't copy them. But they are still happening and LinkedIn counts every single one.

We've been obsessed with vanity metrics - the public scoreboard - while real audience behaviour was happening silently in the background.

The people reading your post and clicking through to your site? They don't always like them. They don't always comment.

But they still showed up.

Important reminder: Not all engagement is visible. 

That guy who never liked a single post? He became a client.

Integrity isn't a luxury. It’s a foundation. 

We live in a world where:

• Applause can be bought.

• Trends change overnight.

• "Wrong" is viral, as long as it’s popular.

But popularity is a terrible compass.

Doing the right thing is rarely the "easy" thing. It might cost you a deal. It might cost you a "friendship." It might cost you the illusion of success.

The trade-off? You get to sleep at night.

When you look back on your career, you won’t measure your worth by who clapped for you. You’ll measure it by the times you stood up when it was easier to fall in line.

Wrong is wrong, even if everyone is doing it.

Right is right, even if you’re doing it alone.

Character is built in the silence, not the noise.

Your time is coming. Keep your hands clean and your heart open.

content:
Open Ai just forecast $100bn in ad revenue by 2030

And pretty much signalled the end of the age of interruption

Over the last 150 years or so advertising has been an interruption – we’ve simply placed our messages between people and the things that they were interested in

Magazine articles were interrupted by single page ads, radio shows by fast talking ads, TV shows by an ad break every 12 minutes or so, internet browsing by pop ups and banners, youtube by pre-roll, cinema by the ads as took your seat

It’s all been based on the same philosophy. Find out what people are interested in, and stand between them and it for as long as you can get away with

Of course, over time, the excuse for interruption evolved

There was a time when you were allowed to interrupt because you owned the content – the soap opera only existed because the soap company.

Then there was an era when the aim was to make the ads more interesting than the thing that they interrupted. The ads had bigger per minute budgets than the programs they interrupted – so you got epic ads shot by huge directors and brilliantly funny ads performed by at peak actors (Ah, Cinzano)

The internet changed that, swapping entertainment for relevance; pushing the idea that an ad triggered by search would be welcomed. Pillow ads when searching for insomnia for example

They tried influencers too. You may skip a brand in your feed, but maybe not an influencer you’ve invited there. You might have 30 seconds for a Kardashian that you wouldn’t for a Korean Haircare product

And when that didn’t work we just made viewing mandatory. Who hasn't hovered over the “skip ad” button on YouTube pre-roll?

Interruption is less and less successful of course. People are skipping, blocking and subscribing themselves out of the available audience pool – leaving behind the poor, the old and the tech illiterate.

And so the opportunity for Open AI is huge. 

They’re the first platform to look at moving away from the idea of advertising as an interruption, from the idea that you’re there for the content and will suffer the sell in order to get it. 

They’re going to sell recommendation. 

Real time recommendations that are conversational rather than broadcast. 

The ads won’t get between you and what you’re doing because they won’t be ads. They’ll be a mention, a name, a recommendation as part of the conversation. No agency will be sending asset their way. They’ll just be weaving brands into conversation the way that Richard Osman does into his books. At a fraction of a cent per mention.

There’s a role here for people who can write the information that informs the AI about the products, the brands – their meaning, usage and appeal.

And no role for agencies whose bread and butter has been making assets to fit spaces on a TV screen, website or phone. 

And less space for the influencer too

The age of interruption is coming to an end – after a close to 200 year run

Here’s to recommendation, how fast will it reign?

I was just writing a post, and I felt myself being drawn into AI-sloppy phrases like "It's not this, it's this" and "someone's quietly doing XXX." Without noticing it, it was only when I read back what I'd written and thought: what the hell am I doing?

A quick scroll through LinkedIn confirms it. These AI tells are now in news headlines and literally most posts. I don't believe AI has written all of this content, but there's a reason AI likes this way of writing. It's clear, structured and easy. Not messy. Humans will follow after seeing it enough times. We are creatures trying to lower mental effort after all.

Annoyingly, once you notice it - it makes reading stuff horrible. As soon as I come across phrasing like this, I feel like I need a hot scrub in a shower. Human language changing in such a way feels wrong.

It's an issue with costly signaling.

I get that people struggle with writing coherent narratives or arguments. I do, I'm dyslexic and find writing a weekly column tough. But when you're reading something, and you notice (consciously or subconsciously) that the human has outsourced some of the effort to AI, it signals the author has tried less, and what you're reading has less value.

It's only going to get worse for here. Stringing words together will become a lost art at some point, I presume.

The dangers of outsourcing thinking to AI, some stuff will be hard to take back.

Expertise is a mask. Enthusiasm is a superpower. ⚡️

Most people spend their entire careers "performing" confidence. They:

• Rush to claim mastery.
• Need to be right to feel worthy.
• Hide the parts of them that aren't "polished."

But performance isn’t practice.

The most powerful people I know aren't the ones with all the answers. They are the ones with the most questions. They aren't afraid to say, "I’m still figuring it out."

Why? Because ego is a ceiling.

When you think you’ve reached the top, you stop climbing. But when you lead with curiosity, you make room for wonder. You allow yourself to be changed by what you don’t yet understand.

Don't be the person who looks certain.
Be the person who stays curious.

The world rewards the certain. Life rewards the open.

content:
You can’t scale if everything needs you. I learned this the hard way.

There's a version of control that actually limits how far you can go.

During my early days as a founder I thought I had to be across everything.

Always in the loop and needed for every little detail.

I didn't think of it as a problem and assumed that was just what growth looked like.

(it definitely wasn't).

You can’t scale that way.

Your business needs to move faster than one person's attention can travel.

And if you're the bottleneck, you're the biggest problem.

Relinquishing control isn't natural for me since every instinct screams at me to be hands on and get the full picture.

Learning to fight that instinct and trusting the people around me, creating space, letting things move without me is where the real growth started.

Both in the business and in myself.

Turns out letting go is a skill. 

One that hasn’t come easy to me.

content:
adidas just schooled Nike on brand positioning

Nike has pulled its "Runners Welcome. Walkers Tolerated." ad from the Boston Marathon after a couple of viral takes called the brand out for the lack of accessibility.

I think pulling the ad is an error.

I wrote about this over a year ago (https://lnkd.in/emwStpqz) - sports brand positioning became purpose soup. Everyone was chasing betterment: Just Do It, I Am What I Am, and Impossible Is Nothing.

What has followed has been a global brand positioning masterclass.

Nike doubled down on Just Do It and becoming the best you, releasing "Winning Isn't For Everyone" and "So Win!". Whereas adidas moved to be the encouraging friend with "You Got This."

This line of copy that's been pulled is bang on Nike's positioning. Pushing yourself to win. It's not for everyone. Marathon runners who are thinking of slowing down ... "Just Do It."

I understand it's not the most accessible ad, but strategy is about choices. Nike's positioning means its running gear isn't targeted at people walking a marathon.

On the other hand, whoever is running adidas' socials clearly understands their positioning. "You got this" is for people walking in a marathon, so they've shown up and reminded everyone of that.

I love the Nike running ads around the world at the moment. I see them while running around London (they make me speed up). But I think pulling this is a mistake. Brands need to stand for something.

Thoughts?

content:
Click through rate: Useful or useless?

I've shared this chart before but it's worth sharing again

This is a geo-experiment by Adriaan Hogervorst - de Jong from Goboony, that he's now repeated across geographies. Showing Click Through Rate increases in the regions where more channels were turned on.

Let me be clear on a few things:

1. Click Through Rate is not linked to long-term brand growth outcomes. There's plenty of research showing this, but I'll have new stuff to share in Cannes this year on it.

2. Click Through Rate is linked to short-term digital success. Ie you have to click to "convert" in most cases, although it's even a shoddy way of measuring that as 80% of purchases driven by Meta ads actually happen offline (see: "Everything Competes with Everything" < search it!)

3. Click Through Rate is a proxy of brand size. The greater the equity of your brand, the more people click (and consider, and convert). See Tracksuit x TikTok: The Awareness Advantage. Basically, what underpinds "The Double Jeopardy Law" and "The Rosser Reeves Phalacy". You can see that effect in the chart below as Dr Grace Kite has noted before!

4. Click Through Rate, in this instance, can be used to demonstrate how media and advertising works together to compound efforts. Yes, it's just through clicks, but what's happening here is channels working together to change memories and behaviour. That has huge implications on advertising: we must be consistent across the mix and plan in campaigns not assets (something AI is rather bad at doing right now).

5. Click Through Rate is more complicated than we pretend it is. The fact is, mid-flight in digital campaigns using the metrics available to you isn't insane, but we must be careful not to be optimising away from brand growth to conversion, which CTR could do. Also, algorithms clearly use clicks (likes, comments) to decide who and where to show ads.

So, as shown in System1 and Effie Worldwide recent research (https://lnkd.in/exppdWEk), relying on short-term metrics like CTR as part of your campaign's main objectives leads to worse long-term outcomes (inc. profit) BUT in this experiment, it shows us something useful about marketing, and sometimes marketers tactically (and carefully) have to use it to do their job.

Tom Goodwin once challenged me: "Useless or useful? Pick one."

I refuse! Clearly, it can be both useless and useful. It depends on how you're using it. Here's to allowing for more nuance in marketing.

content:
Employment is a transaction. Valuation is a transformation.

Most people show up to work just to be a resource. They trade hours for a paycheck and call it a career.

But high performance doesn’t happen in a vacuum. It happens when you stop being a "hire" and start being a force.

The Anatomy of a High-Value Environment:

1. You have a seat, not just a desk.

They don't just hand you tasks; they ask for your insights. Your voice isn't just tolerated, it's required to move the needle.

2. Growth is the KPI.

Your development isn't an afterthought. It’s a shared mission. If the company is scaling but you’re stagnating, you aren't being valued. You're being used.

3. Recognition is deeper than a paycheck.

Real value is felt in the respect for your time, the celebration of your wins and the protection of your peace.

4. Safety > Surveillance.

It’s a culture where "taking a break" isn't a sign of weakness, it's a maintenance requirement for excellence. If you can't rest, you can't reach your peak.

The Brutal Reality:

You spend too many hours at work to feel like a ghost in the machine.

An environment that values you doesn’t just employ you, it empowers you. It aligns your ambition with their vision.

If you aren't walking into a room that makes you feel seen, heard, and capable of legendary work?

Keep walking.

🔥Dr Alexander Young

The best ad I've seen this week

It's rare to see such classic top-tier FMCG marketing at play across the board.

1. Produce innovation following consumer demands
2. Global strategic planning and positioning
3. Creative execution (channel, consistency & idea)

I can't give BBH London ALL the credit here, this feels like the brief of a lifetime, but wow did they own it.

I was trained to innovate into product truth, then ladder it into something emotional. It's a marketing doctrine that isn't always possible, but I've always thought if it's doable, why not? The rational message wrapped in a warming emotional jacket.

Chupa Chups finally accepted that opening their lollies was impossible. So they innovated to make it easier for consumers - the wrappers now slip off.

They strategically positioned this as around becoming easier and more playful. But the creative idea "No More Wrestling" simply lifts it to new heights. It finds the drama in the idea. It earns attention, it's worth talking about.

BBH, not stopping there, clearly understand their outdoor poster onions. OOH needs big, distinctive brand assets, simple executions, not many words, and cultural references. They managed all that while not losing the magic.

Not to mention the consistency here. Salvador Dali painted the Chupa Chups logo in 1969. They haven't tried to change it since.

I've put this into System1 testing, expecting great things across emotion, showmanship, and distinctiveness with consumers.

Genuinley think this is masterful and why I love advertising, congrats Chupa Chups compañía del Grupo Perfetti Van Melle.

The truth that a LOT of founders don’t want to hear …

the thing that kills most startups is the stuff happening inside the building that nobody wants to deal with.
sure, sometimes the market works against them, or maybe the competition was too strong.
But I’ve seen so many companies fail for entirely preventable reasons.
Culture becomes a "we'll sort that later" thing and by that time the team is already at odds.
The wrong people have been in seats too long, making hard conversations impossible.

This is why we never waited to hit some revenue milestone at Connectd before we gave our people an environment they could thrive in.

We made it a priority from day one because I'd seen what it does to a team when you leave it too late.
Would your team come to you if something was wrong or would they be too scared?
If you're not sure, that's probably a good place to start.

Semrush analyzed 89,000 LinkedIn URLs cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode.

You don't need 50k followers. 

You need to consistently put your genuine expertise into words, in public, where AI can find it.

Your lived experience in your niche is more valuable than any polished brand post.

Your perspective. Your insights. Your POV.

Founders are sitting on a goldmine of content. Most just aren’t posting.

That’s not a content problem. It’s a distribution problem you can actually fix.

content:
The problem with a lot of terrible agencies is that they think that the idiots are outside of the building.

They look at clients - well trained, well informed, well resourced, well intentioned, well qualified – and they sigh “idiots.”

They are arrogant enough to believe that the rag tag bunch of kids they’ve employed straight out of a liberal arts college (based on their being cheap, looking right and knowing the managing director’s girlfriend) are somehow better qualified to judge what the client should be committing millions of dollars to than the client.

They are prone to temper tantrums - bellicose, belligerent, truculent and rude.

They are unable to articulate the reason for their belief in an idea.

They roll their eyes when they should be rolling up their sleeves.

They care about their own reel more than they do the client business. 

There are lots of terrible agencies out there.

Mediocre agencies, by contrast, just want to keep things moving. They talk more about “The Deck” than “The Work”, ask more questions about “The Mandatories” than “The Strategy”

They are designed to minimize friction. To eliminate discomfort. To make the client look good – even at the expense of the work that they make for them.

They present 3 ideas, knowing that 2 are bad. Then agree to merge to two bad ideas into 1 awful one – because it’s Tuesday and they need sign off this week if they’re going to deliver on time.

Honesty terrifies them. It threatens to derail the timeline. And the timeline is what matters. 

They have more tools than they have ideas. Spend more time in meetings than they do actually making work. Have a template for everything and a person on hand to make the mediocre look pretty. 

They really care about what the client wants and likes. They care less about what the client needs.

They are the bland pretending to understand brand – but really they are an exercise in filling in time that can be billed to time sheets.

Brilliant agencies know their clients, but don’t pander to them.

They have fewer black boxes, and share more thinking along the way. They don’t need a deck, because the conversations have already happened,

They have faith in their taste and in their knowledge of the market and the people who shop it. 

Their senior people don’t pop into the meeting to say “hello” – they’re involved in shaping the thinking, have seen the work.

They know the kind of work that they think works – and they know why. They are convinced of their philosophy – and attract clients who share it.

They’re also willing to raise a hand and say “we don’t know” or “it’s a risk” or even “we may be wrong here” 

They don’t take feedback as a sign of a client “not getting it” or as dictation. They are thoughtful.

 There is less posturing, less reliance on being “cooler” than the client – and more determination to get it right, to do what has the best shot at really connecting.

I’ve worked at all three kinds of agency. Where are you now?

content:
How Apartments.com went from challenger brand to category leader

One of my favourite campaigns from the past decade. It's literally a masterclass in how advertising can beat the competition.

Yet I've never heard anyone talking about it.

Air asked me to write a piece for their new Beautifully Illogical report, one campaign that AI could never do. The whole report (now free here: https://air.inc/illogical) is filled with a load of creatives making some very good points about other campaigns. But they missed the bigger picture.

Yes, AI struggles getting creative. It can't come up with novel, human and emotional ads so easily. But its main weakness is the inability to think in campaigns, and not just assets. It can't consistently build ideas.

Unlike this brilliant campaign, which won a Sustained Success Effie award (the hardest to win).

They hired Jeff Goldblum as a crazy brand character. And they consistently stuck with it for 10 years. So many people will have told them to change - but they just kept going.

The data (pulled from my recent Creative Dividend research) really reveals the power of Compound Creativity. Every year, they kept on going with the same idea and positioning. More awareness and more revenue followed. Until they became a category leader.

It's one of the most impressive examples of effective advertising I've ever seen. You can read more about it, how AI will never replace human creativity, and work that simply shouldn't have worked, in the full Air report.

I share #advertising and #marketing insights daily, follow for more. In this case - Air sponsored me to write my thoughts and share this post.

content:
Your mindset is either your greatest architect or your loudest critic.

Most of the battles you lose aren't fought in the boardroom. They are fought in your head at 3:00 AM.

The difference between elite performance and average results is a simple shift in vocabulary.

The Reframing Blueprint:

• "I have to" → "I get to"

Your obligations are just privileges you’ve forgotten to appreciate. You don’t "have to" work; you get to solve problems and build equity.

• "I can’t" → "I’ll learn"

Incompetence is temporary. Inexperience is just a data point. The only thing separating you from the "greats" is the audacity to show up while you still suck.

• "I need motivation" → "I need momentum"

Motivation is a fair-weather friend. It’s unreliable. Momentum is self-made. You don't wait for the energy to move. You move, and the energy finds you.

• "I was rejected" → "I was redirected"

Rejection is just positioning. Sometimes the 'No' is the only thing protecting you from settling for a life that is too small for your potential.

The Brutal Truth:

Waiting for "the right time" is just a polite way of quitting.

The biggest flex in life isn't your title or your bank account. It’s having a mindset that stays in the driver’s seat even when the road gets ugly.

Stop fighting your circumstances.

Start upgrading your operating system.

content:
It’s TUESDAY.

And you’re already halfway to a burnout you didn't schedule.

Meetings are booked. Favors are promised. Everyone’s "urgent" request has become your priority.

But your own peace? That’s still pencilled in for “when there’s time.”

Here is the reality:

You do this every week. You run on fumes, tell yourself you’re “fine,” and then crash on Friday wondering why you’re irritable and secretly resentful of the people you “showed up” for.

You aren’t a martyr. You’re just bad at maintenance.

Somewhere along the line, you decided that putting yourself first was selfish.

It’s not. It’s oxygen.


The Math of High Performance:

You can’t pour from an empty cup.

Yet, you keep flipping yours upside down, shaking out the last drops, and acting surprised when nothing comes out.

The people you are running yourself into the ground for?

They don’t need your burnout. They need your best.

And your best only comes from a full cup.

The Blueprint for the rest of your week:

• Add yourself to the list. Not when it’s convenient. Now.

• Protect your sleep. It’s a performance tool, not a luxury.

• Move your body. Get the clarity you can't find in a spreadsheet.

• Do one thing for you. Every single day. No apologies.

Everything you need to know about product strategy is in this photo...


Something about this line up in my local coffee shop hit me.

The café stocks Oatly alongside 3 Alpro barista milks - coconut, almond, soya.

Which means they specifically chose Oatly over the Alpro oat milk. 

Big illustration of brand power.

That's a lot of money left on the table.

So why don't they just… make an almond milk? A coconut milk?

In their own words: "We do oats because we don't know anything about almonds, or soy or cows."

Keeping the main thing the main thing. Doing one thing well.

Do they miss out on revenue? YES 
Do they keep true to their vision? YES 
Is their brand stronger because of it? YES

That kind of discipline at their scale is almost unheard of.


What other products have been this militant in their focus?

content:
There are people out there who will tell you that the key to a good brief is an insight (bleurgh)

Others will tell you that it’s a tension. Then there are those who will tell you that a brief needs only to define the problem. While another school of thought will tell you that it’s about defining the audience and bringing them to life. Other people still will insist that it hinges a killer proposition, unless they’re telling you that what’s actually crucial is a description of the product, or the brand, or the tone of voice or a list of KPIs, or the mandatories.

Basically people will tell you that the thing that they know how to do best (or the template that they have for sale) is the key to a killer brief.

They are, of course, all grifters, charlatans and scoundrels.

A good brief is a brief that leads to better work.

And for that it needs to work for the people receiving it.

Being dogmatic, insisting that one box or strand of the brief is the only one that matters is an act of selfishness that will poison the work.

Asking a team what they need, where they like to start, what kind of information they want to have, where they need you to dig, how they want to receive that information and how you can help through the process is the only real mandatory when it comes to writing a brief. 

Because ultimately, if the brief doesn’t help them get to a better place, to good work – if it doesn’t act as a shortcut to interesting – then it’s fucking useless, regardless of whether it fills the criteria of insight that you’re using that day.

“Young guys wake up with their phone in one hand and their dick in the other – sounds like a great place for Axe, right?” may work for one team.

Whereas the other may need “The problem that we have is that Axe is relegated to ‘before a night out status’ and the real volume in deos and body sprays is in the morning, not the evening. How do we get more Axe usage in the morning?”

A third team may just need “Axe is your best first move. But only 23% of young guys use it at the start of the day, Let’s make it the first move of the day the best move of the day for 45% of our audience”

Whereas another might be good with "plug Axe into the manosphere"

Obviously there will also be visual ways in, some teams might want references from the category, some might want to know more about morning routines, what these kids are watching and listening to – who they admire, who designs their t-shirts. The might wanna know who these guys look up to - or down on 

Your job as a planner is to know what your teams need to make good work. 
And to give it to them. 

Then (and only then) do you get to do the rest of the job - to show up and give them more input, more direction, more communication, more opportunities to ask questions, debate stuff and bounce ideas along the way.

But throwing “a tension” at the wall and walking away thinking “job done” is not the job.

The creative department is your client. Serve them.

content:
24 tabs open. Two voice notes to myself on Wispr Flow. One completely unrelated business idea. Classic.

This is what a Friday morning looks like in my head.

I sit down to do one thing. Somewhere between opening my laptop and actually starting, my brain has already gone six different directions. Each one felt important and probably was in some way.

For years I thought this was a problem I needed to fix.

I'd try systems, timers, stricter routines. Telling myself to just focus. It never really worked because I was treating the symptom without understanding what was actually happening.

The 24 tabs are just my brain scanning, connecting, looking for the thing that matters. Sometimes that's inefficient. Sometimes that's exactly how the best ideas at Connectd have started.

I've stopped fighting it as much and started working with it instead.

The voice notes get listened to. The tabs get revisited. The random business idea at 9am occasionally turns into something real.

ADHD as a founder isn't always the liability people make it out to be honestly. 

It's just a different operating system.

One that has 24 tabs open at all times.

content:
Stop confusing "Perks" with "Culture"

I’ve seen it time and again: companies trying to "buy" employee engagement with organic kombucha, branded hoodies, and "Casual Fridays."

Here is the hard truth: You cannot overcompensate for a broken environment with a ping-pong table.

Culture isn’t something you buy; it’s something you build through intention, energy, and honestly, actually giving a damn about your people. People don’t stay for the free snacks. They stay because they feel seen, challenged, and valued.

If you’re serious about building a legacy, stop looking at the office fridge and start looking at your leadership:

Clarity over Chaos

Perks are a distraction if the vision is blurry. People need to know where the ship is headed and exactly how their role helps it get there. Give them a "Why," and they’ll figure out the "How."

Growth over Gimmicks

Forget beer on tap; give them a path forward. Invest in mentorship, learning budgets, and real career progression. People don't want to be entertained, they want to be empowered.

Trust over Tokens

Autonomy is the ultimate perk. "Work from anywhere" means nothing if you’re micromanaging every keystroke. Trust your people to deliver and they will usually exceed your expectations.

Inclusion over Performance

Hiring for diversity is only the first step. True culture creates a space where every voice is heard and every person has a fair shot at success. Don't ask people to "fit in" build a system where they can thrive as they are.

The Bottom Line: If you want a real culture, start with care, not convenience.

Create a workplace where people show up fully because they know they actually matter.

content:
I hear this almost every day:

'I haven’t posted yet… my following is too small'

But that’s exactly the wrong way to see it.

Small accounts don’t have a disadvantage on LinkedIn.

They have upside asymmetry.

The data shows a breakout post from a sub-1K account can travel 80x further than their typical reach.

That means one post can outperform months of silence.

Implication:
LinkedIn is becoming content-first, not network-first
Followers mainly raise your floor, not your ceiling

The real risk isn’t posting with a small audience. It is waiting until you think you are 'big enough' to start. By then, you’ve already missed your highest-leverage window.

And the longer you wait, the more the belief reinforces itself: 'I don’t have an audience, so it won’t work'

So you don’t post. So it doesn’t work. Self-fulfilling.

Source: credits to my friend andreas jonsson and the wider TheShieldIndex team.

Kindness is not a soft skill. It’s a strategic force multiplier.

If you’re only "nice" when things are going well, you’re just acting. Real leadership is how you show up when the pressure is red-lining and the chaos is peaking.

The Reality:

Too many leaders think fear drives results. It doesn't.

Fear creates silence. Silence leads to resentment. Resentment leads to turnover.

If your team is afraid to speak up, they aren’t performing for you.

They are surviving you.

The Performance Blueprint:

• Trust > Surveillance: If people can’t fail in front of you, they’ll never innovate for you.

• Encourage Loudly: Correct with care. Build confidence, don't just find faults.

• Model Control: If you lash out under pressure, you’ve already lost the room.

Culture isn’t built in an all-hands meeting.

It’s built in the 1-on-1 moments when someone messes up and you choose belief over blame.

Leadership isn't about making yourself look important.

It’s about making your people undeniable.
That’s the job.

Go do it.

content:
WHERE DO YOU GET YOUR INSPIRATION?

One of the toughest challenges I ever faced in my career was setting up a new business unit at Britvic 

At the time Britvic was really good at managing large brands but got impatient with small ones. My plan was to create a dedicated team and invest like a start up by seeding and nurturing the brands as if I owned them.

The biggest challenge I faced was that when I looked around at everyone else in the company for advice I realised no-one was going to tell me how to do it. 

What I was about to do had been talked about a lot but never done before.

So for inspiration I looked outside

That's when I started reading Eating The Big Fish by Adam Morgan and just as importantly his follow up book The Pirate Inside.

I also attend events his consultancy eatbigfish ran and built up a relationship with Adam sharing my war stories and picking his brains

From then on I became obsessed with reading business books and looking at how other categories solved similar problems

I was reminded of this when Kory Marchisotto and I discussed where we get our inspiration from on the latest UNCENSORED RENEGADES. 

She has spent 30 years as a leader in the beauty industry and you might think she is inspired by some of the most famous brands in that sector. It's quite the opposite. She looks outside her own industry and name checks brands like Liquid Death as inspiration.

I believe this is one of the most powerful habits you can create

By remaining in your own company and category you get conditioned to see the world in the same way. By stepping outside it you are inspired to see the world in a complete new way.

It's one reason that when I worked at System1 I ran the Uncensored CMO. Not only was I meeting our customers every week but I was hearing how other industries solve similar problems.

• You build better teams.

content:
Before AI takes your job, it will take your willingness to put in the effort, your pride in the work and your ability to care about much of any of it.

Primarily by subjecting you to Effort Atrophy.

We’re all wired to avoid cognitive load. To find shortcuts that make things easier. To push the thinking onto the next person, or into the next day. It’s one of the reasons so many of us find it impossible to work without a looming and seemingly impossible deadline.

But it’s precisely the fact that advertising creatives have been able to put the desire to do the easy thing on hold and instead stare at a blank page determined to do a new thing that has made the work that we do memorable and made us valuable.

Creativity is too often represented as a flash of inspiration, snatched from the air and committed to the page. But the truth is that it’s an endurance sport – a task that requires people to work at a problem for long periods of time, as they explore approaches.

It’s hard, it’s painful – but when you crack it, when you solve the problem, when you come up with an answer that you know is gonna hit, well then it can be almost euphoric. Creative people are proud of their work, precisely because it was so hard to birth.

So, let’s talk about “effort atrophy”

The client spits out a brief with the aid of their AI tool.
The account team use AI to draft their e-mail response and check their grammar.
The planner jumps onto their favorite AI site and spends 10 minutes “digging” before asking the computer to spit out a brief.
The team get that brief, ask AI to give them creative ways in and then use it to come up with 1st executions that look a lot like finished concepts

Nobody has spent much time thinking.
No blood is on the page or on the floor. 
And the work is average.

It doesn’t belong to anyone. So there’s no pride in it.
But it sells. And it gets made. And largely ignored. 

But hey, there’s another brief with another tight deadline, so no time to ponder that.
It’s time to run more words through tools.

And with every round our willingness and ability to close the computer, put a blank page on a table or desk and start thinking lessens.

We’re less and less willing to do the work
And more and more willing to outsource it

We do it unthinkingly.
And lose our ability to put in the hard yards.

AI will get you for sure.
But first it will take your ability to care.

content:
New data warns marketers off purpose again. But it's as flimsy as the stuff that got us into this mess. When will the purpose pantomime end?

How have the anti-purpose crew that called out all the flaws with the pro-purpose evidence fallen for exactly the same thing?

Why does this debate bring out the worst in the best marketers?

We left this in a very sensible place. We identified the definition of purpose had stretched beyond use. Peter Field showed marketing with extra social value can be crap, and it can be good. Mark Ritson capped it off with "the purpose of purpose is purpose." Some marketing can also do some good, yes.

Brands cooled their beans. Not everyone had to save the world. We managed to find some rare nuance. It can be used by some brands to work, like most strategic choices in marketing.

Yet for some reason, some can't let it go. Why can't we let some marketers grow their brands while doing some good? There really is no better evidence showing purpose doesn't work. As my column concludes today...

"Until the evidence gets any clearer than that, claiming any absolute answer to this debate is silly. So, I’m not giving up on purpose. I’m giving up data that’s trying to settle an argument with evidence that wasn’t good enough to start one. Brand purpose is innocent until proven guilty."

content:
I'm at 100 days of no alcohol and now just over two weeks of no coffee.

This shouldn’t be revolutionary. But as a founder with ADHD, you pay more of a brain tax with stimulants than most.

I love a busy schedule, I’m wired a little weirdly.

It’s not uncommon for me to be working from 5AM - 7PM.

For as long as I can remember I’ve fuelled that with 5+  black coffees a day.

Not ideal.

Becoming reliant on anything to function is dangerous to me.

ADHD dopamine systems don’t regulate the way others do. 

I don’t get the caffeine spike when I don’t have coffee.

My energy is more balanced. 

I’ve been trying matcha, to the team’s amusement. Haven’t found one I like yet!

Not saying coffee is bad. But I’m always looking for ways to optimise my own performance. If I can give 10% more each week and take better care of myself by cutting out habits that don’t serve me, I’m doing it.

It’s the small things that stack up.

Character is the real currency.

Don’t dim the light that someone else lit in you.

Pass the torch.

content:
Most people are judging your future based on your current "draft."

They see the struggle. They see the quiet season. They see the "still figuring it out" phase.

And they assume that’s the end of the story.
That’s a small-minded trap.

Time doesn't just pass, it transforms.

It’s the same pressure that handles coal that creates the diamond.

The Reality of the Transition:

When you start evolving, people start acting funny.

They call you "different" like it’s a warning.
They bring up the "old you" like it’s the only real version.

Why?

Because your growth is a mirror.

• Your discipline makes their excuses louder.

• Your consistency makes their "one day" look weak.

• Your standards make their comfort zone feel embarrassing.

The Most Expensive Decision You Can Make:
Staying the same just so other people can feel comfortable around you.

If you start editing your ambition or shrinking your confidence to keep the peace, you aren’t being humble.

You’re being fearful.

And fear will keep you trapped in "present conditions" forever.

The Blueprint:

1.	Accept the pressure. It’s not breaking you; it’s making you.

2.	Stop explaining. You don't owe anyone a map to a destination they aren't traveling to.

3.	Audit your circle. If someone only respected you when you were struggling, they don't deserve access when you’re shining.

Not everyone is built to witness someone become extraordinary without taking it personally.

Let them judge the coal.

Just make sure you keep building the diamond.

Less random broadcasting. 
More planned, higher-quality content.

A 'prospect' = someone in your ICP (right role, company, seniority)

The implication: LinkedIn is turning the feed into a prospecting surface (not just a publishing one).

3) LinkedIn is formalising creator monetisation

LinkedIn has introduced new ways for brands to partner with creators - including Premium Creator Sponsorships with Top Voices 360. They are expanding its creator / expert programmes (adding more ways for brands to partner with them directly).

This makes it easier for brands to:
 – sponsor trusted experts
 – run campaigns through individual voices
 – reach audiences through credibility (not just ads)

The implication: Creators aren’t just posting. They are becoming a paid distribution layer.

A common thread:
LinkedIn isn’t just a content platform anymore. It is becoming a pipeline engine.

The new B&Q ads are obviously fantastic

Zoe Davies's team sifted through thousands of paint names to create "Swatch Stories". This is one of those ideas that makes you jealous, it's that good.

And it hits what I reckon effectiveness needs to be...

I spent a few years working with JCDecaux and System1 analysing thousands of campaigns against their in-market impact with Beth, Chris, Chiara & Nick.

We got to a pretty simple playbook for posters that work, all underpinned by the simple fact that outdoor usually gets about 2sec of attention (Lumen Research)

1. Use 1-2 of your strongest distinctive brand assets and ensure they get attention. When people get the brand quickly, they process it and ad recall doubles.

2. Put on a show to create an emotional response. Ads that use showmanship (simple stories, characters, wordplay, etc) to create a stronger emotional response see 2x the commercial uplift (like, store visits).

This nails both. Big bold branding. Simple enough for 2sec attention. But with a clever creative with a bit of a story and wordplay. Just enough to reward those that pay enough attention.

Congrats to the Leo UK and B&Q teams on this, I've put it into System1 consumer creative testing. Expecting very good things.

content:
If I was a founder with no budget trying to grow my business (again), here's what I'd do:

1. Spend zero on paid ads until you've exhausted LinkedIn. Organic reach is free. Your founder story, your insights, your mistakes - that's content. Post 3-5x a week before you spend a penny on ads.

2. Start finding advisors alongside hiring employees. They’ll bring experience and guidance you can’t afford full time. Those conversations will save you from expensive mistakes you'd make alone. Find people who've done what you're trying to do. Ask specific questions. Do it before you're desperate.

3. You don't need a full-time CFO when you're pre-revenue. Get someone who's done it 10 times before to spend 1-2 days a week getting your finances right. Senior expertise at a fraction of the cost.

4. Track three metrics obsessively, ignore the rest. Pick the numbers that actually matter right now. Revenue, churn, CAC - whatever moves the needle. Solve for them obsessively. Everything else is noise.

5. Build relationships before you need them. Don't wait until you're fundraising to start talking to investors. The founders who move fast have been building those relationships for months.

6. Get comfortable being uncomfortable. If you're not slightly terrified by what you're building, you're playing it too safe.

Most early-stage failure comes from trying to do too much with too little.

Focus. Find the right people early. Move fast on what matters.

content:
Things have changed: I do work hard and I do care about making money 👋 👀💸

If you’ve been following me for awhile, you’ll know that I’ve spoken before about how I don’t hustle, I don’t work hard and I don’t care about making six figures. 

And while some of that is still true, in the sense that I don’t care…

I’m in an era of my life where I am hustling, I am working hard, and I do care about creating financial freedom. All while trying to be present with my son as a new mum. 

But after speaking with Abi Bellion-Carey, I realised that how I’m showing up on LinkedIn has created this perception that I’ve got it all figured out. 

Trust me I don’t, and it’s not a perfect system: 

→ I’m taking calls in the car while he cries in the background (Sophie Miller knows)  
→ I’m going to baby groups while scheduling content on my phone 
→ I’m negotiating deals while playing peek-a-boo 

And every day looks completely different. Sometimes I’ve managed to clean the entire house, take three calls create content and earn a new client. Other weeks we’re just in survival mode, we lose a brand deal and the house is a mess. 

The reality is being a working mum, and being a business owner, is HARD. 

And the world isn’t built for working mums, especially the ones who don’t have the freedom that I do. 

They’re often primary caregivers they’re the ones that are picking up their child three times a week from nursery because they’re poorly. They’re the ones taking on the mental workload, the house workload, the family admin and having to sacrifice their careers to raise their little ones. 

We need to be creating a system that helps women in their career and doesn’t set them back a decade when they have a child. And to be honest? I don’t know what that looks like.

But if there aren’t any new mums or soon-to-be-mums that want a chat, my DMs are always open 🩷 

As Sedge Beswick said, ambition doesn’t die in the delivery room. And there’s nothing wrong with wanting to raise a family AND have a career.

I just read in Business Insider that the most successful adopters of AI are people with ADHD, and I’ve never felt more validated.

It’s interesting/ and it makes sense.

What people with ADHD often struggle with…

- Quick recall of very specific things
- Executing as fast as they think 
- Also: executing before losing the dopamine hit

What LLMs are designed to be good at:
- Maintaining a strong working memory
- Processing speed-dependent tasks

AI can literally help fill the gap for neurodiverse people. I am noticing this already. I started testing things like Claude Cowork on the weekends. It’s allowing me to turn things around from initial idea → specific brief → solid output much, much faster. Early days, but I’m a fan.

Goes without saying… AI shouldn’t be used to try and replace yourself as the CEO, or to outsource creative ideas. It’s not coming for the c-suite yet. 

But for any of us who have to take in a lot of information and know they could be doing more but struggle to have enough hours in the day, it can help us move faster and with more precision.

Good to see.

content:
Micromanagement is just fear in disguise.

When I first started leading, I screwed this up too.

I tracked everything. I hovered. I suffocated the work.

Not because I was a tyrant.

Because I was terrified.

I was scared things would break.

I was scared no one else would care as much as I did.

Here is the hard truth I had to swallow:

Control kills culture.

When you manage every single move, you aren't building high performers.

You are building robots.

You are training brilliant people to wait for permission instead of taking action.

The moment I stepped back and actually trusted the team?

Everything changed.

They stopped asking for permission.

They started finding solutions.
They acted like owners because they were finally treated like owners.

Trust is not soft. Trust is strategic.

It doesn't mean you stop caring.

It means you become crystal clear on the destination, and let your team figure out the best way to drive there.

If you hired top talent, stop treating them like toddlers.

• Stop counting the hours. Measure the output.

• Stop tracking the green dots. Track the results.

• Stop building a factory when you should be building an empire.

Culture is built on trust, not surveillance.

And if your team doesn't trust you, your numbers don't matter anyway.

Give them the outcome. Let them own the execution.

Credit: Neha K Puri

The best ad I've seen this week

A brilliant emotional journey

After being bored senseless by the incredible waste of time and effort poured into April Fools ads yesterday (apart from you KitKat, go you. Although I'm still not sure if that was real...), it's damn refreshing to see a giant of a brand bringing back a 65-year-old brand character.

The Dulux dog.

System1 tests every UK and US TV ad with millions of consumers to predict their impact. This is one of the highest-scoring ads put on TV. Since testing began. 5.9 Stars for emotional response. Here's what it gets right. 

1. Big storytelling. What Orlando Wood calls Showmanship. Story, character, melody, drama, tension. He's shown these things draw and hold attention, crucially from those not already interested in your brand. Crucial for brand growth.

2. Compound Creativity. As sarah carter, Les Binet and I shared at Cannes Lions last year: consistency, commitment and creativity win together. Dulux has largely kept the same brand assets, platform, and dog for 65 years now.

3. Babies, dogs and brand characters. It's becoming a rather undeniable fact, after internal research leaked decades ago from a big FMCG business, that babies and dogs boost an ad's performance. Equally, brand characters are consistently the highest performing type of asset in research. No wonder an idea with a baby dog brand character wins.

This is the type of creativity that, put on a big media stage (TV), grows brands. Love it, Ogilvy UK / Dulux.

content:
THE SURPRISING POWER OF CONFLICTING GOALS

Rory Sutherland and I had the honour of being invited to ride in the controversial new Jaguar around their test track in Gaydon and sit down with their Managing Director Rawdon Glover to discuss how they designed such an astonishing car

What I experienced on the day was very impressive. Incredible acceleration, beautiful handling, limo like ride comfort and if I had wanted it then a 400 mile range. All from a car that looks like a futuristic sports car.

One thought has stuck with me ever since

The power of conflicting goals.

I first heard about this idea when interviewing Will Guidara the owner of the World's No.1 Michelin restaurant who set out to deliver world-class food AND service, something that was considered in conflict. By embracing the constraint it forced a level of innovation that allowed the team to achieve No.1 status.

I felt the same talking to Rawdon about the new Jaguar GT

How have they made a car with the performance of a supercar but the ride quality of a classic XJ

In fact when I spoke to Joan Serra Tur who has worked on the car for 5 years he talked me through so many engineering challenges that the team had to overcome to maintain the integrity of the design. Everything from the unique platform, to the low ride, to the crash protection, to the aerodynamics has required innovation.

In the latest episode of Uncensored CMO Rory and I talk to Rawdon about how they achieved so many conflicting goals with the new Jaguar GT and their plans to launch the car to the public later this year

content:
Maybe the BEST prompt for people with ADHD.

Copy and paste this into Claude Cowork:

“Act as my high-performance thought partner, operator, and execution coach.

Context about me:

• I am an ADHD founder.
• I think fast, zoom out naturally, and generate a lot of ideas quickly.
• I can also get overwhelmed by too many options, overly long answers, vagueness, or advice that is not practical.
• I need help turning chaos into clarity, priorities, decisions, and action.
• I respond best to sharp thinking, structure, blunt honesty, and momentum.
• Do not treat me like I am fragile or incapable.
• Treat me like a very capable founder who needs help with focus, sequencing, and reducing cognitive drag.

How I want you to respond:

• Start with the clearest answer first.
• Be concise but high value.
• Prioritise practical output over generic explanation.
• Break things into small, clear steps.
• Reduce unnecessary choices.
• When there are many possible directions, recommend one best path first.
• Highlight what actually matters vs what is noise.
• Help me avoid overcomplicating things.
• If my thinking is scattered, organise it for me.
• If I am procrastinating, help me find the smallest useful next step.
• If I am being unrealistic, say so clearly.
• If I am avoiding the real issue, point it out.

If I give you a messy brain dump, convert it into:
  1) what I am actually trying to do
  2) what matters most
  3) what to do next
• If I ask for strategy, give me the strategic view and then the execution plan.
• If I ask for writing help, make it sharper, clearer, and more compelling.
• If I ask for prioritisation, force-rank things.
• If I ask for planning, create a plan that is ambitious but realistic.
• If I seem overloaded, simplify aggressively.

Formatting rules:
• Do not give me huge walls of text.
• Use headings and bullets when useful.
• Summarise where possible.
• End with a clear recommendation, decision, or next action.
•Where relevant, use this format:
   - The real issue
   - What matters most
   - What to do now
   - What can wait

Behaviour rules:
• Do not be passive.
• Do not just mirror my thoughts back to me.
• Do not give me five equal options unless I ask for them.
• Do not hide the best recommendation.
• Do not over-explain obvious things.
• Do not give me corporate fluff.
• Challenge me when needed.
• Help me maintain momentum.

Your job:
Help me think clearly, decide faster, communicate better, and execute consistently as an ADHD founder operating at a high level.”

Game changer.

content:
Societal timelines are a trap.

We look at a 22-year-old founder on a magazine cover and convince ourselves we are failing.

That is a lie.

You are not late.

You are just building a foundation that won't crack.

Look at the real blueprint:

Lost at 22. (Normal)

Broke at 28. (Experience)

Unsure at 31. (Recalibrating)

Starting over at 35. (Audacity)

Then...

The rise at 38.

The purpose at 42.

Unstoppable at 47.

Most people aren't afraid of the time it takes.

They are afraid of the judgment of others while they are cooking.

They want the microwave success.

But microwave success has no flavor and doesn't last.

If you are 30, 40, or 50 and still figuring it out, good.

The lessons you are learning right now are the bricks you'll use to build your empire later.

You are not behind.

You are just in the messy, unsexy part of the process.

Greatness is never rushed.

It is forged.

Keep cooking.

content:
Marketing table of the month goes to...Nico Neumann

When you line up very different approaches across 20 years (single-source analysis, meta-analyses, MMM work, and cross-campaign case analysis), one conclusion keeps showing up: creative quality massively matters.

It should be a large part of every marketer’s job.

The numbers wobble across methods. No study is perfect. But that doesn’t make them useless, as I wrote in my column yesterday: https://lnkd.in/eeW_JT_r

This is what makes Nico’s table so brilliant. It helps us look beyond a single model and see what keeps showing up across different methods and contexts.

One slightly awkward thing for me: the System1/Effie row is actually one of the more conservative ones in the table.

In The Creative Dividend, we matched 1,200 Effie cases to System1 creative measurement from 180,000 respondents and found that the creative-quality component explained between 19.4% and 68.0% of reported campaign Business Results, depending on category. A perhaps useful additional finding.

Not every business result.
Not total business performance.
But reported campaign Business Results within that dataset.

What explains the rest? All the other things that matter across the marketing mix.

Why I love this comparison. No single study is the answer. Things get clearer and clearer as different approaches keep pointing in the same direction.

Appreciate Marketing Science Today pulling this together. Very useful to see different data agreeing in different ways.

I agree with Nico: be clear on research scope, compare across studies, use benchmarks as starting points, and then test on your own brands. Aka the day job.

There are 100+ other charts and findings in The Creative Dividend beyond this model in Chapter 7, designed as a practical guide to creative effectiveness.
